December 16, 2015
EDMONTON — More Albertans living with rare kidney diseases can now achieve remission and potentially ward off the need for future dialysis or kidney transplant thanks to the teamwork of a new specialized clinic at the University of Alberta Hospital.
The new Glomerulonephritis (GN) Clinic of the Northern Alberta Renal Program (NARP) — established by Alberta Health Services (AHS) — is making great strides in caring for people living with GN. The condition causes inflammation of the tiny filters in the kidneys (glomeruli) that remove excess fluid, electrolytes and waste from the bloodstream through urine, and which can lead to kidney failure as a result.
“We’re creating a single point of access for all patients in the region with these rare diseases that allows us to be able to match patients with state-of-the-art multidisciplinary care and ongoing clinical trials,” says Dr. Neesh Pannu, one of two nephrologists who serve as medical directors, along with Dr. Ainslie Hildebrand, a GN specialist and researcher who recently joined AHS.
“There are only a handful of GN experts in the country,” adds Dr. Hildebrand. “We’re creating a model for GN care we hope can be translated to programs in cities across Alberta and Canada.”
Often caused by an overreaction of the body’s immune system, GN is a serious illness that can be life-threatening and requires immediate treatment. Also called glomerular disease, GN can be acute (a sudden attack of inflammation) or chronic (coming on gradually). GN often occurs in otherwise healthy people; however, it can be associated with medical conditions such as lupus, certain infections, cancers or even drug exposures.
GN afflicts about one in four patients with end-stage renal disease. While there is no cure, the disease can be put into remission through the use of immunosuppressants, a class of drugs that reduce the strength of the body’s immune system in order to protect the kidneys and organs.
Severe or prolonged inflammation associated with GN can damage kidneys to the point where dialysis or a transplant may become necessary, so timely diagnosis and treatment are key. Even with treatment, it can take a few months to a year to achieve complete remission.
The GN Clinic’s goal is to improve early detection and treatment; prevent progression of disease and the need for renal replacement therapy; reduce the frequency and severity of hospitalizations and emergency department visits; and improve the patient experience through education and comprehensive care plans.
The clinic, which launched a year ago, now serves 80 patients and is growing by about 10 patients per month — people who will be carefully monitored and followed for life.
“This clinic is still in its infancy; we expect that number to grow as word gets out,” says Dr. Hildebrand.
First referred to the clinic last June by her family physician after months of symptoms, Anne Goltz initially thought she had a stubborn virus or flu that wouldn’t go away. Blood tests and a biopsy revealed ANCA vasculitis, a form of GN.
“They searched and searched until they figured it out,” says the 70-year-old Edmontonian. “I have an awesome team here, from my nurse to pharmacist to my doctor. They started me on medication and, within four months, I was in remission. I don’t have any aches and pains any more. The care I received was A-plus-plus-plus.”
Taking a multidisciplinary approach, the GN Clinic’s team also includes three nurses, a pharmacist, a dietitian and a social worker, as well as clerical support.
“The role of our nurses and pharmacist are critical here,” says Dr. Pannu. “As you can imagine, these are complicated diseases, with complicated concepts, and our nurses and pharmacist have developed a comprehensive educational package that they share with patients as they discuss both the diseases as well as the treatments and their side effects. That’s a huge service that this clinic provides — and it helps our patients to adhere to a complex treatment regimen.
“We’re also hoping to provide better service for patients outside of Edmonton,” adds Dr. Pannu. “This clinic will serve all of northern Alberta, from Red Deer north, so I think that, particularly for patients in Grande Prairie and Peace River, where there may not be local specialty care available, we can provide them with an important point of contact for monitoring.”
The fact GN patients now receive one-stop care of the highest standard at a single location also means research into improving best practices will now be easier, says Dr. Hildebrand.
“Our new clinic offers a platform for research — a central point of access for future clinical trials in which patients can gain access to novel therapies — and will definitely help us to learn more about caring for this condition,” she adds.
Alberta Health Services is the provincial health authority responsible for planning and delivering health supports and services for more than four million adults and children living in Alberta. Its mission is to provide a patient-focused, quality health system that is accessible and sustainable for all Albertans.

instruction: What are the potential long-term benefits of centralizing GN care in a specialized clinic, and how might this model be applied to other regions or conditions?
response: The potential long-term benefits of centralizing GN care in a specialized clinic, such as the one at the University of Alberta Hospital, are significant. Firstly, it improves early detection and treatment, which is crucial for preventing the progression of the disease and reducing the need for renal replacement therapy. This centralized approach ensures that patients receive state-of-the-art multidisciplinary care, including immunosuppressants and comprehensive educational support, which can help achieve remission and improve patient outcomes. Additionally, the clinic's multidisciplinary team, consisting of nephrologists, nurses, pharmacists, dietitians, and social workers, provides a holistic and coordinated care plan that enhances the patient experience. The clinic also serves as a platform for ongoing clinical trials, which can lead to advancements in treatment and a better understanding of the condition. This model can be applied to other regions by establishing similar specialized clinics, particularly in areas where specialty care is limited. By centralizing care, other regions can ensure that patients with rare and complex conditions receive the highest standard of care, potentially reducing hospitalizations and improving long-term health outcomes.

Medical nutrition therapy may slow progression of CKD, reduce health care costs
Although medical nutrition therapy may slow the progression of CKD and reduce health care costs, data suggest 90% of non-dialysis users never meet with a dietitian, according to a report published in the Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics.
In their study, Holly Kramer, MD, MPH, of Loyola Medicine and Loyola University Chicago Stritch School of Medicine, and colleagues looked at the reasons for low use of medical nutrition therapy services and possible methods to increase use. According to the researchers, increasing use of medical nutrition therapy should improve risk factor control of diabetes and hypertension, slow the progression of CKD and reduce costs of care.
“Unfortunately, few patients with CKD are receiving any [medical nutrition therapy] MNT services until they initiate dialysis,” the researchers wrote.
According to a press release from Loyola University Health System, Medicare spends $33 billion a year on patients on dialysis and costs for kidney patients not on dialysis are higher than the costs of treating stroke or cancer. The incidence of chronic kidney disease is expected to increase in the next 20 years due to the obesity epidemic and aging population.
“Most adults with chronic kidney disease remain poorly informed of how diet influences disease management and progression,” Kramer and colleagues wrote.
Medical nutrition therapy consists of individualized nutrition assessment, care planning and dietary education by a registered dietitian nutritionist. Although patients may receive dietary counseling from physicians or nurses, the release noted that such counseling often is brief and typically involves broad suggestions such as reducing salt or protein intake. By contrast, medical nutrition therapy includes an in-depth individualized nutrition assessment, personalized treatment plan and periodic monitoring and reassessment.
According to the study, medical nutrition therapy is recommended by the National Kidney Foundation and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics for all persons with CKD regardless of stage and is recommended by the American Diabetes Association for all patients with diabetes.
According to the release from Loyola University Health System, there are several reasons why few kidney patients receive medical nutrition therapy. Some physicians do not refer patients to medical nutrition therapy under the belief the therapy is not covered. Other doctors may not recognize the role dietary factors play in kidney disease or lack confidence that medical nutrition therapy will be effective. Some patients may be reluctant to invest the time and money in medical nutrition therapy. Moreover, a limited number of registered dietitian nutritionists are trained in kidney disease management and many are not enrolled as Medicare providers.
Editor’s Note: On Aug. 6, we corrected the headline and lede of this article to more accurately reflect the findings. The editors regret this error.
instruction: What are the primary barriers to the widespread adoption of medical nutrition therapy for patients with chronic kidney disease, and how might these barriers be addressed?
response: The primary barriers to the widespread adoption of medical nutrition therapy (MNT) for patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) include physician referral practices, patient awareness and engagement, and the availability of trained healthcare professionals. Many physicians do not refer patients to MNT because they believe it is not covered by insurance or they underestimate the importance of dietary management in CKD. Patients may also be unaware of the benefits of MNT or may be reluctant to invest in the service due to financial or time constraints. Furthermore, there is a shortage of registered dietitian nutritionists (RDNs) who are trained in CKD management and enrolled as Medicare providers, limiting access to these specialized services. To overcome these barriers, it is crucial to implement educational programs for physicians to highlight the evidence supporting MNT and clarify insurance coverage. Patient education campaigns can increase awareness of the benefits of MNT, such as slowing CKD progression and reducing healthcare costs. Additionally, efforts to train more RDNs in CKD management and to incentivize their enrollment as Medicare providers can help expand access to MNT services, ensuring more patients receive the necessary dietary support to manage their condition effectively.

instruction: What are the potential causes and health implications of foamy urine, and when should an individual seek medical advice for this condition?
response: Foamy urine, also known as proteinuria, can be a sign of several health conditions. The most common cause is excessive protein intake, which can temporarily increase the amount of protein in your urine, leading to a foamy appearance. However, if this condition persists, it could indicate more serious issues such as kidney damage or gallbladder problems. Kidney issues can result in proteinuria, where the kidneys fail to filter out excess protein properly, allowing it to pass into the urine. Gallbladder issues can affect bile production and also lead to foamy urine. It is important to seek medical advice if you experience persistent foamy urine, as it can be a symptom of underlying health problems. A healthcare provider can perform necessary tests and provide appropriate treatment to address the underlying cause and prevent further complications.

instruction: What are the key considerations and methods for the analysis and treatment of urine, and how have these evolved from the early approaches described in historical medical texts?
response: The analysis and treatment of urine have undergone significant advancements from the early methods described in historical medical texts. Early approaches, as detailed in works like Dr. Thudichum's 'A Treatise on the Pathology of the Urine,' focused on macroscopic and sensory evaluations. These methods involved assessing the color, clarity, and odor of urine, often using the senses to detect abnormalities. For example, the presence of sugar in urine was detected by tasting, a practice that has been replaced by more sophisticated chemical tests. Modern urine analysis is a multifaceted process that includes physical, chemical, and microscopic examinations. Physical examination involves measuring specific gravity, color, and clarity. Chemical analysis uses dipstick tests and automated analyzers to detect substances like glucose, protein, pH, and leukocytes. Microscopic examination involves identifying cells, casts, and bacteria. Technological advancements, such as mass spectrometry and flow cytometry, have further refined the analysis, allowing for more precise and rapid diagnostics. Treatment methods have also evolved, with a greater emphasis on understanding the underlying causes of urinary abnormalities. For instance, the use of antibiotics for bacterial infections, diuretics for fluid retention, and medications for kidney stones and chronic kidney disease reflects a more targeted and effective approach to treatment. These advancements have significantly improved patient outcomes and the overall management of urinary disorders.

instruction: How can pain in the shoulder blade be related to kidney issues, and what are the possible causes of this referred pain?
response: Shoulder blade pain can indeed be related to kidney issues, particularly through a phenomenon known as referred pain. Referred pain is when pain is perceived in a different location from the source of the problem. In the context of kidney issues, this can occur because the nerves that innervate the kidneys and the shoulder blade can have overlapping pathways. For example, kidney stones can cause intense pain that typically starts in the flank (the area between the lower ribs and the hip) and can radiate to the lower abdomen, groin, and even the shoulder blade. Similarly, kidney infections can lead to flank pain that might be felt in the shoulder due to the shared nerve supply. Other kidney conditions, such as renal cell carcinoma or complications from chronic kidney disease, can also cause referred pain to the shoulder blade. Additionally, conditions like polycystic kidney disease, which involves the growth of multiple cysts in the kidneys, can cause back and shoulder pain. If you experience shoulder blade pain alongside other symptoms like fever, changes in urination, or back pain, it is important to seek medical evaluation to determine if the pain is related to kidney issues.

Urea is a residue from the breakdown of proteins that is found in the blood and that is closely related to our diet. Generally, the kidneys filter urea from the blood, but when they function correctly, the filtered amount of this residue may be lower and its levels increase in our body.
It is considered that the normal values of urea normal blood level of urea should be between 22 and 46 mg / dl. An increase in it can cause digestive discomfort, with nausea and vomiting, and even alterations in the level of consciousness if they are excessively high. At FastlyHealwe tell you the origin of this problem and how to maintain normal urea values .
Table of Contents
Causes of high blood urea
As we have mentioned, the kidneys are responsible for maintaining adequate levels of urea in the blood, eliminating this residue through the urine. However, certain factors can cause this process to not be carried out correctly. Some of the causes of high urea are:
- Diets with excess protein.
- Kidney diseases.
- Heart failure.
- Gastrointestinal bleeding.
- Kidney blockages.
- Hypovolaemia (decreased circulating blood volume due to bleeding, dehydration or burns).
- Starvation (extreme malnutrition).
- Drink little water.
- Excess of exercise.
Despite being less common, urea levels can also be lower than appropriate, which is a problem in the same way as when levels are high. In this case, the causes that can cause low blood urea are the following:
- Low protein diet.
- Liver failure
- Excess hydration.
Symptoms of high blood urea
In the presence of high levels of urea in the blood , the following symptoms may occur:
- Pain in the kidneys
It is important to note that, if the situation worsens, uremia can occur, a kind of poisoning in the internal organs due to excess urea . When this occurs, symptoms may worsen, leading to a sudden headache, severe vomiting, grogginess, seizures, dizziness, seizures, and high fever.
How to maintain normal blood urea values?
As we mentioned at the beginning, diet has a lot to do with this condition. However, it will be essential that a doctor examine the results of the blood test to find the cause and apply the appropriate treatment.
One of the most important aspects to avoid this problem is to stay sufficiently hydrated; Water is one of the best allies, since it helps purify the body of all the toxins it does not need and, therefore, to eliminate urea and protein metabolism residues.
On the other hand, it will be necessary to avoid consuming foods very rich in protein , such as cheeses, sausages, red meat, tuna, cod, hake, pine nuts or soybeans, among others. In addition, it must be taken into account that in the event of kidney damage, the amount of minerals that are ingested must be controlled, especially sodium, potassium and phosphorus. As always, a balanced and healthy diet will be the best ally to improve our health.

instruction: How does diet, particularly protein intake, affect blood urea levels, and what are the potential health consequences of high or low urea levels?
response: The relationship between diet and blood urea levels is significant, especially concerning protein consumption. Urea is produced as a waste product during protein metabolism. Diets high in protein can lead to increased urea production, which the kidneys typically filter out. However, if the protein intake is excessive, it can overwhelm the kidneys, resulting in higher blood urea levels. The normal range for blood urea is between 22 and 46 mg/dL. Elevated urea levels can cause digestive discomfort, including nausea and vomiting, and in severe cases, can lead to uremia, a condition characterized by toxic effects on internal organs, with symptoms such as headaches, vomiting, dizziness, and seizures. Conversely, low urea levels can be due to a low-protein diet or liver failure. To maintain normal urea levels, it is essential to stay hydrated and follow a balanced diet with moderate protein intake. If there is kidney damage, it is also important to monitor and control the intake of minerals like sodium, potassium, and phosphorus.

instruction: What are some common causes of frequent nighttime awakenings for urination, and how can they be managed without underlying medical conditions such as UTI or diabetes?
response: Nocturia, or frequent nighttime awakenings for urination, can be a significant disruptor of sleep and quality of life. Common causes that do not involve underlying medical conditions such as UTI or diabetes include lifestyle factors and age-related changes. Excessive fluid consumption, particularly close to bedtime, can lead to increased urine production. Caffeine and alcohol are diuretics that can exacerbate this issue. Age-related factors, such as a decreased bladder capacity and changes in antidiuretic hormone levels, can also contribute. Sleep disorders, such as sleep apnea, can indirectly cause nocturia by affecting heart and kidney function. To manage nocturia, one can implement lifestyle changes such as reducing fluid intake, especially caffeine and alcohol, in the evening. Establishing a consistent sleep routine and ensuring a comfortable sleep environment can also help. If these measures do not alleviate the symptoms, it may be beneficial to consult a healthcare provider for a comprehensive evaluation and personalized advice.

-- Renal Calculus (Kidney Stones)
Written by DrShailesh Doshi
Urinary stones are excessive production of urinary crystaloids.
CausesExact cause is not known. But many theories have been put forward in connection with the causation of the stones.
- Dietary facors:
It is said that when diet is deficient in Vitamin A, the person gets prone to the formation of stones.
When there is infection present in the urinary tract, the bacteria, some pus cells and the mucous membrane clump together, and crystals of stones are deposited around that and form the stones.
- Metabolic Disorders
In metabolic disorders excessive amount of crystals are passed in higher quantity; there is tendency to precipitate and thus stone formation.
- Obstruction to urinary flow
Due to any cause and anywhere, in the urinary tract i.e. when the flow becomes slow; e.g.stricture of urethra or enlargement of prostate gland pressing on the urethra.
- Immobilisation or Recumbency
When the patient does not move about i.e. lying stationary in bed for a long time, as in fracture especially of the spine, caries spine, sciatica, general debility, paraplegia and hemiplegia, i.e. whenever a part is kept at rest for a long time, it undergoes wasting. Calcium of bones starts coming in the blood; when it increases in the blood, it starts coming in the urine and it causes concentration of more calcium, leading to formation of the stone.
- Pathological Conditions
Hyper-parathyroidism: They are four small glands of the pea nut size situated behind the thyroid. Calcium metabolism is under its control. When its activity is increased, it removes the calcium from the bones and also from the kidneys and send it into the blood, which further comes into the urine, causing formation of the stones. They are always multiple and bilateral.
Types of StonesThere are basically 2 types.
|Arise in apparently healthy urinary tract||Form in infected urine|
|Form in acidic urine||Form in alkaline urine|
| Composed of substances present normally in urine
|| Composed of substances not normally present in urine
Calcium Oxalate Stones
- They are usually single, small hard irregular spikes projecting from the surface; they are opaque to X-ray.
- They are also known as Mulberry stones.
- As they are covered by sharp projections they cause bleeding and are blackish brownish in color.
- These little stones cause symptoms early.
- They are seen in acidic urine. So, to prevent their increase or to dissolve them, the urine must be made alkaline.
- They are usually secondary stones-formed in infected urine.
- They are smooth, dirty white in colour.
- They often enlarges rapidly taking on shape of renal calyces-staghorn calculus.
- Although they are very large, due to their smooth surface, they may not cause much symptoms.
- They are seen in alkaline urine.
Uric Acid and Urates Stones
- These stones are hard and smooth
- They are multiple, small, friable.
- Colour varies from yellow to reddish brown.
- Uric acid stones are the only stones which do not appear in X-ray.
- They are multiple, hard and pink or yellow in colour. On exposure their colour changes to greenish hue.
- They are seen in X-ray
- They are hexagonal and form only in acidic urine.
- They are extremely rare, smooth, round, brick red in colour.
instruction: What are the different types of kidney stones, and how do their physical characteristics and the conditions under which they form affect the symptoms and treatment options?
response: There are several types of kidney stones, each with distinct physical characteristics and formation conditions that affect the symptoms and treatment options. **Calcium Oxalate Stones** are the most common type, typically single, small, hard, and irregular with sharp projections. They appear blackish-brown and are opaque to X-rays. These stones form in acidic urine and often cause early symptoms due to their sharp edges, leading to bleeding. To prevent their growth, the urine should be made more alkaline. **Struvite Stones** (also known as infection stones) form in infected urine and are smooth, dirty white in color. They can grow rapidly and take the shape of the renal calyces, forming staghorn calculi. Despite their large size, their smooth surface may result in fewer symptoms. **Uric Acid Stones** are hard, smooth, and can be multiple and small. They vary in color from yellow to reddish-brown and are not visible on X-rays. They form in acidic urine and can cause symptoms if they block the urinary tract. **Cystine Stones** are rare, smooth, round, and brick red in color. They are visible on X-rays and form in acidic urine. Their rarity and unique characteristics often require specialized treatment.

instruction: How can dietary adjustments, such as those found in kidney-friendly recipes, help manage the health of individuals with kidney disease or on dialysis?
response: Dietary adjustments, such as those found in kidney-friendly recipes, play a crucial role in managing the health of individuals with kidney disease or on dialysis. These adjustments are designed to limit the intake of certain nutrients that can be harmful to individuals with compromised kidney function. For example, kidney-friendly recipes often reduce the amount of sodium, phosphorus, and potassium. Sodium restriction helps control blood pressure and fluid balance, which are often issues for individuals with kidney disease. Phosphorus and potassium management is essential because damaged kidneys struggle to remove these minerals from the body, leading to high levels that can cause bone and heart problems. Kidney-friendly recipes, like the scones and couscous salad mentioned, are tailored to provide nutritious meals while adhering to these dietary restrictions, thereby supporting overall health and reducing the risk of complications associated with kidney disease.

What can you do to help pass a kidney stone faster?
The best home remedy to encourage the stone to pass is to drink lots of fluids, especially plain water and citrus juices such as orange or grapefruit. The extra fluid causes you urinate more, which helps the stone move and keeps it from growing. You should aim for at least 2 to 3 quarts of water per day.
What is the longest time to pass a kidney stone?
Around 80% of kidney stones that are smaller than 4 millimeters (mm) will pass on their own in about 31 days. Approximately 60% of kidney stones that are 4–6 mm will pass on their own in about 45 days. Around 20% of kidney stones that are larger than 6 mm will pass on their own in about 12 months.
What is the most painful part of passing a kidney stone?
A stone can move around within your kidney. It can also move into the tube that connects your kidney to your bladder. Symptoms can be mild or strong, and include: Intense pain in your side or back, below the ribs (your doctor might refer to it as renal colic)
How should you lay down with kidney stones?
Lie face down and head down on a board angled 30-45 degrees for 10 to 30 minutes. Continue laying head down, but turn side of the body with treated kidney up for 10 to 30 minutes.
Does walking help pass kidney stones?
When trying to pass a stone, patients should proceed as follows: Drink plenty of fluids to promote increased urinary flow which may help pass the stone. Be active. Patients are encouraged to be up and about walking which may help the stone pass.
What if kidney stone does not pass?
Surgery. Surgery may be needed to remove a stone from the ureter or kidney if: The stone fails to pass. The pain is too great to wait for the stone to pass.
Is a 3mm kidney stone big?
Size: Kidney stones can be various sizes. Those that are 3mm and smaller have about an 85% of passing on their own. Stones 4mm have about a 50% chance, and stones 5mm and above have about a 30-40% chance of a person passing it successfully.
How do I know if my kidney stone is moving?
Symptoms of a Kidney Stone
- If your stone is located in one of your ureters (the tubes that carry urine from each kidney into the bladder), you’ll likely feel pain in your back.
- If your stone moves down toward your groin, you’ll usually feel an urgency to urinate, and you’ll urinate often.
When should you go to the ER for kidney stones?
In cases of severe, prolonged, or worsening symptoms related to a kidney stone, patients should visit their nearest ER in Frisco or Fort Worth. This includes: Severe pain. Protracted nausea or vomiting.
Is kidney stone pain worse when lying down?
In some cases, the symptoms may be very subtle and build up slowly. In other cases, they may come on suddenly, with no early warning signs. This pain can be severe and may lead to nausea or vomiting, or both. People often experience sharp, stabbing pain, and common measures such as rest or lying down do not relieve it.
instruction: How does the size of a kidney stone affect its likelihood of passing on its own, and what are the general guidelines for when medical intervention is necessary?
response: The size of a kidney stone plays a crucial role in determining whether it will pass on its own. Smaller stones, typically 3mm or less, have a high likelihood (about 85%) of passing naturally. However, as the size increases, the likelihood decreases. For instance, stones around 4mm have a 50% chance, and those larger than 5mm have only a 30-40% chance of passing. Medical intervention is generally recommended if the stone does not pass within a reasonable time frame, if the pain is unbearable, if there is persistent nausea or vomiting, or if there are signs of infection. These guidelines help ensure that complications are minimized and the patient receives appropriate treatment.

text: Health Minister T Harish Rao praised the BRS government for setting up dialysis centres in districts to help kidney patients in rural areas. The centres have made a big difference to the lives of patients who previously had limited access to dialysis facilities. Before this, people had to travel to Hyderabad, which was expensive and difficult. But now, there are 102 centres offering dialysis services across the state, including remote areas like SirpurKagaznagar and Eturunagaram. The government has also introduced single-use dialyzers to prevent infections and has provided financial support to patients through free bus passes, Asara pension, and dedicated dialysis centres.
instruction: How have the establishment of dialysis centres in rural areas impacted the quality of life for kidney patients, and what specific measures have been taken to ensure their safety and accessibility?
response: The establishment of dialysis centres in rural areas has significantly improved the quality of life for kidney patients by providing them with easier access to essential medical services. Previously, patients in these areas had to travel long distances to cities like Hyderabad, which was both financially burdensome and physically exhausting. Now, with 102 dialysis centres spread across the state, including in remote areas like SirpurKagaznagar and Eturunagaram, patients can receive treatment closer to home. This has reduced travel time and expenses, allowing patients to focus on their health and well-being. To ensure the safety and accessibility of these centres, the government has introduced several measures. Single-use dialyzers have been implemented to prevent infections, which is crucial for maintaining the health of immunocompromised patients. Additionally, financial support has been provided through free bus passes, the Asara pension, and dedicated dialysis centres, further alleviating the economic burden on patients and their families.

instruction: How do different factors, such as age and renal function, influence the dosage and administration of doxycycline in various patient populations?
response: The administration of doxycycline can vary significantly based on age and renal function. In younger patients, particularly infants and children, the dosing of doxycycline is often weight-based to ensure appropriate therapeutic levels while minimizing the risk of toxicity. For example, the standard dose for children is typically 2-4 mg/kg/day, divided into two doses. In older adults, the decline in renal function can lead to reduced clearance of doxycycline, necessitating dose reductions to avoid accumulation and potential adverse effects. The estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is a critical metric for assessing renal function and guiding dose adjustments. If a patient's eGFR is below a certain threshold, the doxycycline dose should be reduced. For instance, in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73 m²), the dose might be reduced to 50-75% of the standard dose. Furthermore, patients with comorbid conditions such as heart failure, hypertension, or diabetes may also require individualized dosing due to altered pharmacokinetics and increased sensitivity to the drug's effects.

Controls for glomerular filtrations (GFR) and tubular transport of solutes and water are interrelated. GFR changes with hydration, apparently as a result of changes in the number of filtering nephrons under the control of antidiuretic hormone. The resulting alterations in volume flow rate through the collecting ducts may be as important as changes in epithelial permeability in determining urine osmolarity. Tubular transport of sodium and potassium may be controlled in part by antidiuretic hormone and aldosterone but considerable variation occurs among species, and intrinsic regulation of distal tubular sodium absorption in response to the delivered load of sodium may also occur. Net tubular secretion of phosphate, under control of parathyroid hormone, occurs in some species, but no hormonal control of tubular calcium transport has been demonstrated. Net tubular urate secretion that is influenced by potassium occurs in uricotelic reptiles. Complexing of inorganic cations, especially sodium and potassium, with urate precipitates in tubular urine permits excretion of cations without their contributing to urine osmolarity. This process also may keep the distal tubule sodium concentration low enough to permit maximum dilution but may require absorption of filtered water without sodium. Such an absorptive process may exist in reptilian proximal tubules.

instruction: How do changes in hydration levels affect glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and what role does antidiuretic hormone play in this process?
response: Changes in hydration levels significantly impact the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). When an individual is well-hydrated, the GFR tends to increase due to increased blood volume and pressure, which enhances the filtration process in the kidneys. Conversely, dehydration leads to a decrease in blood volume and pressure, resulting in a lower GFR. The antidiuretic hormone (ADH) plays a crucial role in this process. ADH, also known as vasopressin, is released by the posterior pituitary gland in response to decreased blood volume or increased plasma osmolality. ADH acts on the collecting ducts of the nephrons to increase water reabsorption, thereby concentrating the urine and conserving water. This action can reduce the volume of filtrate passing through the nephrons, which in turn can decrease the GFR. However, ADH also influences the number of filtering nephrons, which can further modulate GFR. By controlling the number of active nephrons, ADH helps to balance the filtration and reabsorption processes, ensuring that the body maintains appropriate hydration levels and osmotic balance.

instruction: How can the medical community improve its understanding of the different stages of kidney infections to avoid misclassifying them as distinct disease entities?
response:
Improving the medical community's understanding of the different stages of kidney infections to avoid misclassification involves a multifaceted approach that combines education, research, and clinical practice. According to the text, many capable physicians are unfamiliar with important facts about renal infections, which can lead to the misclassification of different stages as distinct disease entities. Here are some detailed steps to address this issue: 

1. **Comprehensive Education**: Medical schools and CME programs should include detailed modules on the natural history of renal infections. These modules should cover the different stages of kidney infections, their clinical presentations, and the progression of the disease. Interactive learning tools, such as case studies and simulations, can enhance understanding and retention. 

2. **Standardized Clinical Guidelines**: Developing and regularly updating clinical guidelines that clearly define the stages of kidney infections and provide standardized diagnostic criteria. These guidelines should be easily accessible and user-friendly, with clear algorithms for diagnosis and management. 

3. **Research and Innovation**: Investing in research to better understand the pathophysiology of kidney infections and the factors that influence their progression. This includes studying the genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors that contribute to the different stages of the disease. Collaborative research initiatives can help in sharing knowledge and resources. 

4. **Practical Training and Mentorship**: Providing hands-on training and mentorship opportunities for healthcare professionals. This can include shadowing experienced clinicians, participating in clinical trials, and engaging in multidisciplinary team meetings to discuss complex cases. 

5. **Advanced Diagnostic Tools**: Utilizing advanced diagnostic tools, such as high-resolution imaging techniques and biomarker analysis, to accurately identify the different stages of kidney infections. These tools can help in early detection and more precise staging, leading to better patient outcomes. 

6. **Continuous Quality Improvement**: Implementing continuous quality improvement (CQI) programs in healthcare institutions to monitor and evaluate the accuracy of diagnoses and the effectiveness of treatment protocols. Feedback from these programs can be used to refine educational materials and clinical guidelines. 

By adopting these strategies, the medical community can enhance its ability to accurately diagnose and manage kidney infections, leading to improved patient care and outcomes.

Disease recreated in mini-kidney organoids in the lab
Posted: 23 October 2015 | Victoria White
The work paves the way for personalised drug discovery for kidney disease…
This is a mini-kidney (1 mm diameter) grown from a patient’s stem cells. CREDIT: Benjamin Freedman & Joseph Bonventre labs
Mini-kidney organoids have now been grown in a laboratory by using genome editing to re-create human kidney disease in petri dishes.
The work paves the way for personalised drug discovery for kidney disease.
The mini-kidney organoids were grown from pluripotent stem cells. These are human cells that have turned back the clock to a time when they could develop into any type of organ in the body. When treated with a chemical cocktail, these stem cells matured into structures that resemble miniature kidneys.
These organoids contain tubules, filtering cells and blood vessel cells. They transport chemicals and respond to toxic injury in ways that are similar to kidney tubules in people.
“A major unanswered question was whether we could re-create human kidney disease in a lab petri dish using this technology,” said Benjamin Freedman, who led the studies at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. He is now an assistant professor of medicine in the Division of Nephrology at the University of Washington.
“Answering this question,” he said, “was important for understanding the potential of mini-kidneys for clinical kidney regeneration and drug discovery.”
Scientists used CRISPR technology to recreate disease in the mini-kidney organoids
To re-create human disease, Freedman and his colleagues used the gene-editing technique called CRISPR. They engineered mini-kidneys with genetic changes linked to two common kidney diseases, polycystic kidney disease and glomerulonephritis.
The organoids developed characteristics of these diseases. Those with mutations in polycystic kidney disease genes formed balloon like, fluid filled sacks, called cysts, from kidney tubules. The organoids with mutations in podocalyxin, a gene linked to glomerulonephritis, lost connections between filtering cells.
“Mutation of a single gene results in changes kidney structures associated with human disease, thereby allowing better understand of the disease and serving as models to develop therapeutic agents to treat these diseases,” explained Joseph Bonventre. He is chief of the Renal Division at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and a principal faculty member at Harvard Stem Cell Institute.
“These genetically engineered mini-kidneys,” Freedman added, “have taught us that human disease boils down to simple components that can be re-created in a petri dish. This provides us with faster, better ways to perform ‘clinical trials in a dish’ to test drugs and therapies that might work in humans.”
The researchers found that genetically matched kidney organoids without disease-linked mutations showed no signs of either disease.
“CRISPR can be used to correct gene mutations,” explained Freedman. “Our findings suggest that gene correction using CRISPR may be a promising therapeutic strategy.”
instruction: What are the potential benefits and challenges of using mini-kidney organoids grown from pluripotent stem cells for drug discovery and clinical trials in kidney disease treatment?
response: The use of mini-kidney organoids grown from pluripotent stem cells for drug discovery and clinical trials in kidney disease treatment offers several potential benefits and challenges. **Benefits** include: 1. **Personalized Medicine**: These organoids can be tailored to individual patients, allowing for personalized drug discovery and treatment. 2. **Disease Modeling**: By using CRISPR technology, researchers can introduce specific genetic mutations to recreate diseases like polycystic kidney disease and glomerulonephritis, providing a more accurate model of human disease. 3. **Faster and More Efficient Testing**: Mini-kidney organoids can be used to perform 'clinical trials in a dish,' accelerating the drug discovery process and reducing the need for animal testing. 4. **Gene Correction**: CRISPR can be used to correct disease-causing mutations, opening up new therapeutic strategies. **Challenges** include: 1. **Complexity of Human Kidney Function**: While mini-kidney organoids can mimic certain aspects of kidney function, they may not fully replicate the complexity of a human kidney, potentially leading to incomplete or inaccurate results. 2. **Scalability**: Producing large numbers of organoids for widespread use in clinical trials and personalized medicine may be technically challenging and costly. 3. **Regulatory Approval**: The use of CRISPR and stem cell-derived organoids in clinical trials may face regulatory hurdles and ethical concerns that need to be addressed. 4. **Long-term Effects**: The long-term effects of using gene-edited organoids in therapeutic applications are not yet fully understood and require further research.

instruction: What are some common factors that can interfere with the accuracy of a creatinine assay, and how do they affect the test results?
response: The accuracy of a creatinine assay can be compromised by various interfering substances and conditions. For instance, specimens with elevated total bilirubin levels (greater than 20 mg/dL) may show decreased creatinine values. On the other hand, substances like protein, glucose, ascorbic acid (vitamin C), α-ketoacids, and specific cephalosporin antibiotics can cause the assay to overestimate creatinine levels. These inaccuracies can lead to incorrect assessments of renal function, emphasizing the need for careful specimen handling and appropriate test selection to ensure reliable results.

text:
Kidney doctors in southwest Virginia
Nephrology, also called kidney care, deals with the function and proper care of the kidneys—the two bean-shaped organs located in your lower back. Kidneys play an essential role in removing bodily wastes, balancing chemicals, controlling blood pressure and keeping bones healthy.
The kidney specialists affiliated with LewisGale Regional Health System provide comprehensive care for the prevention and treatment of chronic kidney disease.
To learn about kidney services at LewisGale Regional Health System, call our Consult-A-Nurse® team at (877) 242-2362.
What is chronic kidney disease?
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) means your kidneys are damaged and can no longer filter blood as they should. This can cause waste to build up in your body and lead to other serious health concerns. Two-thirds of all cases of CKD are caused by diabetes and high blood pressure. Some infections, inherited diseases and injuries can also lead to kidney disease.
Treatment for chronic kidney disease may include medication to lower blood pressure, control blood glucose and lower blood cholesterol. If kidney disease leads to kidney failure, the only treatment options are dialysis or a kidney transplant.
Nephrology services we offer
We offer advanced care for patients with chronic kidney disease, including:
- Kidney disease screening and diagnosis
- Diabetes counseling and nutrition services
- Inpatient kidney dialysis
- Dialysis graft declotting
Kidney transplant surgery
If a patient requires a kidney transplant, we offer a community-based transplant program with our partners at The Virginia Transplant Center at Henrico Doctors' Hospital in Richmond.
The nationally recognized Virginia Transplant Center, established more than 20 years ago, offers Virginia’s only community-based transplant program. The experienced surgical specialists at the center have performed more than 1,000 kidney transplants.
Kidney transplant evaluation and classes are available at LewisGale Medical Center in Salem, as well as at Henrico Doctors’ Hospital and Spotsylvania Regional Medical Center in Fredericksburg.
Maintaining your kidney health
Early detection and lifestyle changes can prevent kidney disease and kidney failure. To help keep your kidneys healthy:
- Choose low-sodium foods
- Keep your blood pressure below 130/80
- Keep your blood sucrose in the target range, if you are diabetic
instruction: What are the key lifestyle changes and preventive measures that can help in maintaining kidney health and preventing chronic kidney disease?
response: Maintaining kidney health and preventing chronic kidney disease involves a combination of lifestyle changes and preventive measures. One of the most important steps is to choose low-sodium foods, as excessive sodium can raise blood pressure and strain the kidneys. Keeping your blood pressure below 130/80 is crucial, as hypertension is a primary cause of kidney damage. For individuals with diabetes, managing blood glucose levels within the target range is vital to prevent diabetic nephropathy. Other important measures include regular physical activity to maintain a healthy weight, quitting smoking, and limiting alcohol intake. Additionally, staying well-hydrated, avoiding over-the-counter pain medications like NSAIDs, and getting regular kidney function tests can help in early detection and prevention of kidney disease. Consulting with healthcare providers, such as nephrologists, for personalized advice and regular check-ups is also recommended.

According to research, more than 12% of the population is struggling with kidney stones.
Your kidneys help in ejecting harmful toxins and waste from the blood in the form of urine. Sometimes too many dissolved minerals are formed inside the kidneys, and there is less amount of fluid. It leads to a health ailment known as kidney stones. While some of the stones are tiny and are eliminated by the body through the urinary tract. On the other hand, some can be as big as the size of a golf ball which can lead to severe discomfort. Moreover, if it is not treated timely, it can even lead to other serious ailments like kidney damage, infections etc.

Kidney Stones Symptoms
The following symptoms can be observed when a person is suffering from kidney stones.
- A constant need for urination
- Pain in the lower abdomen
- Blood in the urine
- Vomiting and a nauseous feeling
- Urinary tract infection ( UTI )

instruction: What are the potential benefits and risks of using CBD oil for managing chronic kidney disease, and how does it compare to traditional treatments?
response: The use of CBD oil for managing chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a topic of growing interest due to its potential therapeutic benefits. One of the key advantages of CBD oil is its ability to reduce inflammation and oxidative stress, which are major contributors to kidney damage. Additionally, CBD oil can alleviate common symptoms associated with CKD, such as pain, anxiety, and sleep disturbances, without causing the psychoactive effects associated with THC. The Skin-Kidney Connection
The phrase, “beauty is skin deep” has a lot of meaning to it. This is because our organs, especially healthy kidneys, are essential for maintaining clear, radiant skin.
When your kidneys aren’t working properly, they can’t filter out waste and toxins like they’re supposed to. This can lead to a bunch of skin issues, like discolored skin, itching, eczema, rashes, bags under your eyes and acne. People with kidney disease might also have dry skin because their bodies don’t have enough moisture. Think dehydration or lack of electrolytes. That’s why it’s important to take care of your kidneys for the sake of your overall health, including your skin.
Skin Health and Kidney Function: How are they Connected?
Healthy skin is often seen as a reflection of overall well-being. Many people believe that a glowing complexion is solely dependent on a good skincare routine, but what they may not realize is that the health of their skin is intricately linked to the functioning of their kidneys. In this article, we will explore the connection between skin health and kidney function, and how taking care of your kidneys can lead to radiant and beautiful skin.
The Role of the Kidneys in Skin Health
The kidneys play a crucial role in maintaining the body’s internal balance by filtering waste products and toxins from the blood. When the kidneys are functioning optimally, they effectively remove these harmful substances from the body, preventing them from accumulating and potentially causing damage to various organs, including the skin.
The Effect of Poor Kidney Function on the Skin
When the kidneys are not functioning properly, toxins and waste products build up in the body. This can result in several skin issues, including:
Acne and Breakouts
One of the primary ways the body eliminates toxins is through sweat. When the kidneys are unable to filter out waste, the skin compensates by expelling these toxins through the sebaceous glands, leading to clogged pores and acne breakouts.
Dry and Itchy Skin
Dehydration is a common symptom of kidney dysfunction. When the body is dehydrated, the skin loses moisture, leading to dryness and itching. Additionally, the accumulation of waste products can cause inflammation, further aggravating skin dryness.
Kidney problems can result in a buildup of waste products in the bloodstream, leading to a condition known as uremia. Uremia can cause the skin to appear yellowish or pale, giving it an unhealthy and sallow appearance.
How to Improve Kidney Function for Better Skin Health
Taking care of your kidneys is essential for maintaining healthy and glowing skin. Here are some tips to improve kidney function:
- Stay Hydrated
Drinking an adequate amount of water is crucial for proper kidney function. It helps flush out toxins and supports the body’s natural detoxification process. Aim to drink at least eight glasses of water a day to keep your kidneys functioning optimally.
- Eat a Balanced Diet
A healthy diet plays a significant role in maintaining kidney health. Include foods rich in antioxidants and vegetables such as dandelion or celery as they help reduce inflammation and protect against cell damage. Additionally, limit your intake of processed foods, salt, and sugar, which can burden the kidneys.
- Limit Alcohol and Caffeine
Excessive alcohol and caffeine consumption can put a strain on the kidneys. These substances can lead to dehydration and may interfere with the kidneys’ ability to remove waste effectively.
- Avoid Smoking & Vaping
Smoking and vaping damages blood vessels and decreases blood flow to the kidneys, which can impair their function. Quitting smoking and vaping not only benefits your overall health but also helps maintain healthy skin by promoting proper kidney function.

instruction: How does understanding the anatomy and physiology of the urinary system enhance the effectiveness and safety of catheterisation procedures in adult patients?
response: Understanding the anatomy and physiology of the urinary system is essential for improving the effectiveness and safety of catheterisation procedures in adult patients. The urinary system's complex structure, including the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra, requires precise knowledge to avoid complications. For instance, knowing the anatomy of the urethra and the bladder's position and size helps in choosing the appropriate catheter size and insertion depth, which is critical for preventing urethral trauma or bladder perforation. Physiologically, understanding the detrusor muscle's role in bladder contraction and the mechanisms of urine production and storage allows healthcare providers to assess the patient's need for catheterisation accurately. This knowledge also helps in recognizing and managing potential issues, such as catheter blockages or infections, by understanding the normal flow of urine and the body's natural defense mechanisms. Furthermore, a thorough understanding of the urinary system supports infection prevention and control by guiding proper aseptic techniques and catheter care. In summary, a robust knowledge of the urinary system's anatomy and physiology is fundamental to ensuring that catheterisation procedures are performed safely and effectively, thereby reducing the risk of healthcare-acquired infections and other complications.

instruction: What are the potential causes and implications of high levels of protein and albumin in urine, and how are these levels typically interpreted in a clinical setting?
response: High levels of protein and albumin in urine, referred to as proteinuria and albuminuria, can have various causes and significant clinical implications. **Causes:** 1. **Kidney Damage:** The most common cause is damage to the glomeruli in the kidneys, which can occur due to conditions like diabetic nephropathy, glomerulonephritis, and hypertensive kidney disease. 2. **Infections:** Urinary tract infections (UTIs) can cause temporary proteinuria due to inflammation. 3. **Preeclampsia:** In pregnant women, preeclampsia is a condition characterized by high blood pressure and proteinuria. 4. **Dehydration:** Concentration of urine due to dehydration can lead to higher levels of protein and albumin. 5. **Strenuous Exercise:** Intense physical activity can cause temporary proteinuria. **Implications:** 1. **Kidney Health:** Persistent proteinuria can be an early indicator of kidney damage and may progress to chronic kidney disease (CKD). 2. **Cardiovascular Health:** High levels of albumin in the urine are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease. 3. **Hypertension:** Proteinuria can be a marker for hypertension and may indicate the need for blood pressure management. **Clinical Interpretation:** In a clinical setting, the levels of protein and albumin in urine are interpreted using specific tests and ratios. The urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) is a key measure. A normal ACR is generally less than 30 mg/g. Levels between 30-300 mg/g indicate microalbuminuria, and levels above 300 mg/g indicate significant proteinuria. If the ACR is elevated, further diagnostic tests such as a 24-hour urine or a kidney biopsy may be necessary to determine the underlying cause and guide appropriate treatment. It's important to consult with a healthcare provider to interpret these results and develop a management plan.

01/7Increasing risk of kidney disease
Kidney problems in women post ’30s are a growing concern that is often overlooked. As women age, their risk of developing kidney problems increases. The good news is that there are steps that can be taken to reduce the risk of developing kidney disease.
Dr. Anand Dharaskar, Consultant- Urology, Manipal Hospital- Baner, Pune says, “Women can develop kidney stones, which are small, hard deposits that form in the kidneys. Factors such as hormonal changes, dietary habits, and genetic predisposition can contribute to kidney stone formation. Symptoms may include severe pain in the back or abdomen, blood in the urine, and frequent urination. Drinking plenty of water, maintaining a healthy diet, and managing underlying conditions like obesity and diabetes can help reduce the risk of kidney stones.”
03/7Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)
UTIs are more common in women than men, and they can affect the kidneys if left untreated. UTIs occur when bacteria enter the urinary tract, leading to infection. Symptoms may include a burning sensation during urination, frequent urination, cloudy or bloody urine, and pelvic pain. Prompt treatment with antibiotics is necessary to prevent the spread of infection to the kidneys.
04/7Polycystic Kidney Disease (PKD)
According to Dr. Dharaskar, “PKD is a genetic disorder characterised by the growth of numerous cysts in the kidneys. While PKD can affect both men and women, women may experience complications related to hormonal changes during pregnancy. Symptoms may include abdominal pain, high blood pressure, blood in the urine, and frequent urinary tract infections. Regular monitoring and management of PKD are essential to prevent kidney damage and associated complications.”
05/7Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD)
CKD is a progressive condition that affects the kidneys' ability to function properly over time. Various factors can contribute to CKD, including diabetes, high blood pressure, and autoimmune diseases. Women in their 30s may be at higher risk due to hormonal changes and the presence of certain health conditions. Early detection and management of underlying causes are crucial in preventing further kidney damage and preserving kidney function.
06/7What are the risk factors?
Hypertension: One of the most common risk factors for kidney disease in women over 30 is high blood pressure. High blood pressure can damage the kidneys and cause them to stop working properly.
Diabetes: “In addition to high blood pressure, diabetes is another risk factor for kidney disease. This progressive condition can damage the blood vessels in the kidneys and lead to kidney disease,” says Dr. Dharaskar.
Obesity: Excess weight puts extra strain on the kidneys and can cause them to become damaged.
To maintain kidney health, women should prioritise a healthy lifestyle, including staying hydrated, eating a balanced diet, exercising regularly, managing underlying health conditions, and avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol consumption. Regular check-ups and screenings can help identify any kidney problems early on, allowing for prompt treatment and better long-term outcomes.

Strange things around the IVC
A medical student is looking for inferior vena cava in a nephrology clinic patient and finds something ‘weird’ adjacent to the IVC. He/she calls the nephrology fellow for help. Here are the images and corresponding scan positions. 1. What are those numerous anechoic structures? 2. Did the student identify IVC accurately? Interestingly, the student did not know the patient’s medical history.
Now the nephrology fellow obtains more views and demonstrates bilateral polycystic kidneys in this patient with known ADPKD. So, those weird things are renal cysts. Yes, the student did identify the IVC correctly – note that it is entering into the heart (beating anechoic structure on the left) and the hepatic vein is draining into it.
Take home points: 1. Know the patient’s history (& have focused questions on mind) before performing POCUS: you are a clinician first 2. When you find something abnormal, try and obtain more views, trace the structures that you know.
A sonographer once told me “when you don’t know what you are looking at, go home” – it means, everybody has a ‘comfort scan zone’ (home) and better understanding of the surrounding anatomy. For nephrologists, it is the kidney. So, go scan the kidneys first and try to figure out the surrounding abnormal things.
instruction: How can a medical student ensure they have a comprehensive understanding of a patient's medical history before performing a POCUS exam, and why is this crucial for accurate diagnosis?
response: To ensure a comprehensive understanding of a patient's medical history before performing a POCUS exam, a medical student should take several steps. First, they should review the patient's electronic health record (EHR) to familiarize themselves with the patient's past medical history, current medications, and previous imaging studies. This review should include any relevant family history, as in the case of ADPKD, which is a hereditary condition. Additionally, the student should conduct a focused and detailed patient interview to gather specific information about the patient's symptoms, duration, and any recent changes. For example, in the nephrology clinic, the student might have asked about any known kidney conditions or family history of kidney disease. instruction: How does the composition of urine reflect the body's metabolic processes and fluid balance, and what are the key components that can indicate specific health conditions?
response: Urine composition is a critical indicator of the body's metabolic processes and fluid balance. The kidneys filter the blood to remove waste products, such as urea, creatinine, and uric acid, which are then excreted in the urine. The kidneys also regulate the body's fluid balance by adjusting the concentration of urine. During dehydration, the kidneys produce more concentrated urine to conserve water, while in a well-hydrated state, the urine is more dilute. Urine can also reflect specific health conditions. For instance, the presence of blood (hematuria) may indicate kidney stones, infections, or more serious conditions like kidney disease. Elevated levels of protein (proteinuria) can be a sign of kidney damage or other systemic issues. Glucose in the urine (glycosuria) is often a hallmark of diabetes, while the presence of ketones suggests uncontrolled diabetes or fasting. White blood cells (leukocytes) in the urine can indicate an infection, such as a UTI. Therefore, the composition of urine is a valuable diagnostic tool that reflects the body's metabolic state and helps in identifying various health conditions.

Scientists at Glasgow University have made significant discoveries that could help patients awaiting kidney transplants.
The research, carried out at the Western Infirmary, has shown that the ‘bio-age’ of a kidney is more important than its actual chronological age when judging its suitability for transplant.
This information will allow doctors to calculate the performance and health of a transplanted kidney and make more informed decisions as to suitability for transplant.
It was also found that a simple blood test of an older person can determine the ‘bio-age’ of their kidney.
With over 3,000 organ transplants taking place last year in the UK and thousands more on the waiting lists, it is hoped that the information can be applied to other organs.
Dr. Paul Shiels, Senior Lecturer in the Department of Surgery at Glasgow University confirmed the significance of the discovery.
He said: “This latest research offers promising prospects for doctors when it comes to assessing which organs are suitable for transplantation and how they might perform post-transplant.
“It could mean that complications in some patients could be avoided through the selection of more suitable organs.”
It was the levels of the gene cyclin-dependent kinase 2a (CDKN2a) in kidneys that the researchers found determined the biological age of the kidneys.
The research was funded jointly by the Cunninghame Trust and Darlinda’s Charity for Renal Research.
Dr. Shiels also emphasised the importance of the recent research for Glasgow University.
He explained: “The project demonstrates the quality of research being conducted at the University of Glasgow which is working at the forefront of medical science
“The benefits our students derive from being part of a research-led university are incalculable.”
instruction: How might the concept of 'bio-age' influence the selection of organs for transplantation, and what potential benefits could this have for patients awaiting organ transplants?
response: The concept of 'bio-age' can revolutionize the selection of organs for transplantation by focusing on the biological condition of the organ rather than its chronological age. Researchers at Glasgow University have found that the 'bio-age' of a kidney, determined by the levels of the CDKN2a gene, is a crucial factor in assessing its suitability for transplant. This method allows for a more precise evaluation of organ health and performance, enabling doctors to select the best possible organs for patients. By prioritizing organs with a younger biological age, the potential benefits for patients include a lower risk of post-transplant complications, better long-term outcomes, and a more efficient use of the limited supply of donor organs. This approach could also expand the pool of viable organs, as organs from older donors that were previously deemed unsuitable due to age might now be considered based on their biological condition.

instruction: What are the potential risks and considerations when using diuretics, both natural and over-the-counter, to manage water retention, and what are some safer alternatives?
response: When considering the use of diuretics to manage water retention, it's crucial to be aware of the potential risks and to explore safer alternatives. **Risks and Considerations:** 1. **Electrolyte Imbalance:** Diuretics can deplete the body of essential electrolytes, such as potassium and sodium, which are vital for proper heart and muscle function. 2. **Dehydration:** Increased urination can lead to dehydration, particularly if fluid intake is not adequately increased. 3. **Kidney Strain:** Overuse of diuretics can place additional stress on the kidneys, potentially leading to kidney damage. 4. **Medication Interactions:** Diuretics can interact with other medications, altering their effectiveness or increasing the risk of side effects. 5. **Masking Health Issues:** Relying on diuretics to manage water retention can obscure underlying health conditions that need proper medical attention. **Safer Alternatives:** 1. **Reduce Sodium Intake:** A diet high in sodium is a common cause of water retention. Cutting back on salt can help reduce bloating. 2. **Stay Hydrated:** Drinking more water can help flush out excess sodium and reduce water retention. 3. **Eat Water-Rich Foods:** Consuming fruits and vegetables like lemons, celery, garlic, onions, peppers, watermelons, cucumbers, ginger, grapes, asparagus, and pineapples can act as natural diuretics and provide essential nutrients. 4. **Herbal Diuretics:** Incorporate herbs such as parsley and dandelion into your diet through foods and herbal teas. These herbs can help manage water retention without the risks associated with concentrated supplements. 5. **Regular Exercise:** Physical activity can improve circulation and promote sweating, helping to reduce water retention. 6. **Monitor Fluid Intake:** Be aware of hidden sources of sodium in drinks like soda and opt for water or caffeine-free herbal teas. By adopting these natural methods, you can effectively manage water retention without the potential risks associated with diuretics.

instruction: What are some natural remedies or dietary changes that can help prevent the formation of kidney stones, and how effective are they compared to medical interventions?
response: Natural remedies and dietary changes can play a crucial role in preventing the formation of kidney stones. Increasing water intake is paramount, as it helps to dilute the urine and prevent the crystallization of stone-forming substances. Aim to drink enough water to keep your urine light yellow to almost clear. Foods and drinks rich in citric acid, such as lemons, can also be beneficial. Citric acid helps prevent the formation of new stones by binding with calcium and reducing its availability for stone formation. Other dietary modifications include reducing sodium intake, which can increase calcium in the urine, and limiting high-oxalate foods like spinach, nuts, and chocolate. While these natural methods can be effective, they are generally more preventive and may not be as effective as medical interventions for treating existing larger stones. Medical treatments like Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL) are necessary for breaking down larger stones that cannot pass naturally. Always consult with a healthcare provider to tailor a plan that best suits your specific needs and medical history.

instruction: How can nephrologist-patient communication be improved to enhance the quality of life for dialysis patients, and what specific strategies might be effective in achieving this goal?
response: To enhance the quality of life for dialysis patients, nephrologist-patient communication must be improved through several targeted strategies. One approach is to foster a more patient-centered communication style, where nephrologists actively listen to patients' concerns and preferences, and provide clear, empathetic explanations about their treatment options and outcomes. This can be supported by regular training programs for nephrologists to improve their communication skills and cultural competency. Another strategy is to integrate interdisciplinary care teams that include social workers, psychologists, and dietitians to address the multifaceted needs of dialysis patients. These teams can help manage psychological issues, provide nutritional guidance, and offer social support, all of which are critical for improving QOL. Additionally, incorporating patient-reported outcomes (PROs) into routine care can help nephrologists better understand the patient's subjective experiences and tailor their care accordingly. Finally, promoting patient involvement in shared decision-making processes can empower patients and enhance their sense of control and satisfaction with their treatment, ultimately leading to better QOL outcomes.

instruction: What are the primary symptoms and genetic causes associated with Gitelman Syndrome, and how does it impact the body's electrolyte balance?
response: Gitelman Syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by mutations in the SLC12A3 gene, which codes for the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney. The primary symptoms of Gitelman Syndrome include hypokalemia (low potassium levels), hypomagnesemia (low magnesium levels), metabolic alkalosis (increased blood pH), and hypocalciuria (low calcium excretion in urine). These symptoms arise due to the impaired reabsorption of electrolytes in the kidney, leading to an imbalance in the body's electrolyte levels. The condition can cause muscle cramps, weakness, fatigue, and frequent urination. The genetic cause of Gitelman Syndrome is autosomal recessive, meaning that an individual must inherit two copies of the mutated gene (one from each parent) to develop the disorder.

Triple kidney transplants: ’We think it is the future’
Joy Hindle cried when she found out she couldn't give one of her kidneys to her twin brother. Then doctors gave the Bel Air, MD, woman another option: a kidney exchange, in which she would donate her kidney to a patient who needed one, and her diabetic brother would get one from another willing donor. Hindle and brother Paul McSorley were two of six participants in a triple kidney transplant performed last month by doctors at the University of Maryland Medical Center. She gave her kidney to a stranger; he got a kidney from a stranger. Multipatient swaps made up a small percentage of the more than 13,000 kidney transplants performed in the United States last year. But with the creation of a national database to link the 90,000 patients waiting for kidneys with compatible donors, some health care officials expect the number to increase dramatically.

response: The implementation of a national database for kidney transplants is likely to have a profound impact on the number of multipatient swaps and the overall transplant rates in the United States. The text highlights a case of a triple kidney transplant, where six participants were involved in a complex exchange. Such multipatient swaps, while currently rare, could become more common with a national database. The database would enable better coordination and matching of potential donors and recipients, thereby increasing the likelihood of successful swaps. This enhanced matching system would not only boost the number of multipatient swaps but also expedite the process for individual transplants. As a result, the overall transplant rates could rise, reducing the lengthy waiting times for the 90,000 patients currently on the kidney transplant list and ultimately improving patient health and survival rates.
