instruction: How can lifestyle changes, such as diet and exercise, help in managing chronic kidney disease, and what are some key dietary principles to follow?
response:
Lifestyle changes, such as diet and exercise, play a crucial role in managing chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD is often caused by uncontrolled diabetes and high blood pressure, which can be significantly influenced by lifestyle choices. A healthy diet and regular exercise can help manage blood sugar levels and blood pressure, thereby slowing the progression of CKD.

Key dietary principles to follow include:
- **Calorie and Protein Intake**: Ensure a diet high in calories to maintain energy levels while providing sufficient protein to support bodily functions. However, the protein intake should be carefully managed to avoid overloading the kidneys.
- **Sodium Restriction**: Avoid adding salt while cooking. Instead, sprinkle a small amount of salt before eating. Steer clear of processed foods, canned foods, salted nuts, and products containing baking soda, as they are high in sodium.
- **Potassium Management**: To reduce potassium content, boil vegetables in ample water and drain the excess. Avoid fruits, fruit juices, coconut water, and certain foods like tea, coffee, bajra, maize, ragi, whole wheat flour, jam, jellies, sausages, chocolates, meat, soup, and dried fruits if potassium needs to be restricted.
- **Dairy and Non-Vegetarian Foods**: Limit milk and milk products to 300-500 mg per day. For non-vegetarians, fish and chicken can replace milk and dal, with a recommended intake of 30-50 grams per day.
- **Fat Intake**: Avoid saturated fats and limit oil intake to 25 grams or 5 teaspoons per day.
- **Fruit and Vegetable Consumption**: When potassium is restricted, avoid citrus fruits. Include one portion of fruit (50 calories) as prescribed. All vegetables should be cooked before consumption, and avoid tubers.

A personalized dietary plan from a nutritionist or dietitian can provide more specific guidance tailored to your condition.

text:
By Terry Davis, M.D., family physician, Providence Medical Group - Wilsonville
"Know your numbers" is a message that health care providers have been pushing for years, with positive results. Chances are good that you, your friends and your family members now pay closer attention to your blood pressure and cholesterol numbers. But what about your GFR?
Never heard of it? Most people haven't – but I encourage you to get to know it.
GFR, short for glomerular filtration rate, is a measure of how well your kidneys are doing their job. It's a number that doesn't get much attention, but you'd be wise to watch it - especially if you have diabetes, high blood pressure or other risk factors for kidney disease. A drop in this number may be the first and only indication that your kidneys are starting to have problems. And problems with the kidneys can affect just about every other organ and function of your body.
A moment of appreciation for healthy filtration
The heart gets a lot of press. The lungs get a lot of press. But the kidneys, which play a vital role as your body's filtration system, are underappreciated.
Besides filtering waste products and excess fluid out of your body, these wonderful, hard-working organs also regulate your electrolyte balance, red blood cell production and blood pressure, and can affect your calcium metabolism, as well. Yet as important as they are, we don't pay as much attention to our kidneys as we should - not, that is, until we're faced with the prospect of spending the rest of our life on kidney dialysis. Unfortunately, with type 2 diabetes becoming more common, that prospect is growing more likely for a lot more people.
Doing a number on your kidneys
Some causes of kidney disease can't be controlled - these include family history, genetic conditions, aging and race (African Americans, Native Americans, Hispanic Americans, Asians and Pacific Islanders are at higher risk). But most of the things that lead to chronic kidney disease and kidney failure are things that we do, often unwittingly, to ourselves. Topping the list of controllable risk factors are the following:
- Poorly managed type 2 diabetes: Type 2 diabetes that is not managed well is the leading cause of chronic kidney disease, responsible for about 40 percent of all cases.
- Uncontrolled high blood pressure: Hypertension that is undetected or poorly managed is the second leading cause of chronic kidney disease.
- Too much protein: Compared to the rest of the world, most Americans eat huge amounts of protein, which puts a toxic load on the kidneys.
- Overuse of over-the-counter pain relievers: You don't hear much about this, but non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, such as ibuprofen (Advil) and naproxen (Aleve), put a heavy burden on the kidneys.
- Dehydration: Drinking too little water stresses the kidneys.
- Smoking: On top of all the other harm that smoking does, it's also hard on the kidneys.
Each of these alone increases the risk of chronic kidney disease. A person with several risk factors - for example, a smoker with poorly controlled diabetes who eats a lot of meat and takes ibuprofen frequently - could seriously be looking at kidney failure and dialysis in the future.
And it isn't a pretty future. Dialysis means having to travel to a clinic two or three times a week to be tethered to a machine for half of the day. The machine does the work that your kidneys no longer can do, and it leaves you feeling pretty washed out. You are chronically anemic, you may need hormone injections, and you have to change your diet radically. It is definitely something you want to avoid if at all possible.
That's where knowing your GFR comes in.
What's your number?
GFR is the earliest and most accurate predictor of declining kidney function. Tracking this number gives you the power to detect a problem early enough to do something about it.
Your GFR calculation begins with a blood test for creatinine, a waste product normally filtered out by the kidneys. High levels of creatinine are the first clue to a potential kidney problem, but a complete GFR goes further. It also factors in your age, race, gender and body mass to provide a very accurate measure of your kidneys' functioning. The lower your GFR, the lower your kidney function.
A GFR between 130 and 90 is considered normal for most people, but that can vary depending on a person's body size and race. Kidney disease is ranked in five stages:
- Stage 1: GFR 130 to 90 - A person may be considered in stage 1 if his kidneys are damaged due to injury or other factors, but are still functioning normally
- Stage 2: GFR of 90 to 60 - damaged kidneys with mildly reduced function
- Stage 3: GFR of 60 to 30 - kidney disease with moderately functional kidneys
- Stage 4: GFR of 30 to 15 - severe kidney disease
- Stage 5: GFR below 15 - kidney failure; kidney dialysis or transplant is necessary for survival
A person can progress to stage 4, when dialysis is just around the corner, with no symptoms whatsoever. That's why knowing your GFR is so important: a drop in this number gives you a heads-up that trouble is brewing. When we discover kidney disease earlier, we can intervene with diet and lifestyle changes that can do an enormous amount of good, preserving a lot of kidney function and forestalling or potentially avoiding dialysis.
TLC for your GFR
If some of the risk factors for kidney disease apply to you, ask your doctor to calculate your GFR at your next checkup. If you find that your GFR is abnormal, work closely with your doctor to develop and follow a plan to preserve your kidney function. If your number is healthy - and especially if it's not - start giving your kidneys some much-deserved attention and work on reducing your controllable risk factors:
- Get screened regularly for diabetes and high blood pressure: If you are diagnosed with either of these, work closely with your physician to keep them well under control.
- Don't overdo it on protein: For most people, the U.S. Dietary Guidelines recommend 5 to 6½ ounces of meat, fish or poultry per day from a variety of healthy sources.
- Take fewer pain medicines: For mild aches and pains, try other options such as breathing deeply, drinking water, and applying heating pads or ice.
- Stay hydrated: Drink two quarts of water every day, especially if you already have reduced kidney function.
- Don't smoke: If you do smoke, ask your doctor to help you quit.
instruction: Why is it important to monitor your GFR, and what can a drop in this number indicate about your kidney health?
response: It is essential to monitor your GFR (glomerular filtration rate) because it serves as a critical indicator of kidney health. The GFR measures the rate at which your kidneys filter waste and excess fluid from your blood. A drop in GFR can indicate that your kidneys are not functioning as effectively as they should, which can be the first sign of kidney damage or disease. This is particularly important for individuals with risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and a family history of kidney issues. Kidney disease can progress without symptoms, making early detection through GFR monitoring vital. A decline in GFR can lead to more severe conditions, including chronic kidney disease and kidney failure, which may require dialysis or a kidney transplant. By regularly tracking your GFR, you can identify potential problems early and take proactive steps to manage your health, such as controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, reducing protein intake, and avoiding overuse of pain medications.

instruction: What are the key factors to consider when deciding on prophylactic anticoagulation for adults with nephrotic syndrome, and how do these factors influence clinical decision-making?
response: In making decisions about prophylactic anticoagulation for adults with nephrotic syndrome (NS), several critical factors must be evaluated to balance the benefits and risks. **1. Histological Subtype:** The type of glomerular disease significantly influences the risk of thromboembolic events. Membranous glomerulonephritis (MGN) is associated with the highest risk, followed by focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and minimal change disease (MCD). **2. Severity of Proteinuria:** Higher proteinuria levels are linked to a greater risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and arterial thromboembolism (ATE). **3. Serum Albumin Levels:** Hypoalbuminemia, a common feature of NS, is a strong predictor of thrombosis. **4. Hypercoagulable State:** NS patients often exhibit a hypercoagulable state, which increases the likelihood of thromboembolic events. **5. Duration of NS:** The risk of thrombosis is particularly high in the first six months after diagnosis. **6. Comorbid Conditions:** The presence of comorbidities such as cancer, obesity, and immobility can further elevate the risk. **7. Age and Overall Health:** Older patients and those with poor overall health may have a higher risk of thrombosis. **8. Bleeding Risk:** The potential for bleeding complications must be carefully considered, especially in patients with renal impairment or those on multiple medications. Clinical decision-making should be guided by a thorough assessment of these factors, and the use of evidence-based guidelines, such as those from KDIGO, to tailor prophylactic anticoagulation to each patient's specific needs and risks.

instruction: What are the main dietary changes one should consider to prevent the formation of kidney stones, and how do these changes impact the body's metabolic processes?
response: Preventing kidney stones through dietary changes involves a few key strategies. First, staying well-hydrated is crucial. Drinking plenty of water, aiming for 2-3 liters per day, helps to dilute the substances in urine that can lead to stone formation. This is particularly important as dehydration is a common risk factor for kidney stones. Second, reducing sodium intake is beneficial. A high-sodium diet can increase the amount of calcium in the urine, which is a common component of kidney stones. Therefore, it's advisable to limit the consumption of processed foods, fast foods, and adding extra salt to meals. Third, moderating protein intake, particularly animal protein, is important. High-protein diets can increase the risk of kidney stones by raising the levels of uric acid and reducing citrate levels in the urine. Lean protein sources should be preferred, and excessive consumption of red meat, poultry, and fish should be avoided. Fourth, limiting foods high in oxalate can help prevent calcium oxalate stones, the most common type. Foods like spinach, nuts, chocolate, and beets are high in oxalate and should be consumed in moderation. However, a complete avoidance of these foods is not necessary. Lastly, maintaining a balanced intake of calcium is crucial. Both too little and too much calcium can increase the risk of stone formation. Dietary changes impact the body's metabolic processes by altering the concentration of substances in the urine. For example, increased hydration keeps the urine dilute, reducing the risk of crystal formation, while a low-sodium diet decreases the excretion of calcium in the urine, thus reducing the risk of stone formation. Additionally, a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains can provide essential nutrients that help protect against stone formation.

Lozol: Treating High Blood Pressure with Prescription Medication
Lozol is a prescription medication commonly used in the treatment of high blood pressure, medically known as hypertension. This article provides a detailed overview of Lozol and its role in managing this chronic condition.
What is Lozol?
Lozol is a prescription drug belonging to the class of medications called diuretics, specifically known as a thiazide-like diuretic. It contains the active ingredient indapamide, which helps reduce blood pressure by promoting urine formation and eliminating excess fluid and salt from the body.
How Does Lozol Work?
Lozol primarily works by relaxing the blood vessels and increasing urine production. By reducing the volume of fluid circulating in the bloodstream, Lozol lowers blood pressure and eases the workload on the heart.
While the exact mechanism of action is not fully understood, it is believed that Lozol affects the reabsorption of sodium (salt) and potassium ions in the kidneys, leading to increased urine production. This process helps reduce fluid retention and subsequently reduces blood pressure.
Usage and Dosage
Lozol is available in the form of oral tablets and is typically taken once daily, preferably in the morning. It is essential to follow the prescribed dosage provided by your healthcare professional, as the recommended amount may vary depending on individual factors such as severity of hypertension and overall health condition.
It may take several weeks of consistent use before the full effects of Lozol are experienced. It is crucial to continue taking the medication even if you feel well, as hypertension often shows no symptoms but can still cause severe health complications if left untreated.
Possible Side Effects
As with any medication, Lozol may cause some side effects. Common side effects include:
- Dizziness or lightheadedness
- Dry mouth
- Frequent urination
- Increased thirst
- Low potassium levels (hypokalemia)
If you experience severe side effects or allergic reactions such as rash, difficulty breathing, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, seek immediate medical attention.
Precautions and Interactions
Before starting Lozol, inform your healthcare provider about any existing medical conditions, allergies, or medications you are currently taking. It is essential to disclose this information as some drugs or medical conditions may interact adversely with Lozol.
Certain medications or substances that may interact with Lozol include:
- Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
- Drugs that increase potassium levels
- Diabetes medications
Your healthcare provider will determine whether Lozol is the right medication for you based on your medical history and individual circumstances.

The Future of Transplantation: Implantable Artificial Kidney Research
Vanderbilt University Medical Center nephrologist and associate professor William Fissell, MD is making major progress on an implantable artificial kidney. Join us as we learn the latest on this amazing research project and what the future holds to help those affected by kidney disease.
After registering, you will receive a confirmation email containing information about joining the webinar.
Webinar: The Future of Transplantation: Implantable Artificial Kidney Research

instruction: What are the potential benefits and challenges of developing an implantable artificial kidney, and how might this technology impact the lives of patients with kidney disease?
response: Developing an implantable artificial kidney presents a range of potential benefits and challenges that could transform the lives of patients with kidney disease. **Benefits:** One of the most significant advantages is the potential to provide a more natural and continuous form of kidney function, which could greatly enhance patients' quality of life. Unlike dialysis, which is a periodic and often uncomfortable process, an implantable artificial kidney could offer continuous filtration and waste removal, reducing the physical and emotional toll of chronic kidney disease. This technology could also alleviate the strain on the healthcare system by reducing the need for frequent medical visits and hospitalizations. Furthermore, it could address the critical shortage of donor kidneys, which is a major barrier to kidney transplants. **Challenges:** However, the development of this technology is not without its hurdles. One of the primary challenges is ensuring that the device is biocompatible and can integrate seamlessly with the body's systems to prevent rejection and infection. Another challenge is miniaturizing the technology to a size that can be safely implanted while maintaining its functionality. Long-term reliability and durability are also critical, as the device must function effectively over an extended period. Additionally, the regulatory process for approving new medical devices is rigorous and can be time-consuming, which could delay the availability of the technology. Finally, the high costs associated with research, development, and production pose a significant barrier to widespread adoption. Despite these challenges, the potential benefits of an implantable artificial kidney make it a highly promising area of medical innovation.

Limitations of previous methods
Podocytes are key cellular components of the glomerular filtration barrier in the kidney1. However, they are terminally differentiated and thus incapable of completing successful cell division under normal conditions. As a result, podocyte depletion (reduction in total number per glomerulus or density per glomerulus), is a significant indicator of the development of progressive kidney disease2. Podocyte depletion has, in fact, become a unifying principle of glomerular disease, and to date is routinely assessed by counting podocyte nuclei per glomerular cross-section in histological sections3. Recent studies have, highlighted the limitations of this approach, which include low levels of accuracy and precision, and a high degree of biological variability (particularly in studies in mice).
Stereological methods, both “model-based” and “design-based” (unbiased) methods, produce estimates of podocyte number determined from sampled sections. Model-based methods require knowledge or assumptions of podocyte nuclear size and shape. Generally, these values are assumed, and to the extent these assumptions differ from true values, the estimates obtained are biased. Design-based stereological methods used to estimate podocyte number are extremely time-consuming and have not been adopted by more than a handful of laboratories. Alternative methods for podocyte number estimation using serial histological sections4 (“exhaustive enumeration”) are extremely tedious and laborious.
The combination of tissue clearing and optical sectioning enable new approaches
Fortunately, the advent of new tissue clearing techniques5 in combination with optical sectioning, achievable through confocal, multiphoton or lightsheet microscopy, now make exhaustive enumeration not only attractive but a significant improvement for podocyte quantification, and any other cell of interest, especially those that play central roles in the development and progression of disease.
We have adopted this approach, and developed a novel, time-efficient method to study podocyte depletion using a combination of immunofluorescence, optical clearing, confocal microscopy and 3D analysis6. The technique has been used to quantify features of podocyte depletion in transgenic mice expressing the human diphtheria toxin (DT) receptor constitutively in podocytes, which allows conditional and dose-dependent podocyte death.
Our quantitative morphological tool significantly improves the assessment of podocyte depletion, and allows the study of whole glomeruli across the renal cortex. Differences in podocyte depletion between glomeruli in individual kidneys can be detected, a significant advance in the study of focal glomerular diseases.
Development of a novel method for imaging and quantifying podocyte depletion
Formalin-fixed kidneys are sliced to 800µm thickness, and the slices then subjected to 1hr antigen retrieval using a modified immunofluorescence protocol. Optical clearing is achieved by embedding the slices in agarose which are then dehydrated through changes in methanol, and cleared by several changes of benzyl alcohol, benzyl benzoate (BABB).
By gluing the edges of the dehydrated agarose to a glass petri dish, we immobilise the thick kidney slices on the bottom of the dish, making the specimens amenable to imaging on an upright Leica TCS SP8 MP confocal/multiphoton microscope equipped with the specialised Leica 20x/0.95 NA BABB immersion objective. The BABB mixture used has a refractive index of 1.56, which also permits higher resolution imaging using x40 and x63 oil objectives to be carried out on an inverted microscope when required.
For podocyte enumeration, 800µm thick kidney slices were imaged with stage-tiling in order to access the full cross-section of the kidney. This facilitated systematic imaging across the renal cortex from superficial to juxtamedullary regions to produce unbiased results. Slices up to 2mm thick (which represents the full working distance of this objective) were also imaged, but in general the use of 800µm sections, imaged across 2-3 channels at 1µm intervals provided ideal resolution, working depth and overall imaging time.
The final datasets provided quantifiable podocyte microstructure for analysis, as well as full 3D glomerular visualisation. Using markers for all nuclei (DAPI), podocyte cytoplasm (synaptopodin, SNP) and podocyte nuclei (p57), and the masking and counting features in Imaris (Bitplane AG, Zürich, Switzerland) it was possible to determine for each glomerulus analysed: (i) total podocyte number (ii) mean podocyte volume, (iii) individual glomerulus volume; and from those data calculate (iv) podocyte density (number per volume of glomerulus); (v) mean podocyte nuclear volume; and (vi) mean podocyte cytoplasmic volume.
While the image analysis component was not fully automated and required manual supervision, counting and analysis was significantly better and faster than all other methods thus far. Once confocal images were obtained, values for the above parameters were obtained in approximately 5mins per glomerulus.
Discussion and outlook
Advances in specimen preparation techniques and innovations in imaging continue to push the boundaries of discovery in the life sciences. Our understanding of tissue microstructure and cell and developmental biology has advanced significantly through innovative labelling approaches such as perfusion labelling, improvements in specificity and photostability of fluorescent labels, and tissue clearing techniques.
We now have unprecedented ability to study whole organisms, whole organs and tissues at the cellular and subcellular level. These techniques are applicable to fluorescence widefield, lightsheet and confocal microscopy modalities, all of which are supported by a wide range of high NA, long working distance objectives that match the refractive indices of BABB, Clarity and glycerol.
Moreover, image analysis can be used to efficiently measure number, length, surface area and volume of features of interest. A current challenge arising for many, however, is the handling, analysis and visualisation of these subsequently larger datasets which have now rapidly grown from GB to TB sizes. It is becoming increasingly important to develop better solutions for the rapidly developing discipline of bioimage informatics.

instruction: What are the main limitations of traditional methods used to estimate podocyte number, and how do these limitations affect the accuracy and precision of the results?
response: The traditional methods used to estimate podocyte number, such as counting nuclei in histological sections, suffer from significant limitations that impact the accuracy and precision of the results. One major limitation is the low accuracy and precision, often compounded by high biological variability, especially in studies involving mice. Stereological methods, which are used to estimate podocyte number from sampled sections, can introduce bias if assumptions about podocyte nuclear size and shape are inaccurate. Model-based methods, which rely on these assumptions, can produce biased estimates. Design-based stereological methods, while theoretically unbiased, are extremely time-consuming and have not been widely adopted due to their complexity. Exhaustive enumeration using serial histological sections, while providing more detailed data, is highly labor-intensive and impractical for large-scale studies. These limitations highlight the need for more efficient and accurate methods, such as the combination of tissue clearing and optical sectioning techniques, which can provide unbiased and comprehensive podocyte quantification.

The saying goes that only by knowing oneself and the enemy can one be invincible in a hundred battles. Only by understanding the killers that threaten male health can one be able to fight against them. In order to have a good kidney, male friends should pay attention to relevant precautions.
The bad habit of causing men's kidneys to mourn
1. Drinking too little water
If one does not drink water for a long time, urine output will decrease, and the concentration of waste and toxins carried in urine will increase. Common kidney stones and hydronephrosis in clinical practice are closely related to prolonged periods of non drinking water.
2. Eating too soft bread
There is a food additive called potassium bromate in bread and pastries, which tastes soft when eaten, but excessive consumption can damage the central nervous system, blood, and kidneys.
3. Eating too salty
A salty diet can lead to an increase in blood pressure and the inability to maintain normal blood flow in the kidneys, leading to kidney disease.
4. Abuse of analgesics
Long term or high-dose use of some anti-inflammatory and analgesic drugs, such as painkillers, indomethacin, paracetamol, aspirin, etc., can easily cause kidney damage.
5. Excessive drinking of beverages
Excessive intake of soft drinks and sports drinks can indirectly damage the kidneys. The pH in the human body is 7.2, and these beverages are generally highly acidic. After drinking, the pH in the body changes significantly.
6. Drinking strong tea after drinking
Some people believe that drinking strong tea after drinking alcohol can alleviate alcoholism, but in fact, it is not only ineffective, but also harmful to the kidneys. Experts say that theophylline in tea can quickly affect the kidneys and exert diuretic effects. At this time, alcohol is excreted from the kidneys before it can be further decomposed, causing the kidneys to be stimulated by a large amount of ethanol, thereby damaging kidney function.
instruction: How can understanding the factors that threaten male health help in taking proactive steps to prevent kidney disease, and what precautions can be taken to maintain good kidney function?
response: To effectively prevent kidney disease, it is essential to understand the factors that pose a threat to male health. One of the primary factors is insufficient water intake, which can lead to a reduction in urine output and an increase in the concentration of waste and toxins, potentially causing kidney stones and hydronephrosis. Another factor is the consumption of soft bread containing potassium bromate, which can damage the kidneys along with other systems. To maintain optimal kidney function, men should prioritize adequate hydration, limit the intake of soft bread and salty foods, use analgesics judiciously, reduce the consumption of acidic beverages, and avoid strong tea after drinking alcohol.

The word- diet usually means a specific restricted meal program that facilitates losing weight in a certain period. But some diets are not only for weight loss but for some diseased conditions also. Some diet plans are specially to manage the symptoms of a particular illness. The low oxalate diet (LOD) plan is a basic plan your doctor will advise many times. But do you know what it exactly means?
What are oxalates?
Oxalates are also known as oxalic acid, is a chemical compound naturally found in our body. They are present in a variety of plant foods like green leafy vegetables, fruits, nuts, and seeds. They are present in low quantities in dairy food, meat, and poultry food.
What does our body do to the oxalates?
Oxalates are not so essential for our body, so it binds to the other waste products in food and makes their way to the kidneys to excrete it out. Oxalates often bind to minerals such as calcium and are excreted out of the body through urine and stool.
However, when we consume excessive oxalates, our body fails to flush it through urine, especially if you are not drinking enough fluids. As oxalates increases in the body, they can bind to calcium and block the absorption of minerals, form crystals and eventually kidney stone.
Hence to avoid these consequences, your doctor often advice you to have a low oxalate diet. But what does it mean?
What is a low oxalate diet?
A low oxalate diet refers to a diet from which the amount of oxalate does not exceed 50 grams per day. If you plan your diet properly, then you can do it. In addition to limiting your oxalate intake, staying well-hydrated, moderating your protein intake, and increasing calcium consumption are other essential aspects of a low-oxalate diet. Typically, doctors recommended, to follow the diet for at least 3–6 weeks to see if your symptoms improve.
Which are low oxalate foods?
There are plenty of low oxalate foods that are available easily and can enjoy as a part of a healthy diet. Here are some top low oxalate food that you can add to your diet –
- Dairy products – Milk, cheese, yogurt, butter, and buttermilk
- Fruits – avocado, banana, cherries, mango, papaya, passion fruit, grapes, and melons
- Vegetables – cauliflower, cabbages, radish, mushrooms, cucumber, and peas
- Grains – white rice, barley, oat bran, and corn bran
- Herbs and spices – rosemary, basil, turmeric, cumin, and ginger
- Beverages – water, herbal tea, apple cider vinegar, and wine
- Poultry food – eggs and chicken
- Meat products (Avoid processed meat)
What are the benefits of a low oxalic diet?
When oxalate concentration increase in your body, calcium oxalate stone will develop in your kidney. Various research suggests that almost 75% of kidney stones developed from calcium oxalate. A better pathway to excrete oxalate is from the stool as it will not bind to calcium and prevent the formation of kidney stones.
2: Reduce the risk of cystic fibrosis complication
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a hereditary lung and digestive disorder where the body produces thick and sticky mucus that can clog the lungs and obstruct the pancreas. Though cystic fibrosis is untreatable and unavoidable, we can lower the risk of complications.
In cystic fibrosis patients, doctors always recommend consuming low oxalate foods because to avoid further complications named-hyperoxaluria. The research found that 51% of cystic fibrosis patients had hyperoxaluria, and this is a dangerous risk factor for kidney stones.
3: Prevent underactive thyroid problems
When the body contains excess oxalate, it will store in various tissues and thyroid. This excess oxalate binds to a hormone released from the thyroid – T3 leads to formations of crystals in the thyroid. This crystal reduces the activity of the thyroid gland, leads to the development of various symptoms such as weight gain, fatigue, high cholesterol level, menstrual problems, etc. Hence, it always better to consume oxalate-containing food within a limit.
4: Helpful for autism patients
Researchers have suggested that individuals with autism may be predisposed to oxalate intolerance. Although the metabolic pathways are unclear, individuals with autistic tendencies have seen an improvement in their symptoms when consuming a low oxalate diet.
Tips to follow a low oxalic diet
1: Moderate consumption of high-oxalate diet
Minimizing high-oxalate food from your diet could potentially help to prevent kidney stones. Research suggests that increasing your intake of calcium could boost oxalate excretion and may be more effective against kidney stones. Here are some sample oxalate-calcium combos to try-
- Berries with yogurt
- Broccoli with feta cheese
- Quinoa and chia seeds with milk (to make overnight breakfast quinoa)
2: Enjoy low oxalate foods
Various low oxalate foods help to lower your oxalate levels to enjoy it. In a low oxalate diet, you can include avocado, cauliflower, herbal tea, dairy products, chicken, and meat.
3: Consume calcium-rich foods
Oxalate and calcium bind together to prevent the formation of kidney stones. Therefore it’s recommended to pair your oxalate diet with high-calcium-containing foods like yogurt and cheese.
4: Drink plenty of water
Water helps to flush many toxic substances from your body through your kidney and helps to prevent the formation of kidney stones. It is advisable to drink at least eight 8-ounce glasses of water or fluids per day.
5: Avoid excessive sodium in diet
Sodium causes the body to hold on to water, which counteracts the oxalate-flushing benefits of healthy hydration.
6: Cut down excess vitamin C supplementation
When you consume vitamin C, it breaks down into your body and forms oxalates. If you are taking an excessive amount of vitamin C, then oxalate may get accumulated in your body and will produce various health issues.

instruction: What are the primary benefits of following a low oxalate diet, and how does it help in preventing kidney stones?
response: Following a low oxalate diet (LOD) offers several primary benefits, with one of the most significant being the prevention of kidney stones. Oxalates are naturally occurring compounds found in many plant-based foods. When oxalate levels in the body are high, they can bind to calcium and form calcium oxalate stones in the kidneys. By reducing oxalate intake, the body can better manage and excrete oxalates, primarily through stool rather than urine, thereby lowering the risk of kidney stone formation. This diet is particularly beneficial for individuals who have a history of calcium oxalate kidney stones. Additionally, a low oxalate diet can help reduce the risk of complications in cystic fibrosis patients, prevent underactive thyroid issues, and improve symptoms in individuals with autism. To effectively follow this diet, it is important to limit high-oxalate foods, increase the intake of low-oxalate foods such as dairy products, certain fruits and vegetables, and grains, ensure adequate hydration, consume calcium-rich foods, and avoid excessive sodium and vitamin C supplementation.

What is amiloride (Midamor)?
Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic (water pill) that prevents your body from absorbing too much salt and keeps your potassium levels from getting too low.
Amiloride is used to treat or prevent hypokalemia (low potassium levels in the blood).
Amiloride may also be used for other purposes not listed in this medication guide.

What are the possible side effects of amiloride (Midamor)?
Get emergency medical help if you have any of these signs of an allergic reaction: hives; difficulty breathing; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat.
Stop using this medication and call your doctor at once if you have any of these serious side effects:
- numbness or tingly feeling;
- muscle pain or weakness;
- slow, fast, or uneven heartbeat;
- feeling drowsy, restless, or light-headed;
- urinating less than usual or not at all;
- dry mouth, increased thirst, tiredness, nausea, vomiting;
- shallow breathing;
- tremors, confusion; or
- nausea, stomach pain, low fever, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools, jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes).
Less serious side effects may include:
- mild nausea, loss of appetite;
- gas, stomach pain; or
- skin rash.
This is not a complete list of side effects and others may occur. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088.
Read the Midamor (amiloride) Side Effects Center for a complete guide to possible side effects
What is the most important information I should know about amiloride (Midamor)?
Do not use this medication if you have kidney disease, urination problems, or high levels of potassium in your blood. Do not use potassium supplements or other diuretics while you are taking amiloride.
Before using this medication, tell your doctor if you have heart or liver disease, or a breathing disorder.
Avoid drinking alcohol, which can increase some of the side effects of amiloride.
Avoid a diet high in salt. Too much salt will cause your body to retain water and can make this medication less effective.
Do not use salt substitutes or low-sodium milk products that contain potassium. These products could cause your potassium levels to get too high while you are taking amiloride.
Avoid becoming overheated or dehydrated during exercise and in hot weather. Follow your doctor's instructions about the type and amount of liquids you should drink. In some cases, drinking too much liquid can be as unsafe as not drinking enough.

instruction: How does amiloride (Midamor) work in the body, and what is its primary purpose in medical treatment?
response: Amiloride, marketed under the brand name Midamor, functions as a potassium-sparing diuretic. This means that while it helps the body excrete excess fluids, it also prevents the loss of potassium, which is a common side effect of other diuretics. Amiloride achieves this by blocking the reabsorption of sodium in the distal tubules of the kidneys, which in turn reduces water retention. Its primary medical use is to treat or prevent hypokalemia, a condition where potassium levels in the blood are abnormally low. By maintaining adequate potassium levels, amiloride can help prevent complications such as muscle weakness, irregular heartbeats, and other issues related to electrolyte imbalance.

instruction: How do evidence-based guidelines and surveillance systems like the NHSN contribute to the prevention of infections among hemodialysis patients, and what are the primary threats to their safety?
response: The prevention of infections among hemodialysis patients is significantly enhanced through the use of evidence-based guidelines and surveillance systems like the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN). The CDC provides comprehensive guidelines that cover various aspects of infection control, including hand hygiene, sterile techniques, and the management of vascular access. These guidelines are grounded in scientific evidence and best practices, ensuring that dialysis facilities have the most up-to-date information to protect their patients. The NHSN serves as a critical tool for facilities to track and report infections, allowing them to identify and address issues promptly. By monitoring infection rates and evaluating the effectiveness of prevention strategies, facilities can implement targeted interventions to reduce the incidence of infections. The primary threats to patient safety in hemodialysis settings include bloodstream infections, vascular access infections, and other complications such as sepsis and antimicrobial resistance. These threats can be mitigated through the consistent application of CDC guidelines and the active use of the NHSN for surveillance and quality improvement.

instruction: What are the potential benefits and risks of using ACE inhibitors for managing early stages of kidney disease in individuals with diabetes?
response: Using ACE inhibitors for managing early stages of kidney disease in individuals with diabetes can offer several benefits. One key benefit is the reduction in proteinuria, as evidenced by the case mentioned where an individual's microalbumin levels dropped from 499 to 89 after starting ACE inhibitor therapy. This reduction can help slow the progression of kidney disease. Additionally, ACE inhibitors can help manage blood pressure, which is often elevated in individuals with diabetes and can exacerbate kidney damage. However, there are potential risks to consider. One risk is the possibility of hypotension, or excessively low blood pressure, which can occur as a side effect of these medications. Another critical risk is the potential harm to fetal kidney development if the individual is pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as ACE inhibitors can cause developmental issues in the fetus. Therefore, it is important to weigh these benefits and risks carefully and to regularly monitor kidney function and blood pressure when using ACE inhibitors.

instruction: What are the key differences between simple and complex kidney cysts, and how do these differences affect their medical management?
response: The key differences between simple and complex kidney cysts lie in their composition, potential for malignancy, and the subsequent medical management required. Simple kidney cysts are typically benign and contain only fluid. They are generally asymptomatic and do not pose a risk of becoming cancerous. Therefore, simple cysts often require no specific treatment and can be monitored with regular imaging if they are causing symptoms or are large in size. In contrast, complex kidney cysts can have solid components or irregular walls, which may harbor cancer cells. This increases the risk of malignancy, necessitating more vigilant monitoring and potentially invasive interventions such as biopsy, surgical removal, or further imaging studies. The primary goal in managing complex cysts is to rule out or treat any potential cancer, ensuring early detection and intervention if necessary.

instruction: What are the potential limitations and considerations healthcare professionals should keep in mind when using risk tools and clinical equations, such as the one for estimating GFR, in their practice?
response: When using risk tools and clinical equations like the GFR estimation formula, healthcare professionals must consider several limitations and potential issues. One key limitation is that these tools are based on population-level data and may not accurately reflect individual patient characteristics. For example, the MDRD equation for estimating GFR, which is widely used, may not be precise for patients with conditions that affect creatinine production or excretion, such as muscle wasting or kidney disease. Another important consideration is the potential for bias in the data used to develop these equations, which can lead to underestimation or overestimation of GFR in certain populations, such as older adults or individuals of different racial backgrounds. Additionally, these tools should be used in conjunction with clinical judgment, as they do not replace the need for a thorough patient evaluation. Healthcare professionals should integrate the results from these tools with their own clinical expertise, considering the patient's symptoms, medical history, and other relevant factors. It is also crucial to recognize that these tools are intended for use by trained healthcare professionals and should not be used by patients for self-assessment. The results should be interpreted within the broader context of the patient's health status and care plan, and any decisions should be made in collaboration with the patient and other healthcare providers as necessary.

instruction: What are the primary factors that contribute to the increased bleeding risk in patients with chronic kidney disease who are also at high cardiovascular risk?
response: In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) who are also at high cardiovascular risk, several primary factors contribute to the increased bleeding risk. According to the study by Ocak et al. (2018), these factors include: 1) **Impaired Platelet Function**: CKD can lead to platelet dysfunction, reducing the ability of platelets to adhere and aggregate, which is crucial for hemostasis. 2) **Altered Coagulation Factors**: CKD often results in an imbalance of coagulation factors, such as reduced levels of factors II, V, VII, and X, which can impair the coagulation cascade. 3) **Medication Use**: Patients with CKD and high cardiovascular risk are often on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapies, which further increase the risk of bleeding. 4) **Uremic Toxins**: Accumulation of uremic toxins in the blood can interfere with normal hemostatic processes, exacerbating bleeding tendencies. 5) **Inflammation**: Chronic inflammation associated with CKD can also contribute to increased bleeding risk by affecting vascular integrity and coagulation pathways.

instruction: What are the potential causes and symptoms of elevated pus cells and RBCs in a urine test, and what steps should be taken to address this condition?
response: Elevated pus cells and RBCs in a urine test can indicate several potential causes, including urinary tract infections (UTIs), kidney infections, kidney stones, or other inflammatory conditions. To address this condition, it is essential to visit a healthcare provider for a proper diagnosis. The doctor may prescribe antibiotics if an infection is confirmed. House Call: Hypertension and your kidneys Pt. 1
BRIDGEPORT, W.Va (WDTV) - Welcome back to UHC’s House Call on WDTV. In the first part of our three part series, Hypertension and Kidney Disease, Dr. Lewis Akers, Nephrologist at UHC Nephrology, joins us to talk about hypertension and how it can affect your kidneys.
1). How does high blood pressure affect the kidneys?
High blood pressure can constrict and narrow the blood vessels, which eventually damages and weakens the vessels throughout the body, including in the kidneys. The narrowing reduces blood flow.
If your kidneys’ blood vessels are damaged, they may no longer work properly. When this happens, the kidneys are not able to remove all wastes and extra fluid from your body. Extra fluid in the blood vessels can raise your blood pressure even more, creating a dangerous cycle, and cause more damage leading to kidney failure.
2). How common are high blood pressure and kidney disease?
Almost 1 in 2 U.S. adults—or about 108 million people—have high blood pressure.
More than 1 in 7 U.S. adults—or about 37 million people—may have chronic kidney disease (CKD).
High blood pressure is the second leading cause of kidney failure in the United States after diabetes.
3). Who is more likely to have high blood pressure or kidney disease?
High blood pressure
- You are more likely to have high blood pressure if you:
- are older. Blood pressures tends to increase with age. Our blood vessels naturally thicken and stiffen over time.
- have family members with high blood pressure. High blood pressure tends to run in families.
- have unhealthy lifestyle habits. Unhealthy habits such as eating too much sodium (salt), drinking too many alcoholic beverages, or not being physically active can increase your risk of high blood pressure.
- are African American. High blood pressure is more common in African American adults than in Caucasian, Hispanic, or Asian adults.
- are male. Men are more likely to develop high blood pressure before age 55; women are more likely to develop it after age 55.
- In addition to high blood pressure, other factors that increase your risk of kidney disease are:
- a family history of kidney failure
- race or ethnicity—African Americans, Hispanics, and American Indians tend to have a greater risk for CKD
High blood pressure can be both a cause and a result of kidney disease.

instruction: How does the cycle of high blood pressure and kidney damage contribute to the progression of kidney disease?
response: High blood pressure and kidney damage contribute to the progression of kidney disease through a dangerous cycle. High blood pressure constricts and narrows the blood vessels, including those in the kidneys. This narrowing reduces blood flow and damages the blood vessels, leading to impaired kidney function. When the kidneys are damaged, they cannot effectively remove wastes and extra fluid from the body. The accumulation of extra fluid in the blood vessels further raises blood pressure, which in turn causes more damage to the kidneys. This cycle can continue, leading to a progressive decline in kidney function and eventually kidney failure.

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a long-term condition where the kidneys don't work as well as they should.
It's a common condition often associated with getting older. It can affect anyone, but it's more common in people who are black or of south Asian origin.
CKD can get worse over time and eventually the kidneys may stop working altogether, but this is uncommon. Many people with CKD are able to live long lives with the condition.

How to keep your Kidneys Safe
What is Acute Kidney Injury?
Acute is a term used to describe something that has occurred over hours or
days (as opposed to chronic which means months or years).
Kidney Injury describes evidence of damage to the kidneys usually with a
change in kidney function tests and passing only small amounts of urine.
What are the symptoms?
In the early stages, there may not be any, but symptoms may be related to the illness which causes the AKI, such as diarrhoea and vomiting, low blood pressure with light headedness and passing only small volumes of urine.
It’s very important that AKI is detected early and treated promptly as in some cases it can be very serious. In the large majority of cases early detection and treatment will result in resolution of the AKI.
Kidney function is usually assessed by testing the blood for waste products This includes creatinine which comes from our muscles and can build up if the kidneys are not functioning well. The hospital laboratory is then able to provide an estimate of the efficiency of the kidneys. It is also important to test the urine to look for evidence of kidney damage or inflammation.
Who is at risk of Acute Kidney Injury?
We are all at risk of Acute Kidney Injury. It is very common when people become seriously unwell, and affects 1 in 5 people admitted as an emergency to hospital.
The kidneys require an adequate blood pressure to function.
If blood pressure drops a lot then cells in the kidneys are damaged and they may not function properly again, even when blood pressure returns to normal.
Some people are more at risk than others, for example those people who already have abnormal kidney structure or function. This may be related to other long term conditions such as diabetes or high blood pressure. If there is evidence of abnormal kidney function which lasts for more than 3 months then this is called Chronic Kidney Disease.
instruction: What are the primary risk factors for developing Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD), and how does the prevalence of CKD vary among different demographic groups?
response: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a long-term condition characterized by reduced kidney function. The primary risk factors for developing CKD include advanced age, as the condition is more common in older individuals. People of black or South Asian origin are also at a higher risk, with higher prevalence rates observed in these demographic groups. Other significant risk factors include diabetes and hypertension, which can damage the kidneys over time. The prevalence of CKD can vary significantly among different demographic groups, with black and South Asian populations being more affected, potentially due to genetic predispositions, lifestyle factors, and access to healthcare.

instruction: How do recurring kidney stones impact a person's quality of life, and what psychological or emotional support systems can help manage the stress and discomfort associated with frequent stone passages?
response: The recurrent experience of kidney stones can have a profound impact on a person's quality of life. The physical pain and discomfort are often described as excruciating and can lead to frequent hospital visits, missed work, and a general sense of unease. Emotionally, the unpredictability of when the next stone will form can create chronic anxiety and stress, affecting mental health and overall well-being. To cope with these challenges, it is essential to build a robust support system. Psychological support, such as counseling or therapy, can be invaluable in helping individuals manage the emotional toll. Support groups, either locally or online, can provide a network of individuals who understand the experience and can offer practical advice and emotional support. Lifestyle changes, including increasing fluid intake, maintaining a balanced diet low in sodium and high in fiber, and engaging in regular physical activity, can also help reduce the frequency of stone formation. Additionally, staying informed about the latest treatments and prevention strategies can empower individuals to take control of their health and reduce the burden of recurring kidney stones.

Patients with nephrolithiasis and blood hypertension have higher calciuria than those with isolated nephrolithiasis or hypertension?
Schleicher M. M. 1, Reis M. C. 2, Costa S. S. 2, Palmeira Rodrigues M. 3, Casulari L. A. 3
1 Department of Nephrology, Medical School (ESCS) Federal District General Hospital Brasilia, DF, Brazil

Aim. The aim of this study was to determine urinary excretion of calcium, uric acid and sodium and to evaluate insulin resistance in patients with nephrolithiasis and blood hypertension, isolated and in association, and in healthy controls, in absence of obesity and diabetes.
Methods. The study included 83 non-obese or diabetic patients: 17 with nephrolithiasis and hypertension (group D); 25 with nephrolithiasis (group C); 17 with hypertension (group B) and 24 healthy controls (group A). Urinary analysis was done in 24-hour urine collection and insulin resistance was evaluated through the HOMA-IR index.
Results. Calciuria was higher in group D in relation to groups A (P<0.01), B (P<0.01) and C (P=0.01). There was no significant difference between groups A and B (P=0.32), A and C (P=0.10) and B and C (P=0.68). Correlation analysis between urinary calcium detected strong correlation with uric acid in group A, regular in groups B and C and, strong with sodium in groups B and C. No differences were detected in uric acid and sodium excretion or insulin resistance among groups.
Conclusion. Patients with blood hypertension and nephrolithiasis present higher calciuria than healthy people, with hypertension or with lithiasis and do not have the positive correlation observed in these latter groups with renal excretion of uric acid and sodium. These results suggest that impaired renal calcium reabsorption in non-obese or diabetic individuals is involved in the association between hypertension and urolithiasis.
instruction: What factors might contribute to higher calciuria in patients with both nephrolithiasis and hypertension compared to those with only one of these conditions or healthy individuals?
response: Higher calciuria in patients with both nephrolithiasis and hypertension compared to those with only one of these conditions or healthy individuals can be attributed to several physiological and metabolic factors. The study by Schleicher et al. found that patients with both conditions (group D) had significantly higher calciuria compared to healthy controls (group A), isolated hypertension (group B), and isolated nephrolithiasis (group C). This finding suggests that the combination of hypertension and nephrolithiasis may exacerbate the renal handling of calcium, leading to increased urinary calcium excretion. One key factor is impaired renal calcium reabsorption, which is more pronounced in patients with both conditions. This impaired reabsorption can be due to alterations in the renal tubules that affect the reabsorption of calcium, possibly influenced by the pathophysiology of both hypertension and nephrolithiasis. Furthermore, the study noted that the correlation between urinary calcium and uric acid or sodium was different in group D compared to the other groups, indicating that the renal mechanisms for calcium excretion are distinct in these patients. This suggests that the interplay between hypertension and nephrolithiasis may disrupt normal renal function, leading to higher calciuria.

instruction: What are the key components of effective clinical pathways in dialysis care, and how can they be implemented to improve patient outcomes and quality of life?
response:
Clinical pathways in dialysis care are essential for standardizing and optimizing patient care. The key components of effective clinical pathways include:
1. **Blood Pressure Management**: Regular monitoring and adjustment of antihypertensive medications to control blood pressure, which is crucial for preventing cardiovascular events.
2. **Infection Prevention**: Implementing rigorous infection control protocols, such as hand hygiene, sterilization of equipment, and vaccination programs, to reduce the risk of infections.
3. **Anemia Treatment**: Regularly assessing hemoglobin levels and adjusting erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) and iron supplements to manage anemia effectively.
4. **Nutritional Support**: Providing personalized dietary plans and supplements to address malnutrition and maintain optimal nutritional status.
5. **Bone Health**: Monitoring and managing bone mineral metabolism, including calcium, phosphorus, and parathyroid hormone levels, to prevent bone disorders.
6. **Dialysis Adequacy**: Ensuring that dialysis treatments are adequate and effective by monitoring clearance of toxins and fluid balance.
To implement these pathways effectively:
- **Multidisciplinary Teams**: Assembling a team of nephrologists, nurses, dietitians, and social workers to provide comprehensive and coordinated care.
- **Patient Education and Engagement**: Educating patients about their condition, treatment options, and the importance of adherence to the care plan.
- **Continuous Quality Improvement**: Regularly reviewing patient outcomes and updating the pathways based on new evidence and feedback.
- **Technology Utilization**: Leveraging electronic health records (EHRs) and clinical decision support systems to standardize care and monitor adherence.
By focusing on these components and strategies, clinical pathways can enhance the quality of care, improve patient outcomes, and enhance the overall quality of life for dialysis patients.

instruction: What are the key components of a routine urine test and how do they contribute to diagnosing kidney diseases?
response: A routine urine test is an essential part of diagnosing kidney diseases, as it provides a comprehensive overview of various parameters that reflect kidney function. The key components of this test include urine color, transparency, pH, red and white blood cells, epithelial cells, casts, protein, specific gravity, and urine sugar qualitative. These components are crucial for several reasons. For instance, the presence of protein in the urine (proteinuria) is a significant indicator of kidney damage, particularly to the glomeruli. Red blood cells (hematuria) can point to inflammation or injury within the kidneys. The pH level of the urine helps assess the kidneys' ability to maintain acid-base balance, while specific gravity indicates the kidneys' capacity to concentrate urine. Additionally, the presence of casts, which are cylindrical structures formed in the kidney tubules, can provide insights into the type and extent of kidney damage. Urine transparency and color can also signal potential infections or other abnormalities. By analyzing these components, healthcare providers can detect early signs of kidney disease and tailor appropriate treatments.

instruction: What are the potential risks and benefits of hypervolemia in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis, and how can these be managed effectively?
response: Hypervolemia in peritoneal dialysis patients presents a complex interplay of risks and benefits that require careful management. **Risks** associated with hypervolemia include: 1. **Pulmonary Edema**: Fluid accumulation in the lungs can lead to respiratory distress and hypoxia. 2. **Congestive Heart Failure (CHF)**: Increased intravascular volume can overload the heart, potentially causing heart failure. 3. **Hypertension**: Excess fluid can elevate blood pressure, exacerbating cardiovascular conditions. 4. **Hemoconcentration**: This can increase blood viscosity and the risk of clotting. 5. **Renal Insufficiency**: Iatrogenic hypervolemia and increased renal vein pressure can lead to renal dysfunction. **Benefits** of hypervolemia include: 1. **Enhanced Tissue Perfusion**: Increased intravascular volume can improve blood flow to vital organs. 2. **Prevention of Vasospasm**: Hypervolemia can help prevent vasospasm, which is beneficial in certain clinical scenarios. 3. **Management of Hyponatremia**: Dilution of excess water in the plasma can help manage hyponatremia. **Effective Management** strategies include: 1. **Volume Management**: Regular body composition assessments and fluid balance monitoring to prevent overhydration. 2. **Treatment of Hypervolemia**: Use of diuretics, ultrafiltration, and adjustments to dialysis prescriptions to remove excess fluid. 3. **Glucose Sparing Strategies**: Reducing glucose exposure in dialysis solutions to minimize fluid retention and metabolic complications. 4. **Blood Pressure Monitoring**: Frequent monitoring to detect and manage hypertension early. 5. **Neurological Assessments**: Regular evaluations to detect signs of increased intracranial pressure or other complications. 6. **Induced Hypertension**: In specific cases, controlled induction of hypertension may be necessary. 7. **Automated Intravenous Routine**: Careful management of intravenous fluid administration to avoid hypervolemia and related complications. 8. **Educational Programs**: Educating patients and healthcare providers on the signs and symptoms of hypervolemia and the importance of adherence to fluid management plans.

Dialysis vascular access (DVA) care is being increasingly provided in freestanding office-based centers (FOC). Small-scale studies have suggested that DVA care in a FOC results in favorable patient outcomes and lower costs. To further evaluate this issue, data were drawn from incident and prevalent ESRD patients within a 4-year sample (2006-2009) of Medicare claims (USRDS) on cases who receive at least 80% of their DVA care in a FOC or a hospital outpatient department (HOPD). Using propensity score matching techniques, cases with a similar clinical and demographic profile from these two sites of service were matched. Medicare utilization, payments, and patient outcomes were compared across the matched cohorts (n = 27,613). Patients treated in the FOC had significantly better outcomes (p < 0.001), including fewer related or unrelated hospitalizations (3.8 vs. 4.4), vascular access-related infections (0.18 vs. 0.29), and septicemia-related hospitalizations (0.15 vs. 0.18). Mortality rate was lower (47.9% vs. 53.5%) as were PMPM payments ($4,982 vs. $5,566). This study shows that DVA management provided in a FOC has multiple advantages over that provided in a HOPD.

instruction: What are the potential benefits of providing dialysis vascular access care in freestanding office-based centers compared to hospital outpatient departments, and how do these benefits impact patient outcomes and costs?
response: The provision of dialysis vascular access (DVA) care in freestanding office-based centers (FOC) compared to hospital outpatient departments (HOPD) has been shown to offer significant advantages, both in terms of patient outcomes and cost-effectiveness. A study utilizing Medicare claims data from 2006-2009 demonstrated that patients receiving DVA care in FOCs had better clinical outcomes. Key findings included fewer hospitalizations (3.8 vs. 4.4), lower rates of vascular access-related infections (0.18 vs. 0.29), and fewer septicemia-related hospitalizations (0.15 vs. 0.18). The mortality rate was also lower in FOCs (47.9% vs. 53.5%). These improved outcomes can translate to better patient health and quality of life. Moreover, the cost analysis revealed that FOCs were more cost-effective, with lower PMPM payments ($4,982 vs. $5,566). These cost savings can be substantial, potentially reducing financial strain on patients and the healthcare system. Therefore, the benefits of providing DVA care in FOCs are multifaceted, enhancing patient care and economic efficiency.

instruction: How does the urinary system maintain homeostasis, and what are the specific functions of the kidneys in this process?
response: The urinary system, specifically the kidneys, maintains homeostasis through several key functions. First, the kidneys filter blood to remove metabolic wastes and excess substances, such as urea, uric acid, and excess salts, which are then excreted as urine. This filtration process helps to detoxify the blood and maintain a healthy internal environment. Second, the kidneys regulate the body's fluid balance by controlling the amount of water and electrolytes that are reabsorbed or excreted. This is crucial for maintaining blood volume and pressure. Third, the kidneys help to regulate the pH of the blood by excreting excess hydrogen ions and reabsorbing bicarbonate ions, which helps to maintain the proper acid-base balance. Finally, the kidneys play a role in the production of hormones such as erythropoietin, which stimulates the production of red blood cells, and renin, which helps to regulate blood pressure. These functions collectively ensure that the body's internal conditions remain stable and optimal for cellular activities.

The health benefits of celery start with the ABCs, as in the vitamins A, B, and C. The leaves are a good source of vitamin A. Celery stalks contain more than one B vitamin as well as vitamin C. Important minerals are also included in the health benefits of celery, such as amino acids, folic acid, potassium, and many more.
Another one of the important health benefits of celery is its ability to act as a natural diuretic. Fluids in the body need to be properly balanced and including celery in the diet can help. The fact that it is a good source of potassium adds to this benefit, as some diuretics deplete potassium. Many people also prefer incorporating something natural into their diet as opposed to taking medication. Nutritional fiber is an important part of the diet, and celery is a good source of fiber, which can help prevent constipation.
Speaking of diet, another health benefit of celery is that it also makes a healthy crunchy snack for those on a low fat diet. It is a staple for many when attempting to reduce fat intake for general purposes as well as to lose weight. The texture and the natural saltiness can help ease cravings for other crunchy, salty foods that may not be as healthy.
Celery may also help ease cravings for sugar. One of the health benefits of celery is that it is low on the glycemic index, which means the carbohydrates within it are broken down slowly, resulting in a slower release of sugar into the blood. This makes it a good choice for those who suffer from diabetes. This also makes celery beneficial for losing weight as spikes in blood sugar can hurt weight loss efforts.
Other health benefits of celery include the ability to aid in lowering both cholesterol and blood pressure. More health benefits of celery include properties that aid in kidney function and may also lessen the risk of kidney stones. It is also said to help fight cancer, possibly slow the expansion of tumors, and fight free radicals, which are known to harm cells throughout the body.
Celery also provides a great way to add flavor to food such as soups and salads. The health benefits of celery make it a great choice for seasoning favorite dishes. It is one vegetable that isn’t prone to losing so much of its nutritional value when cooked. It is often juiced and sold as a health food as well. It can be mixed with other juices to create flavorful combinations and can be included in smoothies to give them an extra healthy punch.
instruction: How can incorporating celery into one's diet help manage fluid balance and potentially reduce the need for diuretic medications?
response: Celery can be a beneficial addition to a diet aimed at managing fluid balance and potentially reducing the need for diuretic medications. As a natural diuretic, celery helps the body eliminate excess fluids through increased urine production, which can be particularly useful for individuals dealing with fluid retention. One of the key benefits of celery in this context is its high potassium content. Potassium is essential for maintaining proper fluid balance and can help counteract the potassium depletion often caused by diuretic medications. By incorporating celery into meals, individuals can support their body's natural processes for fluid regulation. Moreover, celery's low calorie and high fiber content make it a healthy snack option that can also aid in weight management and prevent constipation. This multi-faceted benefit makes celery a valuable addition to a health-conscious diet.

Ames, M. K., Vaden, S. L., Atkins, C. E., Palerme, J.-S., Langston, C. E., Grauer, G. F., … Webb, T. (2022, November 9). JOURNAL OF VETERINARY INTERNAL MEDICINE.
The influence of aldosterone breakthrough (ABT) on proteinuria reduction during renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibition for spontaneous proteinuric chronic kidney disease (CKDP ) has not been determined in dogs.Determine whether ABT occurs in dogs with CKDP and if it is associated with decreased efficacy in proteinuria reduction during RAS inhibitor treatment.Fifty-six client-owned dogs with CKDP and 31 healthy client-owned dogs.Prospective, multicenter, open-label clinical trial. Dogs were treated with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker alone or in combination at the attending clinician's discretion and evaluated at 5 time points over 6 months. Healthy dogs were used to determine the urine aldosterone-to-creatinine ratio cutoff that defined ABT. The relationship of ABT (present at ≥50% of visits) and proteinuria outcome (≥50% reduction in urine protein-to-creatinine ratio from baseline at ≥50% of subsequent visits) was evaluated. Mixed effects logistic regression was used to evaluate the relationship between clinical variables and outcomes (either successful proteinuria reduction or ABT).Thirty-six percent (20/56) of dogs had successful proteinuria reduction. Between 34% and 59% of dogs had ABT, depending on the definition used. Aldosterone breakthrough was not associated with proteinuria outcome. Longer duration in the study was associated with greater likelihood of successful proteinuria reduction (P = .002; odds ratio, 1.6; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.2-2.2).Aldosterone breakthrough was common in dogs receiving RAS inhibitors for CKDp but was not associated with proteinuria outcome.
instruction: What factors might influence the occurrence of aldosterone breakthrough in dogs with proteinuric chronic kidney disease, and how can these factors be managed to optimize treatment outcomes?
response: Aldosterone breakthrough (ABT) is a significant concern in the management of proteinuric chronic kidney disease (CKDP) in dogs, particularly when using renin-angiotensin system (RAS) inhibitors. The occurrence of ABT can be influenced by various factors, including the specific RAS inhibitor used, the duration of treatment, and the individual dog's physiological response to the medication. According to the study by Ames et al. (2022), ABT was observed in a substantial proportion of dogs (34% to 59%) but was not directly linked to a reduction in treatment efficacy for proteinuria. To optimize treatment outcomes and manage ABT, veterinarians can implement several strategies: (1) extending the duration of treatment, as the study found that a longer treatment period was associated with a higher likelihood of successful proteinuria reduction (P = .002; odds ratio, 1.6; 95% CI, 1.2-2.2); (2) regularly monitoring urine aldosterone-to-creatinine ratios to detect ABT early and adjust treatment accordingly; (3) considering the use of combination therapy with both angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) to enhance the blockade of the RAS; and (4) individualizing treatment plans based on the dog's specific needs and response to medication. Regular follow-up visits and comprehensive monitoring are essential to ensure the best possible outcomes for dogs with CKDP.

instruction: How do UREA + ELECTROLYTES SERUM TEST and ESTIMATED GLOMERULAR FILTRATION RATE TEST differ in assessing kidney function, and are they equally effective for this purpose?
response: The UREA + ELECTROLYTES SERUM TEST and the ESTIMATED GLOMERULAR FILTRATION RATE (eGFR) TEST are both used to assess kidney function, but they do so in different ways and provide different types of information. The UREA + ELECTROLYTES SERUM TEST measures the levels of urea and electrolytes (such as sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate) in the blood. Urea is a waste product of protein metabolism, and its levels can indicate how well the kidneys are filtering waste from the blood. Electrolytes are essential for various bodily functions, and their levels can also reflect kidney function. However, this test is not as specific or sensitive as the eGFR test for assessing kidney function. The eGFR test, on the other hand, estimates the glomerular filtration rate, which is a measure of how well the kidneys are filtering blood. It is calculated using a formula that takes into account serum creatinine levels, age, sex, and sometimes race. The eGFR test is more accurate and provides a more comprehensive assessment of kidney function. Therefore, while the UREA + ELECTROLYTES SERUM TEST can provide some information about kidney function, it is not as effective as the eGFR test for this purpose.

instruction: What are the potential benefits and drawbacks of using icodextrin in peritoneal dialysis solutions for patients with kidney disease?
response: The use of icodextrin in peritoneal dialysis solutions, such as Extraneal, offers several potential benefits for patients with kidney disease. One of the primary advantages is its ability to provide sustained ultrafiltration over a longer dwell time. This is particularly beneficial for patients who require more extended periods of fluid removal to manage fluid overload and hypertension. Additionally, icodextrin solutions are glucose-free, which can be advantageous for patients with diabetes, as they help minimize glucose absorption and maintain better glucose control. However, there are also potential drawbacks to consider. Icodextrin is more expensive than traditional glucose-based solutions, which can be a significant financial burden for patients and healthcare systems. Moreover, there is a risk of adverse reactions, such as allergic responses or peritonitis, although these are relatively rare. Patients may also experience metabolic changes, including elevated blood levels of maltose, which can interfere with some blood glucose monitoring systems, leading to inaccurate readings.

SAN FRANCISCO. (KFSN) -- Progress on a new artificial kidney has been so promising the FDA has fast-tracked its development. That's potentially life-saving news for the 100,000 people the National Kidney Foundation says are on a waiting list for a transplant right now. Only 20,000 kidneys will be available for them this year.
David Anderson has walked into a dialysis clinic 2,300 times since 1999. He comes four times a week for hours, while a machine does what his kidneys should: remove toxins from his blood.
"It's a very time-consuming experience and when my treatment today is finished, I'm going to be tired. Not a whole lot will get done tonight," detailed Anderson.
Shuvo Roy, a bioengineering professor at UC San Francisco, told Ivanhoe, "Over the course of the last few years, we've advanced the membrane technology, we've developed cell engineering, and currently, we are in animal testing."
Roy is developing an implantable bio artificial kidney.
It would go in the same place as a donor kidney. Anderson's doctor, Lynda Frassetto, M.D., a professor of Medicine at UC San Francisco, said the need is critical.
"This would allow us to build kidneys and then we could just put them in to people. Really, it would just be a totally astounding thing for us to be able to do that," said Dr. Frassetto.
"I would participate in trials or get an artificial kidney this evening if that were available," Anderson told Ivanhoe.
The government estimates kidney failure costs Medicare more than $30 billion a year and takes up eight to nine percent of its budget. Anderson's treatment alone is close to three and a half million. Professor Roy and Dr. Frassetto said any investment in artificial kidney technology will eventually save money and lives.
