Finerenone - oral
Finerenone - oral
Finerenone is used by people with type 2 diabetes and kidney disease to lower the risk of dialysis, death from heart disease, heart attacks, and the need to go to the hospital for heart failure. It works by blocking a chemical (aldosterone) in your body which in turn lowers the amount of sodium and water the body retains.
Take this medication by mouth with or without food as directed by your doctor, usually once daily.
To reduce your risk of side effects, your doctor may direct you to start this medication at a low dose and gradually increase your dose. Follow your doctor's instructions carefully.
If you are unable to swallow whole tablets, you may crush the tablet and mix it with water or soft foods (such as applesauce). Drink/eat the entire mixture right away. Do not prepare a supply for future use.
The dosage is based on your medical condition and response to treatment.
Use this medication regularly to get the most benefit from it. To help you remember, take it at the same time each day.
Do not increase your dose or use this drug more often or for longer than prescribed. Your condition will not improve any faster, and your risk of side effects will increase.
Avoid eating grapefruit or drinking grapefruit juice while using this medication unless your doctor or pharmacist says you may do so safely. Grapefruit can increase the chance of side effects with this medicine. Ask your doctor or pharmacist for more details.
Dizziness or lightheadedness may occur. If either of these effects lasts or gets worse, tell your doctor or pharmacist promptly.
Remember that this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has judged that the benefit to you is greater than the risk of side effects. Many people using this medication do not have serious side effects.
Tell your doctor right away if you have any serious side effects, including:
A very serious allergic reaction to this drug is rare. However, get medical help right away if you notice any symptoms of a serious allergic reaction, including:
This is not a complete list of possible side effects. If you notice other effects not listed above, contact your doctor or pharmacist.

Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to FDA at 1-800-FDA-1088 or at www.fda.gov/medwatch.
In Canada - Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You may report side effects to Health Canada at 1-866-234-2345.

This medication may increase your potassium levels. Before using potassium supplements or salt substitutes that contain potassium, consult your doctor or pharmacist.
This drug may make you dizzy. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can make you more dizzy. Do not drive, use machinery, or do anything that needs alertness until you can do it safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. Talk to your doctor if you are using marijuana (cannabis).
Before having surgery, tell your doctor or dentist about all the products you use (including prescription drugs, nonprescription drugs, and herbal products).
During pregnancy, this medication should be used only when clearly needed. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor.
It is unknown if this medication passes into breast milk. Because of the possible risk to the infant, breastfeeding is not recommended while using this medication and for 1 day after the last dose. Consult your doctor before breastfeeding.
See also How to Use and Precautions sections.
Drug interactions may change how your medications work or increase your risk for serious side effects. This document does not contain all possible drug interactions. Keep a list of all the products you use (including prescription/nonprescription drugs and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Do not start, stop, or change the dosage of any medicines without your doctor's approval.
Some of the products that may interact with this drug are:
Other medications can affect the removal of finerenone from your body, which may affect how finerenone works. Examples include adagrasib, certain azole antifungals (such as ketoconazole, voriconazole), ceritinib, clarithromycin, cobicistat, nefazodone, certain HIV protease inhibitors (such as nelfinavir, tipranavir), ritonavir, telithromycin, among others.
If someone has overdosed and has serious symptoms such as passing out or trouble breathing, call 911. Otherwise, call a poison control center right away. US residents can call their local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. Canada residents can call a provincial poison control center.
Do not share this medication with others.
Lab tests (such as potassium blood levels) should be done while you are taking this medication. Keep all medical and lab appointments. Consult your doctor for more details.
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose. Take your next dose at the regular time. Do not double the dose to catch up.
Store at room temperature away from light and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep all medications away from children and pets.

instruction: How does finerenone help reduce the risk of kidney disease complications in patients with type 2 diabetes, and what is the mechanism of action behind its effectiveness?
response: Finerenone is a non-steroidal selective mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) antagonist designed to help reduce the risk of kidney disease complications in patients with type 2 diabetes. The primary mechanism of action involves blocking the mineralocorticoid receptor, which is activated by the hormone aldosterone. When aldosterone binds to this receptor, it can lead to increased sodium and water retention, higher blood pressure, and inflammation and fibrosis in the kidneys. By inhibiting this receptor, finerenone helps to mitigate these adverse effects, thereby reducing the progression of kidney disease. This reduction in kidney damage can significantly lower the risk of severe complications such as the need for dialysis, cardiovascular events like heart attacks, and hospitalization for heart failure. Patients should take finerenone as directed by their healthcare provider, starting with a low dose and gradually increasing if necessary, to ensure optimal therapeutic outcomes and to minimize potential side effects.

instruction: What precautions should individuals with kidney or heart problems take when increasing their fluid intake, and why is it important to follow a doctor's advice in these cases?
response: When individuals with kidney or heart problems consider increasing their fluid intake, they must take several precautions. Kidney issues can impair the body's ability to filter and excrete excess fluids, potentially leading to electrolyte imbalances and fluid buildup. Heart problems, especially those involving congestive heart failure, can also be exacerbated by excess fluid, as the heart may struggle to pump the increased volume effectively. This can result in symptoms such as swelling, shortness of breath, and increased blood pressure. It is imperative to follow a doctor's advice, as they can provide tailored recommendations based on the individual's medical history and current health status. Doctors may advise maintaining a stable fluid intake or even reducing it to prevent complications. Always seek professional medical guidance before making any changes to your fluid intake to ensure it is safe and appropriate for your specific condition.

instruction: What are the primary symptoms of kidney stones, and how do they vary based on the size and location of the stone?
response: The primary symptoms of kidney stones include severe pain, frequent and painful urination, nausea and vomiting, and blood in the urine. The pain typically starts in the back, just below the ribs, and can radiate to the abdomen, groin, and even the genital area. The intensity of the pain depends on the size and location of the stone. Smaller stones may cause only mild discomfort or no symptoms at all, while larger stones can cause excruciating pain that comes in waves. The pain can be so intense that it feels like contractions during childbirth. Frequent and painful urination occurs as the body tries to expel the stone, and this symptom can also indicate a bladder infection if accompanied by a fever. Nausea and vomiting are common due to the stimulation of the Vagus nerve by the pain. Blood in the urine can result from the stone scratching the kidney or ureter, which is usually detected through a urinalysis. If you experience these symptoms, it is important to seek medical attention to confirm the diagnosis and receive appropriate treatment, which may include hydration, medication, or surgical intervention.

instruction: What are the primary markers that indicate a worsening of kidney disease, and what changes in treatment might be necessary if these markers are observed?
response: Key indicators of a worsening kidney disease are an increase in proteinuria (protein in the urine) and a rise in serum creatinine levels. These markers reflect declining kidney function. If these changes are noted, several adjustments in treatment may be necessary. For instance, stringent blood pressure control becomes crucial, as hypertension can exacerbate kidney damage. Additionally, it is important to avoid nephrotoxic substances such as pain killers and certain alternative medications. In some cases, a kidney biopsy may be recommended to diagnose specific conditions like IgA Nephropathy, which can guide more targeted treatment strategies. Your nephrologist will provide personalized advice and adjustments to your treatment plan based on these markers.

Kidney Health Outreach for Manitoba
Kidney Health Outreach provides education about kidney health to communities across Manitoba. We receive requests from communities, organizations or health-care providers to provide educational workshops about keeping kidneys healthy.
We generally present to adults including general community presentations, small group presentations or presentations for health-care workers.
Is Kidney Health Outreach available for health fairs?
The team is available to participate in local community health fairs. They will set up a booth and provide information and answer questions about kidney health to people of all ages.
How is the education provided?
The team does a presentation and engages with audiences to ask questions and talk about kidney health.
- Interactive quiz games
- Kidney displays
- Handouts such as posters and pamphlets
Who provides the education?
Kidney Health Outreach has a team of kidney health professionals who provide educational information about keeping your kidneys healthy. The team includes: a nurse, dietitian, exercise specialist, pharmacist and an aboriginal liaison social worker. Different members of the team deliver education based on the request and availability.
How long are the presentations?
The presentation can range from one hour to three hours depending on how much and the type of education that is being asked about.
Who do I call for more information?
For more information about workshops and availability for health fairs please call:
Request a Kidney Health Outreach Workshop
To plan and arrange for a workshop in your community, please contact us as much in advance as possible (ideally six to eight weeks). We try to accommodate as many requests as we can, although may not be able to honour every request.
instruction: Who comprises the team of Kidney Health Outreach, and what are the specific roles of each member in delivering educational workshops and health fairs?
response: The Kidney Health Outreach team in Manitoba is made up of a diverse group of kidney health professionals, including a nurse, dietitian, exercise specialist, pharmacist, and an aboriginal liaison social worker. Each member has a unique role in delivering educational workshops and health fairs. The nurse educates the audience on kidney anatomy, function, and medical management, while the dietitian provides insights into kidney-friendly diets and nutrition. The exercise specialist offers guidance on physical activities that promote kidney health, and the pharmacist discusses the safe use of medications and their effects on kidney function. The aboriginal liaison social worker ensures that the educational content is culturally appropriate and accessible to indigenous communities. During health fairs, the team sets up a booth to provide information, answer questions, and engage with attendees through interactive quiz games, kidney displays, and handouts such as posters and pamphlets.

instruction: What are the key factors that might influence a nephrologist's decision to affiliate with multiple hospitals, and how does this benefit patient care?
response: Several key factors might influence a nephrologist's decision to affiliate with multiple hospitals. One major factor is the opportunity to expand their patient base, as affiliating with multiple hospitals allows them to reach a larger number of patients. Another factor is the ability to access a wider range of resources and technologies, which can enhance the quality of care they provide. For example, different hospitals may have specialized equipment or treatment protocols that are not available at a single institution. Additionally, affiliating with multiple hospitals can provide professional networking opportunities and the potential for collaboration with other specialists, which can lead to improved patient outcomes. For patient care, this benefits by ensuring that patients receive the most comprehensive and specialized care possible, as nephrologists can leverage the strengths and resources of each hospital to address the unique needs of their patients.

instruction: What are the key nutritional components that make dog food suitable for managing kidney disease, and how do they benefit dogs with this condition?
response: The key nutritional components that make dog food suitable for managing kidney disease include reduced protein, low phosphorus, low sodium, and increased omega-3 fatty acids. These components benefit dogs with kidney disease in several ways. Reduced protein helps minimize the workload on the kidneys, as they have to process fewer waste products. Low phosphorus levels prevent the accumulation of phosphorus in the blood, which can lead to further kidney damage. Low sodium helps manage blood pressure and reduces the risk of hypertension, a common complication in dogs with kidney disease. Increased omega-3 fatty acids, such as those found in fish oil, can help reduce inflammation and improve overall kidney function. For example, Royal Canin Renal Support contains 14% protein, 0.2% phosphorus, and 0.35% sodium, which are tailored to support dogs with chronic renal insufficiency.

Rare Disease Spotlight: C3 Glomerulopathy
C3 glomerulopathy (C3G), a rare kidney disease, affects only two or three people out of every one million. That’s only a couple people out of the entire population of San Jose, California or Austin, Texas.
Although C3G only affects a select few, without treatment it can lead to severe kidney damage and failure, necessitating expensive dialysis or transplant. To date, there is no specific, effective therapy.
What is C3G?
C3 glomerulopathy is a relatively new classification. At a 2013 consensus meeting, scientists recommended that two rare diseases, dense deposit disease (DDD) and C3 glomerulonephritis (C3GN) be subgrouped under a new heading, C3G.
The two diseases that comprise C3G both involve a high presence of a protein called C3G in the renal glomeruli. The glomeruli are the filtering units of the kidney.
In patients with C3G, proteins in the blood get broken down in such a way that breakdown products get lodged in the kidney, setting off reactions that injure the glomeruli. Injured glomeruli can’t filter blood as well, which hampers urine production. As this continues, toxins build up and damage kidney tissue.
What are the symptoms of C3G?
Common symptoms of C3G include:
- Blood in the urine (hematuria)
- Excess protein in the urine (proteinuria), evidenced by dark, foamy urine
- Reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR; reduced ability of the kidney to filter the blood and make urine), elevated creatinine
- Swelling (edema) of hands, feet, and/or ankles
- High blood pressure
- Decreased urine output
How is C3G diagnosed?
Doctors may order a urine test to check for proteinuria and hematuria. A blood test can measure serum creatinine levels; unusually high levels may indicate kidney damage. A blood test can also reveal glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), which shows how well the kidneys filter waste from the body. C3G disease severity depends on low eGFR and high proteinuria.
The only way to diagnose C3G specifically, however, is with a kidney biopsy. Kidney deposits stain for the complement protein C3. When examined under an electron microscope, the doctor can see breakdown deposits indicative of C3G.
How is C3G treated?
While there is no treatment for C3G, certain steps can help slow the progression of kidney damage over time.
Blood pressure and cholesterol medication is a good start. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEI) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) both control blood pressure as well as reduce the amount of protein in urine.
Controlling high fat lipids (cholesterol) in your body helps reduce kidney damage as well as lower heart disease risk. Reducing sodium content and protein in the diet may also reduce stress on the kidneys.
Studies suggest that mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) can decrease the rate of kidney damage in patients with C3G. A study out of Oregon Health Science University in Portland, Oregon, found that MMF combined with corticosteroids induced remission in 67% of the 30-patient cohort.
Another study looked at the effect of MMF on Southeast Asians with C3G. After six months of therapy, 23% of the patients (4 out of 17) showed complete remission, or a return of serum creatinine levels to baseline. Seven patients (41%) achieved partial remission.
Eculizumab (Solaris®), a drug designed to treat rare blood disease, may be effective in slowing proteinuria and kidney disease progress, but it only works about 50% of the time according to nephrologist Paolo Cravedi, MD, a nephrologist for Mt. Sinai, commented in an article for Pharmaceutical Technology.
Biorasi currently finished 12 to 16 months of enrollment in a rare kidney disease C3G phase II study to evaluate the safety and biologic activity of a new drug. Biorasi has 19 nephrology (kidney) clinical sites.
We know people affected by C3G need better treatment options. It is a disease with unmet medical needs that tends to manifest in childhood.
As a CRO that understands the challenges involved in researching rare disease treatments, we’re here to help drug developers deliver the most effective clinical trials possible—on time and on budget.
Speak with one of our rare disease experts today to find out how we can help you develop your next rare disease program.
instruction: What are the primary symptoms of C3 Glomerulopathy (C3G), and how do these symptoms affect the patient's quality of life?
response: C3 Glomerulopathy (C3G) is characterized by several primary symptoms that can severely affect a patient's quality of life. These symptoms include blood in the urine (hematuria), excess protein in the urine (proteinuria) which can be seen as dark, foamy urine, a reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and elevated creatinine levels, swelling (edema) in the hands, feet, and ankles, high blood pressure, and decreased urine output. Hematuria and proteinuria can cause significant psychological distress, as patients may worry about the progression of their kidney disease. Edema can lead to physical discomfort and difficulty in performing daily activities, while high blood pressure can increase the risk of heart disease and stroke. What to do when you have to pee?
What if you really need to hold your pee?
- Do a task that will actively engage your brain, such as a game or crossword puzzle.
- Listen to music.
- Stay sitting if you are already sitting.
- Read a book.
- Scroll through social media on your phone.
- Keep warm, since being cold can give you the urge to urinate.
Can you come if you have to pee?
During sexual activity, some women experience an expelling of fluid at orgasm. Some researchers claim only urine is expelled. Others believe that the paraurethral glands create a fluid that’s similar to the male ejaculate made in the prostate.
What triggers the need to urinate?
As your bladder fills, nerve signals sent to your brain eventually trigger the need to urinate. When you urinate, these nerve signals coordinate the relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles and the muscles of the urethra (urinary sphincter muscles). The muscles of the bladder tighten (contract), pushing the urine out.
How do you relieve bladder pressure?
- physical therapy.
- antihistamine medication to help with urgency.
- pentosan polysulfate sodium, which may block irritants in urine.
- tricyclic antidepressants, which can relax the bladder.
- over-the-counter pain medications.
- surgery, in rare cases.
What does it mean when a girl has to pee a lot?
Examples include excess caffeine intake through coffee, tea, and certain soft drinks. Share on Pinterest Frequent trips to the toilet can be caused by a variety of conditions, including excessive caffeine intake, bladder stones, and UTIs. However, frequent urination may also be due to a number of medical conditions.
What drinks make you pee a lot?
OAB: Drinks That May Increase the Urge to Go
- Caffeinated drinks such as coffee, colas, energy drinks, and teas.
- Acidic fruit juices, especially orange, grapefruit, and tomato.
- Alcoholic drinks.
- Carbonated beverages, sodas, or seltzers.
Can urine and sperm come out together?
No. While sperm and urine both pass through the urethra, they can’t come out at the same time.
How do we know when to pee?
Your bladder is full of receptors that tell your brain how full your bladder is. Basically, there’s an invisible “fill line” in your bladder. When your urine reaches that point, your brain receives a signal that indicates you need to pee. This happens when your bladder is only a quarter of the way full.
Why do I feel like peeing after peeing?
UTIs happen when bacteria or something else infects parts of your urinary system, which includes your bladder, urethra and kidneys. Besides frequent urination, signs of a UTI include a burning feeling when you pee, discolored urine and constantly feeling like you have to pee (even after peeing).
What is the fastest way to cure a urine infection?
Here are seven effective bladder infection remedies.
- Drink more water. Why it helps: Water flushes out the bacteria in your bladder.
- Frequent urination.
- Pain relievers.
- Heating pads.
- Appropriate dress.
- Cranberry juice.
How do you know if something is wrong with your bladder?
Changes in bladder habits or symptoms of irritation Pain or burning during urination. Feeling as if you need to go right away, even when your bladder isn’t full. Having trouble urinating or having a weak urine stream. Having to get up to urinate many times during the night.
Is it good to pee alot?
It’s considered normal to have to urinate about six to eight times in a 24-hour period. If you’re going more often than that, it could simply mean that you may be drinking too much fluid or consuming too much caffeine, which is a diuretic and flushes liquids out of the body.
How do you adjust your body when you need to Pee?
Making Physical Adjustments Remain fairly still to avoid jarring or shaking your body. Limit how much you drink when you need to pee. Reposition your body so you aren’t pressing on your bladder. Pass gas, if you have to. Warm your body and avoid getting into water.
How much time should you spend between Pee breaks?
Slowly extend the amount of time between pee breaks. If you start your schedule by urinating every 2 hours, move to 2.25 hours between restroom visits the next week, then 2.5 hours the week after that.
What do you do when you have a hard time peeing?
Holding in Urine Visualize closing your urethra. Reposition your body. Pass gas, if you have to. Stay warm. Avoid jarring or shaking your body. Avoid thinking of water, waterfalls, or rain. Minimize drinking anything while you need to pee. Think of a distraction. Resolve the situation if possible.
How do you train your bladder to stop leaking urine?
Training Your Bladder Keep a “pee diary” for about 1 week to chart your habits. Set a comfortable urination schedule. Slowly extend the amount of time between pee breaks. Do Kegel exercises to strengthen your pelvic floor muscles. Talk to your doctor about any bladder control issues.
instruction: How do different beverages, such as caffeine and alcohol, affect the frequency and urgency of urination, and what are some healthier alternatives?
response:
Beverages like caffeine and alcohol can significantly impact the frequency and urgency of urination due to their diuretic properties. Caffeine, present in coffee, tea, and energy drinks, stimulates the kidneys to produce more urine, leading to increased trips to the bathroom. Alcohol, on the other hand, inhibits the release of an antidiuretic hormone, which normally helps the body retain water, thus increasing urine production and potentially causing dehydration and a more urgent need to urinate.

For healthier alternatives, consider water, which is essential for maintaining proper hydration and does not have any diuretic effects. Herbal teas, such as chamomile or ginger, can provide a calming and hydrating option without the diuretic properties of caffeine. Decaffeinated coffee and tea are also good choices if you enjoy the taste but want to avoid the increased urination associated with caffeine. Additionally, coconut water is a natural, hydrating beverage that can help replenish electrolytes without the diuretic effects of caffeine or alcohol.

World Vegetarian Day (Oct 1), Vegetarian Awareness Month throughout October, and Meatless Mondays are among some of the activities drawing more attention to vegetarian eating. As the number of patients with chronic kidney disease requiring dialysis treatments or transplantation continues to grow, so does the demand for registered nurses to become a nephrology nurse to fulfill patient needs. With their clinical expertise in providing care to patients with abnormal kidney functions in a technologically advanced nursing specialty, it is estimated that nephrology nurses are needed to treat over 661,330 patients each year with diabetes or kidney disease by the National Kidney Foundation. If you are interested in initiating dialysis treatments, educating patients on at-home care, intervening to prevent complications, and helping patients achieve their rehabilitative potential after a renal transplant, the following is a step-by-step guide on how you can become a nephrology nurse.
Earn a Bachelor’s Degree in Nursing
The first step towards reaching your professional aspirations as a nephrology nurse is to receive the proper training at the bachelor’s degree level from an accredited nursing program. In general, four-year BSN programs are intended to develop the leadership and critical thinking skills that are needed for more advanced nursing positions. You will take courses related to nursing theory, nursing management, human anatomy, developmental psychology, microbiology, health assessment, pathophysiology, pharmacology, nursing research, and clinical practicum. It is highly recommended that nephrology nurses have a BSN to open more professional doors in certification and have enhanced skills for better job prospects. If you already have earned an ADN degree, there is also the option to complete the RN-BSN program with an accelerated curriculum.
Start Working as a Registered Nurse in Nephrology
In all states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories, it is required that nurses possess a valid nursing license as a Registered Nurse to practice. Although processes will vary greatly from state to state, most will require applicants to meet specific educational requirements from an accredited institution, submit an application, complete a background check, and pass the comprehensive National Council Licensure Examination (NCLEX-RN). Once you have received good test results, you can start working as a registered nurse without supervision. You will need to work for at least three years as an RN and obtain at least 3,000 hours in a nephrology setting before moving on to the next step.
Pursue Certification as a Certified Nephrology Nurse (CNN)
After you have gained the necessary experience in home hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, inpatient critical care, inpatient acute kidney injury, Chronic Kidney Disease management, kidney transplant, and apheresis as a registered nurse, you can apply for certification to become a Certified Nephrology Nurse through the Nephrology Nursing Certification Commission. Before being accepted, you will need to complete a minimum of thirty contact hours of approved continuing education credits in nephrology within three years prior to application. Once you have been accepted, you will need to pass a 200-question examination in four years with a correct response rate of over 70% to receive certification.
Related Resource: Cardiac Care Nurse
Overall, nephrology nurses are in demand for providing direct care to patients with kidney-related health concerns that stem from diabetes, substance abuse, kidney disease, high blood pressure, and other increasingly common medical causes. Using this step-by-step guide to become a nephrology nurse, you will unlock opportunities for providing essential dialysis and renal transplant care in acute care centers, home health services, outpatient clinics, transplant units, hospitals, and more.

response: To become a Certified Nephrology Nurse (CNN), a registered nurse must follow several key steps and meet specific requirements. First, earning a Bachelor’s Degree in Nursing (BSN) from an accredited program is highly recommended. This degree provides essential training in nursing theory, management, and clinical skills, which are crucial for advanced positions. After completing the BSN, the next step is to obtain a valid nursing license as a Registered Nurse (RN) by passing the National Council Licensure Examination (NCLEX-RN). Once licensed, the RN must gain at least three years of experience, accumulating a minimum of 3,000 hours in a nephrology setting. This experience should cover various aspects of nephrology care, including home hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, inpatient critical care, acute kidney injury management, chronic kidney disease (CKD) management, kidney transplant, and apheresis. Additionally, the RN must complete 30 contact hours of approved continuing education in nephrology within three years prior to applying for certification. Finally, the RN must pass a 200-question examination with a correct response rate of over 70% to earn the CNN certification. This certification is important for career advancement in nephrology nursing as it demonstrates specialized knowledge and expertise, enhancing job prospects and opening doors to advanced roles in nephrology care.

instruction: How does the body regulate sodium levels, and what are the potential health consequences of consuming excessive amounts of sodium, particularly for individuals with high blood pressure?
response: The regulation of sodium levels in the body is a complex process primarily managed by the kidneys, which adjust the reabsorption and excretion of sodium to maintain homeostasis. The kidneys are influenced by hormones such as aldosterone, which increases sodium reabsorption, and atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), which promotes sodium excretion. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) plays a crucial role in this process. When blood pressure drops, the kidneys release renin, which activates angiotensin, leading to the release of aldosterone and the reabsorption of sodium and water, thus increasing blood volume and pressure. For individuals with high blood pressure, consuming excessive amounts of sodium can have severe health consequences. High sodium intake can lead to fluid retention, increased blood volume, and elevated blood pressure, which can exacerbate hypertension and increase the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attack and stroke. Moreover, chronic high sodium intake can place additional stress on the kidneys, potentially leading to kidney damage and failure. Research also suggests that very high sodium intake (over 5,000 mg per day) may increase the risk of stomach cancer. Therefore, it is crucial for individuals with high blood pressure to limit their sodium intake to recommended levels (1,500 mg per day) to reduce these health risks.

Kidney stones are the solid masses that are made up of crystals. Kidney stones are basically formed in your kidneys. They can move anywhere along the urinary tract and get stuck. The urinary tract consists of these parts:
In this blog, you will get to know about the types of kidney stones one by one.
Calcium Oxalate Stones
Calcium oxalate stones are the most common type of kidney stones. Oxalate is a natural substance that is present in many foods. The body uses food for energy. After your body uses what it requires, the waste products travel via the bloodstream to kidneys and flush out through urine. If there is plenty of waste in too little liquid, there are chances that kidney stones will form. The crystals can stick together and can form a solid mass. Oxalate is a type of substance that can form crystals in the urine. This happens if there is too much of the oxalate in the body. There are certain risk factors that can cause your body to develop calcium oxalate stones. The risk factors include:
- Dehydration, not drinking enough liquid
- If your diet is too high in protein
- Some medical conditions such as dent disease
Kidney stones are common if you are having inflammatory bowel disease. This condition will affect your body’s ability to absorb fat. If the fat is not absorbed in a nice way, then the fat will bind to calcium and it will leave oxalate behind.
By these methods, you can lower the chances of calcium oxalate stones:
Drinking enough liquids
The one thing you can do is to drink plenty of liquids, like water. Drinking plenty of water will make your urine thin and it will make harder for chemicals to build up. The doctor will suggest the right amount of fluid for you.
Eat less sodium
A diet that is high in sodium can cause calcium to build up in your urine. Too much of calcium present in the urine can lead to the formation of the new stones. It can cause the bones to weaken.
Avoid taking vitamin C supplements
Consult your doctor before taking any vitamin C supplements. Too much of vitamin C can cause high amounts of oxalate in urine.
Struvite stones are a hard mineral deposit that can form in your kidneys. These stones form when minerals like phosphate and calcium crystallize inside kidneys and stick together. Bacteria in the urinary tract are responsible for the formation of struvite. Struvite stones can grow quickly. They will eventually block your bladder, ureter, kidney. Bacteria present in your urinary tract produce struvite when they break down the waste product into ammonia. Struvite stones form when your urine is alkaline. If you are having a urinary tract infection which will make your urine alkaline.
Treatment of Struvite Stones
It’s better to treat struvite stones in time as they have a tendency to grow in size. They can possibly damage your kidney and can lead to infections. People who are more prone to contracting UTI’s have higher chances of forming struvite kidney stones.
Doctors are able to treat these infections with the help of shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) or with percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PNL). PNL is a suitable treatment for people having trouble with the stones and if they are too large to break down by SWL. The doctor will make a small incision in your back and will insert a scope. The stone will be removed via an incision.
SWL uses shock waves that are directed from the machine outside your body which will break up the stones into tiny pieces. After the treatment is done, the pieces of stone will pass via your urinary tract, you might have to go through this procedure more than once.
Cystine stones tend to reoccur and are usually larger than other kidney stones. You should talk to your doctor if you are suffering from kidney stones. There are things that you can follow (lifestyle and dietary changes) to reduce the risk of developing more kidney stones. Cystinuria which is a rare disorder is the major cause of cystine stones. This disorder causes a natural substance which is cystine to leak into the urine. These stones can get stuck in the bladder, kidneys or anywhere in the urinary tract.
Treatment of Cystine Stones
The goal of the treatment is to reduce the formation of stones by reducing the amount of cystine in your urine. With less cystine present in urine, there are lesser chances of forming cystine kidney stones. You can take pain relievers while waiting for the stone to pass out of your body. If the stone is big and painful, you may require surgery to remove it. There are various types of surgeries to help reduce the formation of cystine kidney stones:
So, these were the main types of kidney stones that can harm your body. You should consult as your doctor as soon as possible.

instruction: What are the primary risk factors for developing calcium oxalate kidney stones, and how can these be mitigated through lifestyle and dietary changes?
response: Calcium oxalate kidney stones, the most common type, are primarily influenced by factors such as dehydration, a high-protein diet, and certain medical conditions like dent disease and inflammatory bowel disease. Inflammatory bowel disease can lead to poor fat absorption, leaving excess oxalate in the body. To mitigate these risk factors, it is essential to make specific lifestyle and dietary adjustments. Drinking plenty of water is crucial, as it helps dilute the urine and prevents the accumulation of waste products that can form crystals. Reducing sodium intake is also important, as high sodium levels can increase calcium excretion in the urine, contributing to stone formation. Additionally, consult your doctor before taking vitamin C supplements, as they can raise oxalate levels. By implementing these changes, you can effectively reduce the risk of developing calcium oxalate kidney stones.

instruction: What are the primary diagnostic methods used to evaluate renal disease, and how do they help in determining the anatomical location of the disease (pre-renal, post-renal, intrinsic)?
response:
The primary diagnostic methods for evaluating renal disease include urinalysis, measurement of glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and various imaging techniques such as ultrasonography, CT scans, MRI, and radionuclide perfusion scans. These methods are crucial for determining the anatomical location of the disease:

1. **Pre-renal Disease**: This type of renal dysfunction is often caused by conditions that reduce blood flow to the kidneys, such as hypotension or dehydration. Key diagnostic indicators include increased BUN and creatinine levels, and normal urinary sediment. Urinalysis typically shows no significant abnormalities, and imaging studies may not reveal specific changes, but they can rule out other causes.

2. **Post-renal Disease**: This is typically due to obstruction in the urinary tract, such as from kidney stones, prostate enlargement, or tumors. Imaging studies are essential for diagnosis. Ultrasonography can detect hydronephrosis, while CT scans are highly effective for identifying stones. MRI can provide detailed images of the urinary tract and surrounding structures.

3. **Intrinsic Renal Disease**: This involves damage to the kidney tissue itself, such as glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, or renal artery stenosis. Urinalysis is a critical tool, often showing hematuria, proteinuria, and cellular casts. GFR measurements help assess kidney function, and imaging studies like ultrasonography can reveal abnormalities in kidney size and structure. MRI and MRA are useful for detecting renal artery stenosis. Renal biopsy is often necessary for a definitive diagnosis of intrinsic renal diseases.

By combining these diagnostic methods, healthcare providers can accurately determine the location and nature of renal disease, guiding appropriate treatment and management strategies.

How does Asparagus work?
There is some scientific evidence that asparagus can increase urine production (diuretic). Asparagus is a good source of dietary fiber, folic acid, vitamin C, vitamin E, vitamin B6, and several minerals.
Are there safety concerns?
Asparagus is safe when consumed as a food. However, there isn't enough information to know if asparagus is safe when used for medical purposes.
Asparagus can also cause allergic reactions when eaten as a vegetable or used on the skin.
Do not use medicinal amounts of asparagus if:
- You are pregnant or breast-feeding.
- You have kidney disease.
- You have water retention from heart disease.
- You are allergic to plants such as onions, leeks, garlic, and chives.
instruction: What are the potential health benefits of consuming asparagus, and how does its diuretic property contribute to these benefits?
response: Consuming asparagus can provide a range of health benefits, primarily due to its high content of essential nutrients and its diuretic properties. Asparagus is rich in dietary fiber, which aids in digestion and can help prevent constipation. It also contains vitamins such as folic acid, vitamin C, vitamin E, and vitamin B6, which are vital for maintaining overall health, including immune function, skin health, and red blood cell production. The diuretic effect of asparagus is particularly noteworthy, as it increases urine production. This can be beneficial for reducing fluid retention and swelling, which is often associated with conditions like premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and certain types of edema. The increased urine output can also help in the excretion of toxins and waste products from the body, potentially reducing the risk of kidney stones and supporting kidney health. However, it's important to note that individuals with certain conditions, such as kidney disease or water retention from heart disease, should consult a healthcare provider before consuming asparagus in medicinal amounts.

instruction: How important is it to determine the specific type of kidney stone a person has, and what are the different types of supplements or treatments that can be used based on the stone's composition?
response: Determining the specific type of kidney stone a person has is crucial for effective treatment and prevention. Different types of kidney stones require different management approaches. For instance, calcium oxalate stones, which are the most common, may be managed with increased fluid intake, a low-sodium diet, and reducing oxalate-rich foods. On the other hand, uric acid stones, which form in acidic urine, can be treated with medications to alkalinize the urine, such as sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) or potassium citrate. Struvite stones, often associated with urinary tract infections, may require antibiotics and surgical intervention. Cystine stones, which are rare, may be treated with medications like thiols to dissolve the stones. By identifying the stone type, a healthcare provider can recommend the most appropriate supplements and treatments, thereby reducing the risk of recurrence and complications.

instruction: How does the consumption of caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee impact the risk of forming kidney stones, and what are the underlying mechanisms behind this effect?
response: Drinking both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee can lower the risk of developing kidney stones, although the magnitude of the effect differs. A study in the Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology found that consuming at least one cup of caffeinated coffee daily reduces the risk of kidney stones by 26 percent, while decaffeinated coffee reduces the risk by 16 percent. The mechanisms behind this protective effect are multifaceted. Coffee increases urinary output, which helps to flush out potential stone-forming substances. It also contains compounds like antioxidants and phytochemicals that may have anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidative properties, potentially reducing the formation of kidney stones. Furthermore, the presence of citric acid in coffee may play a role in preventing the crystallization of calcium and other minerals that contribute to stone formation.

instruction: What are the key components of an effective treatment plan for managing proteinuria in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease, and why is it important to address proteinuria specifically?
response: An effective treatment plan for managing proteinuria in patients with Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) should focus on several key components. First, it is crucial to control blood pressure, as hypertension can exacerbate kidney damage and increase proteinuria. Medications such as ACE inhibitors or ARBs are often prescribed for their renoprotective effects. Second, lifestyle modifications, including a low-protein diet, reduced sodium intake, and regular physical activity, can help manage proteinuria and slow the progression of CKD. Third, addressing the underlying cause of CKD, such as diabetes or glomerulonephritis, is essential. For example, tight glycemic control in diabetic patients can reduce proteinuria. Finally, specific therapies like Micro-Chinese Medicine Osmotherapy and Toxin-Removing Treatment can be considered, especially for patients who have not responded well to conventional treatments. Addressing proteinuria is important because it is a marker of kidney damage and can lead to further kidney function decline, increasing the risk of kidney failure. Reducing proteinuria can help preserve kidney function and improve overall health outcomes.

Background and objectives: A genetic cause can be identified for an increasing number of pediatric and adult-onset kidney diseases. Preimplantation genetic testing (formerly known as preimplantation genetic diagnostics) is a reproductive technology that helps prospective parents to prevent passing on (a) disease-causing mutation(s) to their offspring. Here, we provide a clinical overview of 25 years of preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic kidney disease in The Netherlands.
Design, setting, participants, & measurements: This is a retrospective cohort study of couples counseled on preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic kidney disease in the national preimplantation genetic testing expert center (Maastricht University Medical Center+) from January 1995 to June 2019. Statistical analysis was performed through chi-squared tests.
Results: In total, 98 couples were counseled regarding preimplantation genetic testing, of whom 53% opted for preimplantation genetic testing. The most frequent indications for referral were autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (38%), Alport syndrome (26%), and autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (9%). Of couples with at least one preimplantation genetic testing cycle with oocyte retrieval, 65% experienced one or more live births of an unaffected child. Of couples counseled, 38% declined preimplantation genetic testing for various personal and technical reasons.
Conclusions: Referrals, including for adult-onset disease, have increased steadily over the past decade. Though some couples decline preimplantation genetic testing, in the couples who proceed with at least one preimplantation genetic testing cycle, almost two thirds experienced at least one live birth rate.

instruction: What are the primary genetic kidney diseases for which preimplantation genetic testing is most frequently requested, and what factors might influence a couple's decision to decline this testing?
response: The primary genetic kidney diseases for which preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) is most frequently requested are autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (38%), Alport syndrome (26%), and autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (9%). These conditions are significant causes of renal failure and can have a substantial impact on the quality of life for affected individuals. Factors that might influence a couple's decision to decline PGT include personal beliefs, ethical considerations, the emotional and financial burden of the testing process, and concerns about the success rate and potential risks of the procedure. Additionally, the availability and accessibility of alternative reproductive options, such as adoption or use of donor gametes, can also play a role in their decision-making process.

instruction: What is the function of the uriniferous tubule in the kidney, and how does it contribute to the overall process of urine formation?
response: The uriniferous tubule is a critical component of the kidney's nephron and plays a vital role in the process of urine formation. It is composed of several segments, including the proximal convoluted tubule, the loop of Henle, the distal convoluted tubule, and the collecting tubule. The primary function of the uriniferous tubule is to process the glomerular filtrate, which is the fluid that has been filtered from the blood by the glomerulus. As the filtrate moves through the tubule, specific segments are responsible for different functions. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs a significant portion of water, glucose, and electrolytes, while the loop of Henle helps to create a concentration gradient in the medulla of the kidney, which is essential for the reabsorption of water in the collecting tubule. The distal convoluted tubule further regulates the reabsorption and secretion of ions and maintains the body's acid-base balance. Finally, the collecting tubule gathers the processed filtrate and delivers it to the renal pelvis, where it joins other collecting tubules to form urine, which is then excreted from the body.

Charles Jennette, MD, professor of pathology and laboratory medicine, and professor of medicine, has received the Robert H. Heptinstall Lifetime Achievement Award from the Renal Pathology Society (RPS). The honor was presented February 29 at the RPS Annual Meeting in Los Angeles, Ca.
Jennette’s service, teaching and research activities focus on kidney disease. From 1999–2019, he was Kenneth M. Brinkhous Distinguished Professor and Chair of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine.
Jennette is executive director of the UNC Nephropathology Laboratory, which evaluates approximately 2,000 renal biopsy specimens per year, and is co-director, with Ronald J. Falk, MD, of the Glomerular Disease Collaborative Network, which coordinates kidney disease research by approximately 300 nephrologists throughout the Southeastern United States.
Jennette’s research and scholarship are directed at understanding the causes, and improving the diagnosis and treatment of kidney diseases, especially those caused by inflammatory and immunologic mechanisms. He has published over 300 journal articles, over 140 book chapters, and 18 books.
Jennette is editor of Heptinstall’s “Pathology of the Kidney” and serves on the editorial boards of professional journals dealing with pathology or kidney diseases. He has given over 450 national and international invited presentations, including more than 20 named lectureships. Notable awards include the Renal Pathology Society Jacob Churg Award for Outstanding Contributions in Renal Pathology, the European Society of Pathology Honorary Diploma for Outstanding Achievements in Nephropathology, the UNC Medical Alumni Distinguished Faculty Award, and the Distinguished Service Award of the Association of Pathology Chairs.
The RPS promotes excellence in diagnosis, fosters basic, clinical and translational research, encourages training and education in renal disease, sponsors US based and international conferences and symposia, and brings news and updates pertaining to renal pathology to its members around the world.

This approach not only improves patient outcomes but also enhances their overall quality of life.

instruction: How does the traditional Ayurvedic concept of Moothrashmari compare with the modern medical understanding of renal calculi, and what are the key differences in their approaches to management and treatment?
response:
The traditional Ayurvedic concept of Moothrashmari and the modern medical understanding of renal calculi share some similarities but differ significantly in their approaches to management and treatment. According to Ayurveda, Moothrashmari is a condition characterized by the formation of stones in the urinary system, leading to severe pain and discomfort. The term 'Ashmari' is derived from 'Ashma' (stone) and 'Ari' (enemy), emphasizing the intense pain and the disease's malevolent nature. Ayurveda considers Moothrashmari one of the 'Mahagada' (great diseases), highlighting its potential to disrupt the anatomy and physiology of the urinary system. Treatment in Ayurveda focuses on using herbs and natural remedies to dissolve and expel the stones. Kshara, a type of alkali, is particularly noted for its Lekhana (scraping), Bhedana (penetrating), Pachana (digesting), Shodhana (purifying), and Tridoshaghna (balancing the three doshas) properties. The study 'Effect of Mulakakshara in the management of Moothrashmari (renal calculi)' demonstrates the effectiveness of using Mulaka (Raphanus sativus) Kshara in treating this condition.

In contrast, modern medicine defines renal calculi as solid concretions or crystal aggregations formed in the kidneys from dietary minerals in the urine. These stones are classified by their location (nephrolithiasis, ureterolithiasis, cystolithiasis) and chemical composition (calcium-containing, uric acid, struvite, etc.). The modern approach to managing renal calculi involves a combination of pharmacological interventions, dietary modifications, and, in severe cases, surgical procedures such as lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, and percutaneous nephrolithotomy. The goal is to relieve pain, prevent complications, and remove the stones. While both systems aim to alleviate symptoms and prevent recurrence, Ayurveda emphasizes a holistic and natural approach, while modern medicine relies on advanced diagnostic tools and interventions.

instruction: How does diet influence the pH level of urine, and what are the potential health implications of an overly acidic or alkaline urine pH?
response:
Diet significantly influences the pH level of urine, which in turn can have important health implications. The pH of urine typically ranges from 4.6 to 8.0, with a common value around 6.0. An alkaline urine pH (greater than 7) is often associated with a diet rich in vegetable proteins, dairy, and citrus fruits. These foods contain compounds that, when metabolized, produce bicarbonate, which increases the pH of the urine. Alkaline urine can lead to the formation of phosphate and carbonate crystals, which may contribute to the development of kidney stones. Additionally, an overly alkaline urine can be a sign of a urinary tract infection or metabolic or respiratory alkalosis.

On the other hand, an acidic urine pH (less than 7) is typically the result of a diet high in animal proteins. The metabolism of these proteins produces acids, such as sulfuric acid, which lower the pH of the urine. Acidic urine can lead to the formation of oxalate and urate crystals, which can also contribute to kidney stone formation. Moreover, overly acidic urine can be indicative of conditions such as renal tuberculosis, diarrhea, or other forms of acidosis. Monitoring and managing urine pH through dietary adjustments can help prevent these health issues and maintain overall kidney function.

Cyst on Kidney, circular fluid-filled cysts develop on or in the kidneys. It is possible that kidney cysts are associated with serious disorders that can affect the kidneys. Simple kidney cysts, on the other hand, are noncancerous and rarely cause complications.
What causes simple kidney cysts is not known. Most kidney cysts are confined to the surface of the kidney, but multiple cysts can develop in either kidney. Simple kidney cysts, on the other hand, are not the same as polycystic kidney disease cysts.
Simple kidney cysts are often discovered during an imaging test for a different medical condition, such as kidney cancer. Patients without symptoms or signs of kidney cysts usually don’t require treatment.
The kidneys are generally found on either side of the center back, right beneath the ribs, in the human body. The size of a kidney is about the same as a fist. The kidneys perform a variety of functions, including:
- regulating the fluid and salt content of the blood
- removing waste materials and generating urine
- hormones that aid in blood pressure management, red blood cell formation, and calcium levels
- maintaining the mineral, salt, and acid balance in the blood through managing body chemistry
- Vitamin D is activated to maintain bones healthy.
Cyst on Kidney – what are they?
As the name suggests, a cyst consists of a closed sac filled with air or liquid. Located at the base of the spine, kidneys are bean-shaped organs that help regulate the body’s salt and water levels. Additionally, they remove waste products by filtering the blood and excreting uric acid.
Nephrons are small working parts found inside the kidneys that are responsible for the kidney’s function. An individual nephron is made up of two parts: A filter, and a tube, respectively. nephrons remove extra water and waste products from the blood as it passes through the kidneys to be filtered, which then leaves the body as urine.
It is common for simple kidney cysts to be small, round sacs filled with watery fluid that are surrounded by a thin wall. If you’re getting older, cysts can form on the kidney’s surface, or in the nephrons.
Who is at risk for simple kidney cysts?
Simple kidney cysts become increasingly frequent as people get older; up to half of all people 50 and older have at least one kidney cyst. Most people only have a cyst in one kidney, but as we get older, the frequency of cysts and the chance of developing cysts in the second kidney increases.
Is it Possible for Simple kidney Cysts to be Dangerous?
Kidney cysts are usually always non-cancerous. They’re referred to as “simple” because there’s a slim chance they’ll turn into something more serious. Some cysts, on the other hand, have thickened walls, may seem irregular on X-rays, and may be linked to kidney cancer.
Cyst on Kidney Symptoms
Symptoms of simple kidney cysts are frequently absent. In reality, the majority of people who have them are completely unaware of their existence. If cysts rupture (break open) and begin to bleed, become infectious, or grow large enough to push on other organs in the abdomen, they become a problem.
Simple kidney cysts usually have no symptoms or indicators. Symptoms of a small kidney cyst that has grown large enough include:
- Upper abdominal ache with a fever
- Pain between the ribs and the hip, in the stomach, or in the back.
- Urination on a regular basis (having to go the bathroom often).
- Urine with blood in it, or urine that is black.
When should you see a doctor?
If you have signs or symptoms of a kidney cyst, make an appointment with your doctor.
Cyst on Kidney Causes
The cause of simple kidney cysts is unknown. According to one idea, kidney cysts form when the kidney’s exterior layer weakens and creates a pouch (diverticulum). The pouch fills with fluid, detaches, and becomes a cyst.
Kidney cysts form when a nephron’s tube grows larger and fills with fluid. Researchers aren’t sure what causes this, but they do know that simple cysts aren’t passed down down the generations. Simple kidney cysts are thought to arise as a result of damage or microscopic obstructions in the tubules.
What is the treatment for simple kidney cysts(Cyst on Kidney)?
Simple kidney cysts don’t always need to be treated. It may be required to reduce or remove a cyst if it is exerting too much pressure on another organ or altering the way a kidney works. Simple kidney cysts are most often treated with one of two procedures:
Aspiration and sclerotherapy: The doctor punctures the cyst and drains the fluid with a long needle inserted beneath the skin. To diminish the cyst, a powerful solution is put into it. If necessary, this operation can be repeated.
Surgery to remove a cyst is typically performed laparoscopically, using thin instruments entered via small incisions in the abdominal wall.
Simple kidney cysts become more common as you become older, although they can happen at any age. Men are more likely to have simple kidney cysts.
Simple kidney cysts are unavoidable. Drink plenty of water and limit your salt intake to less than 2,300 mg per day to lower your risk (less than 1,500 mg if you are older than 51, African-American, or have high blood pressure or long-term kidney disease).
instruction: What are the potential risks and complications associated with simple kidney cysts, and under what circumstances might medical intervention be necessary?
response: While simple kidney cysts are typically benign and asymptomatic, they can occasionally lead to complications. These complications may arise if the cysts grow large enough to press on other organs, rupture, or become infected. Symptoms that may indicate a problem include upper abdominal pain, fever, pain between the ribs and the hip, frequent urination, and blood in the urine. If a cyst is causing significant symptoms or affecting kidney function, medical intervention may be necessary. Treatment options include aspiration and sclerotherapy, which involves draining the cyst and injecting a solution to prevent regrowth, or laparoscopic surgery to remove the cyst. Simple kidney cysts are more prevalent in older adults, particularly those over 50, and are more common in men. To reduce the risk of developing kidney cysts, it is recommended to stay well-hydrated and maintain a low-sodium diet.

Why did you decide to investigate rates of acute care utilization across racial-ethnic groups in children with glomerular disease?
In reviewing the literature previously on health disparities in kidney disease, there’s a lot described in end stage kidney disease (ESKD) and dialysis and transplant patients, but not a lot described in patients who have other kidney pathologies, those, say, who are at risk to go on and develop end stage kidney disease or who have glomerular disease, so diseases of the filters of the kidney itself that can get leaky and cause other problems. There’s reason to believe there’d be disparities in those diseases. One, we know that African Americans are at increased risk of glomerular disease, because of the APOL 1 gene. Also these diseases impact patients’ lives significantly, they often have a lot of complications, and the medications that they are required to take can also have a lot of complications like infections, blood clots, things like that, that would cause them to be in the hospital. With all of this in mind, there’s reason to think that there are disparities that haven’t been previously described before.
How did you go about conducting the study and what were the main findings?
We use the CureGN network. It’s a large multinational prospective cohort study. It gives us a large sample with a diverse population to really study health disparities. Since glomerular disease is so rare, you need a lot of patients from a lot of different places to really have a large enough sample size to investigate these outcomes, especially when you’re going to divide them amongst racial-ethnic groups. We had a nice database to look at. We did recurrent event proportional models to see how often they were getting admitted to the hospital or visiting the emergency room and seeing if there were differences in these rates across racial-ethnic groups.
Further, not just looking at the actual rates, but we wanted to understand what the causes would be of different rates if we were to see them. That’s when we adjusted for confounders, and we did them sequentially so that we could understand what exactly the factors are that were causing differences that we saw. So, was it socioeconomic status, was it their overall health status? Was it the type of glomerular disease that they had? Or was it how severe their disease was?
We overall found that African American children did have increased rates of acute care utilization, so hospitalization or emergency department (ED) visits, but that is largely explained by their increased risk of having severe disease, in addition to their likelihood of being on public insurance. While there were differences amongst racial-ethnic groups, with Black children, being more likely to need acute care utilization, it is not inherent in race itself, but more because of their likelihood of having lower socioeconomic status and more severe disease.
Were any findings unexpected?
This is actually sort of what we hypothesized. I think it really speaks to the social determinants of health that we all know affect kidney disease. We know that race itself is a social construct, there’s no genetic basis for race. There’s nothing that’s going to be inherent about the race that is going to make patients at risk for being hospitalized more. But it’s really about the interplay of genetic propensity, their social factors, access to care, their socioeconomic status, health, literacy, etc, that all cause interplay of social determinants of health that lead to worse outcomes. I think this kind of proved what we were already suspecting but has given us a basis of how do we start intervening on these disparities to improve outcomes and make health more equitable.
instruction: How does the CureGN network facilitate the study of health disparities in glomerular disease, and what unique advantages does it offer compared to other research methods in this field?
response: The CureGN network offers unique advantages in studying health disparities in glomerular disease by leveraging a large, multinational, and diverse patient cohort. This extensive database is essential for researching rare conditions like glomerular disease, as it provides the necessary sample size to detect meaningful differences across racial-ethnic groups. The network's design allows for sophisticated statistical analyses, such as recurrent event proportional models, to assess the frequency of hospitalizations and emergency department visits. Moreover, the ability to adjust for various confounders, including socioeconomic status, overall health status, and disease severity, provides a deeper understanding of the factors contributing to disparities. For instance, the study revealed that while African American children had higher rates of acute care utilization, this was primarily due to their higher risk of severe disease and public insurance status, rather than inherent racial factors. These insights highlight the importance of addressing social determinants of health to reduce disparities and improve patient outcomes.

instruction: How can dietary changes and hydration levels impact the formation of kidney stones, and what are some preventive measures one can take to avoid this condition?
response: The formation of kidney stones can be significantly influenced by both dietary choices and hydration levels. Dehydration is a major risk factor for kidney stone formation, as it leads to concentrated urine, which facilitates the crystallization of minerals such as calcium, oxalate, and uric acid. To prevent kidney stones, it is crucial to stay hydrated, aiming for urine that is clear or light yellow. In terms of diet, reducing the intake of foods high in oxalate, such as spinach, nuts, and chocolate, can help prevent calcium oxalate stones. Increasing your consumption of citric acid-rich foods, like lemons, can also be beneficial as citrate can inhibit stone formation. Additionally, limiting sodium intake is important, as high sodium levels can increase calcium excretion in the urine. Maintaining a balanced diet with adequate calcium intake from sources like dairy or leafy greens is also recommended, as insufficient calcium can paradoxically increase the risk of kidney stones. These preventive measures can help reduce the likelihood of developing kidney stones and promote overall kidney health.

instruction: What are the potential side effects of chronic diuretic use, and how can these be managed to minimize health risks?
response: The prolonged use of diuretics can result in a range of side effects that can impact various systems in the body. One of the primary concerns is dehydration, as diuretics increase urine production, leading to a loss of fluids and essential electrolytes such as potassium, sodium, calcium, and magnesium. Low levels of these electrolytes can cause symptoms like muscle weakness, cramps, and heart palpitations. To minimize these risks, patients should be vigilant about maintaining adequate hydration and may need to take electrolyte supplements. Another potential side effect is the elevation of blood sugar levels, particularly in individuals with diabetes, which can be managed through regular blood glucose monitoring and adjustments to medication. Furthermore, some diuretics may cause other side effects such as lethargy, chest tightness, and anxiety. If these side effects are significant, it may be necessary to switch to a different diuretic or explore alternative treatments. Regular medical follow-ups are crucial to monitor and manage these side effects, ensuring that the benefits of diuretic therapy outweigh the risks.

Background: Low physical performance in patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis is associated with a high mortality rate. We investigated the clinical relevance of gait speed and handgrip strength, the two most commonly used methods of assessing physical performance. Methods: We obtained data regarding gait speed and handgrip strength from 277 hemodialysis patients and evaluated their relationships with baseline parameters, mental health, plasma inflammatory markers, and major adverse clinical outcomes. Low physical performance was defined by the recommendations suggested by the Asian Working Group on Sarcopenia. Results: The prevalence of low gait speed and handgrip strength was 28.2 and 44.8%, respectively. Old age, low serum albumin levels, high comorbidity index score, and impaired cognitive functions were associated with low physical performance. Patients with isolated low gait speed exhibited a general trend for worse quality of life than those with isolated low handgrip strength. Gait speed and handgrip strength showed very weak correlations with different determining factors (older age, the presence of diabetes, and lower serum albumin level for low gait speed, and lower body mass index and the presence of previous cardiovascular events for low handgrip strength). Patients with low gait speed and handgrip strength had elevated levels of plasma endocan and matrix metalloproteinase-7 and the highest risks for all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events among the groups (adjusted hazard ratio of 2.72, p = 0.024). Elderly patients with low gait speed and handgrip strength were at the highest risk for poor clinical outcomes. Conclusion: Gait speed and handgrip strength reflected distinctive aspects of patient characteristics and the use of both factors improved the prediction of adverse clinical outcomes in hemodialysis patients. Gait speed seems to be a better indicator of poor patient outcomes than is handgrip strength.

instruction: How do gait speed and handgrip strength, two commonly used methods of assessing physical performance, reflect different aspects of patient characteristics in hemodialysis patients, and what implications do these differences have for clinical outcomes?
response: In the context of hemodialysis patients, gait speed and handgrip strength serve as valuable tools for assessing physical performance, each reflecting distinct aspects of patient health and predicting different clinical outcomes. Gait speed, defined as the ability to walk a certain distance in a given time, is a comprehensive measure of physical function and is closely linked to overall health and quality of life. The study found that patients with low gait speed were more likely to be older, have diabetes, and have lower serum albumin levels, all of which are markers of poor systemic health. Moreover, low gait speed was associated with worse quality of life, highlighting its importance in evaluating the patient's overall well-being. Handgrip strength, which measures the strength of the hand muscles, primarily reflects muscle function and body composition. Patients with low handgrip strength were found to have a lower body mass index and a higher prevalence of previous cardiovascular events, indicating that this measure is more specific to muscle strength and cardiovascular health. Both measures were associated with elevated levels of plasma endocan and matrix metalloproteinase-7, markers of inflammation and tissue damage, but the combination of low gait speed and handgrip strength was the strongest predictor of poor clinical outcomes, including higher risks of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events. This suggests that while gait speed and handgrip strength are useful individually, their combined use provides a more robust assessment of physical performance and a better prediction of adverse clinical outcomes, especially in elderly hemodialysis patients.

How Your Kidneys Work
- The two kidneys are vital organs, performing many functions to keep your blood clean and chemically balanced.
- The kidneys are bean-shaped organs, each about the size of a fist. They are located near the middle of the back, just below the rib cage.
- Kidneys are sophisticated trash collectors. Every day, the kidneys process about 200 quarts of blood to sift out about 2 quarts of waste products and extra water. The waste and extra water become urine, which flows to the bladder through tubes called ureters. The bladder stores the urine until you go to the bathroom.
- The wastes in your blood come from the normal breakdown of active muscle and from food eaten. The body uses the food for energy and self-repair. After the body takes what it needs from the food, waste is sent to the blood. If the kidneys did not remove these wastes, the wastes would build up in the blood and damage the body.
- The actual filtering occurs in tiny units inside the kidneys called nephrons. Every kidney has about a million nephrons. In the nephron, tiny blood vessels called capillaries intertwine with tiny urine-carrying tubes called tubules.
- The tubules first receive a combination of waste materials and chemicals that the body can still use. The kidneys measure out chemicals like sodium, phosphorus, and potassium and release them back to the blood to return to the body. In this way, the kidneys regulate the body's level of these substances. The right balance is necessary for life, but excess levels can be harmful.
- In addition to removing wastes, the kidneys release three important hormones:
o Erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates the bones to make red blood cells;
o Renin, which regulates blood pressure; and
o The active form of vitamin D, which helps maintain calcium for bones and for normal chemical balance in the body.

response: The regulation of essential chemicals like sodium, phosphorus, and potassium by the kidneys is a vital process for maintaining the body's overall health. The kidneys, which are sophisticated filtration systems, process about 200 quarts of blood each day, filtering out waste products and excess water to produce about 2 quarts of urine. This filtration occurs in the nephrons, which are the functional units of the kidneys. Each nephron contains a network of tiny blood vessels and urine-carrying tubes. This regulation ensures that the body maintains the correct balance of these chemicals, which are essential for various physiological functions, including nerve signaling, muscle contractions, and fluid balance. Proper regulation is crucial because an imbalance in these chemicals can lead to serious health problems, such as muscle weakness, heart arrhythmias, and metabolic disorders.

Diabetic Foot Health Care
What Is Diabetes?
Diabetes is a chronic condition that occurs when there are abnormally high levels of
glucose or sugar in the blood. This is caused by the body not producing sufficient
or no insulin, so that the cells do not respond normally to the insulin that is
produced. Insulin is a hormone that is produced by the pancreas. It is needed for
glucose to enter the body cells and be converted to energy.
Diabetes can have serious health complications, including heart disease, stroke,
kidney failure and limb amputation. It can take 15 years off a person’s life if not
The cause of diabetes is not known for certain, however, the modern western diet
high in refined sugar may release excessive sugar levels in the body, causing high
blood sugar peaks.
There Are Two Main Types of Diabetes.
Type 1 Diabetes Or Insulin Dependent Diabetes
~ Occurs when the pancreas no longer produces the insulin needed
~ Represents about 15% of all cases of diabetes
~ Is an autoimmune condition not generally caused by lifestyle factors
~ Is one of the most common chronic childhood diseases
~Type 1 diabetes is increasing by about 3% every year
Type 2 Diabetes Or Non-Insulin Dependent Diabetes
~ Occurs when the pancreas is not producing enough insulin or the insulin is not
~ Represents up to 90% of all cases of diabetes
~Risk factors include increasing age, family history, ethnic background and obesity
~Lifestyle factors such as poor diet, being overweight and lack of physical activity
contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes
Symptoms Of Diabetes
Symptoms of diabetes can include excessive thirst and urination, unexplained weight
loss, weakness & fatigue, irritability. Diabetes symptoms are usually diagnosed with
a routine blood test.
When blood glucose reaches higher levels, symptoms can include blurred vision,
infections that don’t heal or heal very slowly, tingling, burning and numbness in the
feet. This is caused by nerve damage and called peripheral neuropathy.
Complications Caused By Type 2 Diabetes
The complications caused by type 2 diabetes may include increased risk of heart
disease and stroke, blindness, kidney failure, limb amputation and neuropathic pain.
Diabetes, Heart Disease & Stroke
Diabetes is also often associated with high blood pressure and high blood fats or
cholesterol and triglycerides which are know to cause an increased risk of heart
attack and stroke. Medical research tells us that over two-thirds of all cardiovascular
