Dr. Sylvester Ikhisemojie
When any person has the experience of passing urine that foams, it is sometimes an unsettling event. Most often, this happens a lot when someone passes urine in a large volume and quickly into a vessel or urinal. The speed with which the urine is passed, the turbulence such passage causes and the composition of the receiving vessel all play a role in determining how the urine appears and how much foam is in it.
If the water closet bowl contains some soapy lotion for example, the urine will mix with some of that and appear foamy. However, such an occurrence will only be occasional as soap will not always be found in the bowl nor will urine always be voluminous and passed with a lot of force. The addition of a forceful passage occurs when a particular individual is pressed like it can be after a long road journey where it may not be expedient to stop at intervals to relieve oneself.
When urine foams consistently, it is a sign that there is protein in it and it may then be time to see a doctor and complain about such an observation. To be sure, many of us would occasionally pass out some protein in the urine but it should never be a regular occurrence. That may be a problem after rigorous exercise, for example or following a major illness, but it should stop at some point. When protein is present all the time in the urine, it means the kidneys are not working properly. The kidneys are the filters of unwanted impurities from the blood. In the main, they should do all the necessary filtration but retain the proteins because proteins are important to the body for so many functions. If they fail to do this or are unable to do so, then something is seriously amiss. It is often indicated by the presence of albumin in the urine. Albumin is a component of the total amount of protein circulating in our blood.
Sometimes, urine can appear foamy when the person passing it is dehydrated and has not had enough fluid to drink for that day. The body’s requirement for water is more in the tropics than in the temperate regions of the world for obvious reasons and the need to drink water is correspondingly more. Many people do not take enough fluids for a variety of reasons but it is important to make up on the deficit incurred once one is able to. That helps to avoid a state of dehydration and the passing of urine that can appear darker than normal and foamy as well. The various factors we have mentioned above can be responsible for foaming urine but as emphasised also, once it gets to be more noticeable over time, it only means that the kidneys are practically leaking protein. They are failing in their duty of adequately filtering the urine such that there is the tendency at that point towards kidney failure. In people with pre-existing conditions of hypertension and or diabetes, this often represents a problem that could end up with regular dialysis and even kidney transplantation.
There are some other reasons why your urine could produce foam other than dehydration and speed of passage. An inflammatory condition in the kidneys such as might be found in a condition known as glomerulonephritis can often cause this malady. The long name means there is a swelling response of the small functional units of the kidneys such that their cells allow the passage of large particles through them including proteins. These proteins then escape into the urine and such urine demonstrates their presence by foaming. Intensive exercise in perfectly healthy people can also lead to this possibility and that is one of the reasons why top athletes and soldiers are fed reinforced meals essentially made of high percentage proteins. In the military stores of the world’s largest armies, these are stored in advance as “meals ready to eat” or MRE. It is largely to replenish the protein stores that might be lost during intense combat.
Sometimes, a stone anywhere along the urinary tract can also cause the passage of protein in the urine that can cause it to foam. Some of this is because it may impede the flow of urine such that it can get attacked by bacteria thereby leading to protein loss. Sometimes, the physical injury caused by the stone as it scrapes the walls of the pathway can also liberate some protein into the urine either directly or through associated bleeding. In the same way, people on treatment with aspirin can also have this problem as can yet others who have been exposed to intense cold. Low blood pressure, which is associated with certain conditions, like severe diarrhoea and vomiting, can also cause this. This can be seen also in people who have endured severe blood loss from injuries or operations. Lastly, even people undergoing emotional turmoil and stress have been observed to pass protein in their urine in a situation known as proteinuria.
When you pass foaming urine, it is rational to consider the possibility of the common causes first. Urinating with a fast stream is a top contender. Urinating into a toilet bowl that has some soap in it is another and so is inadequate intake of water and other fluids. However, if foamy urine is associated with other symptoms or it is recurrent, it will be wise to see a doctor and get examined properly. Symptoms such as nausea, a shortness of breath and unexplained tiredness often help show the need to see a doctor. The same holds true for general swelling of the body, an itchy skin and the frequent passage of urine. There may also be vomiting. So that if somebody has any combination of these symptoms as well as a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure or kidney disease, such people should not delay before they see a doctor. In particular, diabetes and other causes of raised blood sugar often have more glucose particles circulating in their blood.
Since glucose is a large compound just like protein, the kidneys may have trouble properly filtering them. When the kidneys cannot do the filtration properly, both the glucose and protein will escape into the urine causing it to foam. When the blood sugar level is not well regulated as in poorly controlled diabetes, there is a constant feeling of thirst, a dry mouth, and a frequent need to urinate. There may be in addition, unexplained hunger, unexplained weakness, a dry mouth and blurring of the vision. As a result, the presence of protein in the urine can be diagnosed by testing a urine sample for the amount of protein in it. If the levels are high, a 24-hour urine sample is requested which, which is all the urine produced in an entire day and sent to a laboratory for analysis which will attempt to compare the amount of albumin in the blood to the level of creatinine, another protein. If the ratio between the former and the latter is above average, it would mean that there is kidney disease.
Very often, foaming urine can be reversed by simply drinking more water and the appearance should then cease within a few days. If that does not happen, and there are some of the symptoms we mentioned earlier in association with it, then you must see a doctor. Other than increased water intake, changes can be made to the diet as well as regular exercise and weight control. If you do smoke and or take large amounts of alcohol, it is important to stop those habits. Finally, if there is associated high blood pressure or diabetes, medications must be prescribed to control those conditions. Often it is a combination of all the measures described above that will do the magic and it is important to know that at certain levels and with adequate discipline, some of the conditions that will cause the urine to foam are reversible.

instruction: What are the common reasons for urine to appear foamy, and how can these be distinguished from more serious underlying health conditions?
response: Foamy urine can result from various factors, ranging from benign to more serious. Common reasons include the speed and force of urination, the presence of soapy substances in the toilet, and dehydration. Rapid urination can create turbulence, leading to foam. Soapy residues can mix with urine, causing it to foam. Dehydration, especially in hot climates, can result in concentrated urine that appears foamy. However, consistent foamy urine may indicate a more serious underlying condition, such as proteinuria. Proteinuria, the presence of protein in the urine, can be a sign of kidney problems. Conditions like glomerulonephritis, where the kidney's filtering units are inflamed, can allow proteins to pass into the urine. Other causes include intense exercise, urinary tract stones, and certain medications. If foamy urine is recurrent or accompanied by symptoms like nausea, shortness of breath, unexplained fatigue, swelling, itchy skin, frequent urination, or a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure, or kidney disease, a medical evaluation is advisable. Diagnosis typically involves urine tests to measure protein levels and possibly a 24-hour urine to assess kidney function. Treatment may include increased fluid intake, dietary changes, regular exercise, and managing underlying conditions like hypertension or diabetes.

According to the Education Portal website, a dialysis nurse is a registered nurse who works with patients who either suffer from kidney disease or kidney failure. These patients routinely undergo dialysis treatment, which is an artificial process used to remove waste and unhealthy fluids from the kidneys.
A dialysis nurse can work in a dialysis clinic, hospital or private physician's office. A minimum of two years experience as a registered nurse is generally required. She must know how to use a dialysis machine, which extracts a patient's blood, cleans it and returns it to the body. According to the Best Nursing Degree website, Lorry Schoenly, a dialysis nurse follows the direct instructions of each patient's physician: She administers blood products or fluid therapy in accordance with the doctor's orders. She also provides information about the procedure and answers general questions for patients about dialysis.
The Education Portal website notes that dialysis nurses must undergo training to learn how to use a dialysis machine correctly. A dialysis nurse hooks patients up to dialysis machines for frequent treatments. The nurse must know precisely how the machine operates and recognize immediate warning signs if it starts to malfunction. The nurse continuously monitors each patient's vital signs during the dialysis procedures. Dialysis nurses also assess the effectiveness of dialysis procedures, communicate problems to doctors and maintain a clean, safe environment for patients.
instruction: What are the primary responsibilities of a dialysis nurse during a dialysis treatment, and how do they ensure the safety and effectiveness of the procedure?
response: The primary responsibilities of a dialysis nurse during a dialysis treatment include preparing the patient and the dialysis machine, initiating and monitoring the treatment, and ensuring the overall safety and effectiveness of the procedure. They must be proficient in operating the dialysis machine, which involves extracting, cleaning, and returning the patient's blood. Dialysis nurses continuously monitor the patient's vital signs and the machine's performance, ready to address any technical or physiological issues that may arise. They follow the specific instructions and orders provided by the patient's physician, administering necessary treatments such as blood products or fluid therapy. To ensure safety and effectiveness, dialysis nurses receive specialized training on the use of the dialysis machine and maintain a clean, sterile environment to prevent infections. They also play a crucial role in patient education, providing information and support to help patients understand the dialysis process and manage their condition.

Nationwide, more than 400,000 Americans have kidney disease so bad that they need regular dialysis – meaning they have to connect to a machine for several hours at least three times a week to clean their blood of toxins.
“They have to come at a certain time, so it’s very scheduled, very regimented, and their time is not their own,” says Dr. Robert LaClair, a nephrologist, or kidney specialist at St. Peter’s hospital in Helena.
“The way we do dialysis in this country, no one would be saying, ‘this is the way we should be doing things.’ No one would,” LaClair says.
When he came to St. Peter’s five years ago, LaClair decided he was going to do things differently. He was going to encourage as many of his patients as possible to dialyze at home.

instruction: What are the potential benefits and drawbacks of home dialysis compared to in-clinic dialysis, and how might this alternative approach improve the quality of life for patients with severe kidney disease?
response: The potential benefits of home dialysis compared to in-clinic dialysis are numerous and can significantly enhance the quality of life for patients with severe kidney disease. One of the key advantages is the reduction in the need for frequent travel to a dialysis center, which can be both time-consuming and physically draining. Home dialysis allows patients to integrate their treatment into their daily lives, maintaining a more normal routine and reducing the disruption to work, family, and social activities. Moreover, home dialysis can be performed more frequently, which can lead to better management of fluid and electrolyte balance, fewer symptoms, and a lower risk of hospitalization. However, there are also potential drawbacks to consider. Home dialysis requires a substantial initial investment in training and equipment, and patients must be capable of managing the technical aspects of the treatment, which can be challenging for some. There is also the risk of technical issues or complications that may require prompt medical intervention. Despite these challenges, the ability to dialyze at home can empower patients, giving them more control over their treatment and potentially leading to better overall health and well-being.

instruction: What are the primary roles and functions of the protein known as KIRREL3 or NEPH2 in cellular processes?
response: KIRREL3, or NEPH2, is a protein that belongs to the family of cell junction proteins, which are critical for the formation and maintenance of cell-cell interactions. In the kidney, KIRREL3 is expressed in podocytes, specialized cells in the glomerulus that are essential for the filtration of blood. Specifically, KIRREL3 helps to form the slit diaphragm, a specialized cell junction that acts as a filtration barrier, preventing the passage of large molecules and cells into the urine. Beyond its role in the kidney, KIRREL3 is also expressed in the nervous system, where it may contribute to the formation and stabilization of synapses, supporting neuronal communication and function. The protein's involvement in these processes underscores its importance in maintaining tissue integrity and function in both the renal and nervous systems.

instruction: What factors can influence the results of a urine creatinine test, and how do these factors affect the interpretation of the results?
response: The accuracy and interpretation of urine creatinine test results can be influenced by multiple factors, primarily age and lean body mass. Creatinine is produced by muscle metabolism, and the amount produced is directly related to the amount of muscle mass an individual has. Younger individuals and those with more muscle mass will generally have higher creatinine levels. Additionally, age can affect kidney function, which in turn can influence creatinine clearance. Abnormal results can be indicative of various conditions, such as renal disease, muscle disorders, or dehydration. However, these results should be interpreted with caution, considering the individual's age and muscle mass. For instance, a high creatinine level in a young, muscular individual may not be cause for concern, whereas the same level in an older individual with less muscle mass might suggest renal impairment. It is crucial to discuss the results with a healthcare provider to get a proper interpretation and to rule out any potential health issues.

instruction: What are the key factors that healthcare providers should consider when selecting a knowledge database for evidence-based drug dosing recommendations for patients with impaired kidney function?
response:
When healthcare providers are selecting a knowledge database for evidence-based drug dosing recommendations for patients with impaired kidney function, they should focus on the following key factors to ensure the database meets their clinical needs and enhances patient care:

1. **Evidence Quality and Reliability**: The database should be based on high-quality, peer-reviewed evidence and regularly updated to incorporate the latest clinical research. This ensures that the dosing recommendations are current and based on the best available evidence.

2. **Broad Drug Coverage**: The database should include a comprehensive list of drugs, covering both frequently prescribed medications and less common ones. It should also provide dosing recommendations for various stages of kidney impairment, from mild to severe, to address a wide range of clinical scenarios.

3. **Ease of Use**: The user interface should be intuitive and user-friendly, allowing healthcare providers to quickly and easily access the necessary information. This can reduce the risk of medication errors and improve patient safety.

4. **EHR Integration**: Integration with electronic health record (EHR) systems is essential for seamless workflow and real-time dosing recommendations. This integration ensures that dosing adjustments are based on the most up-to-date patient data, enhancing the accuracy and relevance of the recommendations.

5. **Customizability**: The database should offer the flexibility to tailor dosing recommendations to individual patient needs, including factors such as age, weight, and other comorbidities. This customization can help optimize treatment plans for each patient.

6. **Support and Training**: The database provider should offer robust support and training resources, such as user guides, training sessions, and responsive customer support, to ensure that healthcare providers can effectively utilize the database.

7. **Compliance with Standards**: The database should adhere to relevant regulatory standards and guidelines, ensuring that the recommendations are in line with best practices and legal requirements.

By evaluating these factors, healthcare providers can select a knowledge database that provides reliable, evidence-based drug dosing recommendations, ultimately improving the care and outcomes for patients with impaired kidney function.

Medical questions & health advice by licensed doctors
"What are reasons for my kidneys to be hurting?"
I'm a 33 year old female. Very suddenly yesterday evening, my left kidney started hurting. The pain started out as an annoying pain, but then it started intensifying over the next 30 minutes. I started to feel awful and extremely nauseous. Fearing that I was getting a kidney infection, I drank several glasses of water and cranberry juice. I then went to sleep and woke up today feeling fine, with no pain in my left kidney. Over the last month I extremely changed my diet, cut out all fattening and high caloric foods and I have lost 10 pounds. I used Alli for about 2 weeks and then discontinued using it. Ever since I changed my diet, I have not been drinking the usual amount of 5 glasses of water a day that I usually drink. Is it possible that I was getting a kidney infection, or could there be something else causing the pain?
Sudden pain is always of concern, especially if it worsens or persists or is accompanied by other concerning symptoms, like fever or nausea and vomiting. I recommend talking to your primary care doctor as soon as possible. One concerning possibility would be kidney stones. These manifest as severe pain in the flank which moves into the abdomen and down the leg, sometimes to the groin. Classic of kidney stone pain is that it is crampy in nature and comes and goes, with periods of severe pain alternating with episodes without pain. I am particularly concerned about this possibility, because kidney stones sometimes occur more frequently in people who are experiencing rapid weight loss or dieting. Another would be a kidney infection, also known as pyelonephritis. This usually begins as a urinary tract infection with the typical symptoms of burning with urination and then progresses. Kidney infections have severe pain in the abdomen or in the lower back just under the ribs. Often there is fever as well. It sounds like you should call your primary care doctor as soon as possible to help you figure out what is going on. If fever or severe pain returns, you should go instead to the emergency room.

instruction: How can one differentiate between the symptoms of a kidney infection and kidney stones, and what are the recommended steps for seeking medical attention for these conditions?
response:
Differentiating between a kidney infection and kidney stones involves recognizing the specific symptoms associated with each condition. Kidney stones typically cause severe, crampy pain in the flank (the area between the ribs and the hips) that may move into the abdomen and down the leg, sometimes reaching the groin. The pain from kidney stones often comes and goes, with periods of severe pain alternating with periods of relief. Other symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and blood in the urine. On the other hand, a kidney infection (pyelonephritis) usually starts with symptoms of a urinary tract infection, such as burning with urination, and then progresses to severe pain in the abdomen or lower back just under the ribs. Kidney infections are often accompanied by fever, chills, and sometimes nausea and vomiting.

If you suspect either condition, it is important to seek medical attention. For kidney stones, if the pain is severe or if you experience symptoms like fever or blood in the urine, you should call your primary care doctor or go to the emergency room. For a kidney infection, if you have a fever, chills, or severe pain, you should also contact your doctor immediately or go to the emergency room. Both conditions can be serious and require prompt medical evaluation and treatment.

instruction: How do different types of kidney stones form, and what dietary and lifestyle changes can be made to prevent their recurrence?
response: Kidney stones form when there is an imbalance in the levels of certain minerals and salts in the urine, leading to their crystallization and aggregation. The most common types of kidney stones are composed of calcium and oxalate, though they can also be made of uric acid, cystine, or struvite. Calcium oxalate stones form when there is excess calcium and oxalate in the urine, often due to dietary factors, dehydration, or certain medical conditions like hyperparathyroidism. Uric acid stones form in acidic urine, often in people with high protein diets or gout. Cystine stones are rare and result from a genetic disorder called cystinuria, while struvite stones are associated with urinary tract infections. To prevent the recurrence of kidney stones, it is important to stay well-hydrated, reduce sodium and animal protein intake, and limit foods high in oxalate such as spinach, nuts, and chocolate. Regular exercise and maintaining a healthy weight can also help. In some cases, medications may be prescribed to manage specific types of stones, such as allopurinol for uric acid stones or thiazide diuretics for calcium oxalate stones.

instruction: How does gout impact the risk of developing chronic kidney disease, and what measures can be taken to mitigate this risk?
response:
Gout has been identified as a potential risk factor for the development of chronic kidney disease (CKD), particularly CKD stage ≥3. The relationship between gout and CKD is multifaceted. Chronic hyperuricemia, a hallmark of gout, can lead to the formation of urate crystals in the kidneys, causing inflammation and progressive renal damage. This is supported by studies showing that patients with gout have a higher prevalence of psoriasis and an increased risk of total joint replacement, both of which can be associated with systemic inflammation. Moreover, the presence of gout is often accompanied by other comorbidities, such as hypertension and diabetes, which are also risk factors for CKD.

To mitigate the risk of CKD in patients with gout, a comprehensive approach is recommended. This includes:
1. **Urate-Lowering Therapy (ULT):** Medications like allopurinol are effective in reducing serum uric acid levels and have been shown to lower the risk of developing CKD. It is important to adjust the dose of allopurinol based on the patient's renal function to avoid toxicity.
2. **Lifestyle Modifications:** Patients should adopt a diet low in purines, maintain a healthy weight, and engage in regular physical activity. These changes can help reduce uric acid levels and improve overall health.
3. **Regular Monitoring:** Regular blood tests to monitor serum uric acid levels and kidney function are essential. Imaging techniques, such as ultrasound, can also be used to detect early signs of kidney damage.
4. **Patient Education:** Educating patients about the importance of adherence to treatment and lifestyle changes can improve outcomes. Nurse-led care, as shown in a British study, can significantly improve the proportion of gout patients who achieve target serum urate levels.
5. **Management of Comorbidities:** Addressing other health issues, such as hypertension and diabetes, is crucial in reducing the overall risk of CKD. Effective management of these conditions can help preserve kidney function.

Reasons to Support an Atlanta Non-Profit that Helps People with Kidney Disease
In your search for an Atlanta non-profit to support, you’ll find many worthy organizations that help a variety of people, from veterans to cancer patients. If you decide to contribute to charity, consider assisting one that helps people with kidney disease, like American Kidney Services. We’re an Atlanta non-profit that collects donations of used clothing and household items and forwards the funds they generate to organizations that provide direct financial support to people with kidney disease. The money we raise with Atlanta residents’ donated goods helps people through incredibly difficult times, and often, it even saves lives.
Chronic kidney disease is the gradual loss of kidney function. Failing kidneys can no longer properly filter toxins and waste from the blood stream, control the production of red blood cells, or do other vital tasks. For that reason, people with kidney disease need medications and frequent treatments, like dialysis, to live. Even with health insurance, the cost of these treatments can add up and become nearly impossible to afford.
That’s why your donations to Atlanta non-profit organizations that assist kidney disease patients are so important. Your contributions relieve some of the stress that people with kidney disease and their families face when they’re struggling to afford treatment in addition to necessities like rent and electricity. The financial aid Atlanta non-profit organizations like ours provides helps patients focus on receiving treatment, and, in short, it helps keep them alive.
To make a donation of used clothing or household goods to our Atlanta non-profit, simply call us or fill out the online form, and we’ll pick your items up for free from your home. We’ll remind you when our collection trucks will be in your neighborhood, and you’ll be able to leave your items out by your mailbox in a bag or box labeled “AKS.” You can also take your donations to a nearby Value Village or to any of our hundreds of drop boxes.
Contributing to charity is a wonderful way to help the world, the nation, and the communities of Atlanta. Non-profit organizations like American Kidney Services work hard every day to help people in need, but we can’t do it without your generous support.
For more information on American Kidney Services, an Atlanta non-profit, please contact us today.
instruction: What are the primary challenges faced by individuals with chronic kidney disease in managing their medical expenses, and how do non-profit organizations like American Kidney Services help alleviate these financial burdens?
response: Individuals with chronic kidney disease face significant challenges in managing their medical expenses. The disease necessitates frequent and often costly treatments such as dialysis and medications, which can be a substantial financial burden even with health insurance. Additionally, the high cost of these treatments can make it difficult for patients to afford other essential expenses like rent, utilities, and food. Non-profit organizations like American Kidney Services play a crucial role in alleviating these financial burdens. They collect donations of used clothing and household items, which are then sold to generate funds. These funds are directed towards providing direct financial assistance to individuals with kidney disease, helping them cover the costs of treatment and other essential needs. By doing so, these organizations not only help reduce the financial stress on patients and their families but also enable them to focus on their health and treatment, potentially improving their quality of life and overall outcomes.

instruction: What diagnostic steps should be taken to determine the underlying cause of blood in urine and potential obstruction, and why is it important to address the obstruction?
response: To diagnose the underlying cause of blood in the urine and potential obstruction, a series of diagnostic steps should be followed. Initially, a thorough medical history and physical examination are necessary to evaluate symptoms and risk factors. A urinalysis should be performed to check for red and white blood cells and to identify any signs of infection. An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis is a key diagnostic tool that can provide detailed images of the urinary tract, helping to detect obstructions like kidney stones or tumors. In some cases, more advanced imaging techniques such as a CT urogram or a cystoscopy may be required for a more comprehensive assessment. It is crucial to address any identified obstruction because it can lead to urine stagnation, which increases the risk of urinary tract infections and can cause significant complications, including kidney damage, chronic pain, and recurrent infections. Prompt management of the obstruction is essential to prevent these serious health issues.

instruction: What are the primary indications and contraindications for the use of potassium chloride, and how should it be administered to ensure optimal effectiveness and safety?
response:
The primary indications for potassium chloride include the treatment of hypokalemia, which can be induced by diuretics, and managing digitalis intoxication without AV block. The medication is available in extended-release tablets and effervescent powder forms. It should be taken with meals and fluids to enhance absorption and reduce gastrointestinal (GI) irritation. The extended-release tablets should be swallowed whole, but Klor-Con M tablets can be split in half or mixed with 4 ounces of water. Effervescent tablets or powder should be dissolved in a beverage before consumption. For prophylactic use, a daily dose of 20 mEq is recommended, while therapeutic doses range from 40 to 100 mEq daily, divided into multiple doses with a maximum of 20 mEq per dose. 

Contraindications for potassium chloride include hyperkalemia, chronic renal disease, acute dehydration, heat cramps, severe tissue destruction, adrenal insufficiency, familial periodic paralysis, acidosis (for potassium chloride products), and alkalosis (for potassium bicarbonate products). Additionally, the tablets are contraindicated in patients with esophageal compression due to an enlarged left atrium or decreased GI motility. 

To ensure optimal effectiveness and safety, it is crucial to monitor the patient's potassium levels, clinical status, acid-base balance, and ECG. Discontinue the medication if gastrointestinal bleeding, ulceration, or other disturbances occur. Special caution is advised in patients with renal or cardiac disease, the elderly, pregnant women (Category C), and nursing mothers. Potential drug interactions include hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride, and potassium-containing salt substitutes, as well as an increased risk of serious GI reactions with anticholinergics or other agents that decrease GI motility. Common side effects include hyperkalemia, GI discomfort and irritation, diarrhea, and rash (rare). Tablets can cause esophageal and GI ulceration, bleeding, obstruction, and perforation.

instruction: What are the primary reasons for ensuring adequate fluid administration in patients with kidney issues, and what are the potential consequences of insufficient fluid intake?
response: Ensuring adequate fluid administration in patients with kidney issues is vital to support kidney function and prevent complications. The primary reasons for this include maintaining adequate blood flow to the kidneys, which is essential for their ability to filter waste products and excess fluids from the blood. Adequate fluid intake helps the kidneys produce sufficient urine, which is necessary for the elimination of metabolic waste and maintaining electrolyte balance. If fluid intake is insufficient, the kidneys may not receive enough blood, leading to reduced urine output and potential dehydration. Dehydration can worsen kidney function by decreasing the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and increasing the risk of acute kidney injury. Moreover, inadequate fluid intake can lead to the accumulation of toxins and electrolyte imbalances, which can cause systemic issues such as hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and uremia. Therefore, it is crucial to monitor and adjust fluid intake to support kidney health and prevent these complications.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:
April 16, 2021
Kidney patients and docs ask congress to expand research and innovation
Amidst COVID-19, Largest American Kidney Organizations Back Strategic Funding for NIH and KidneyX
Washington, D.C.: The American Association of Kidney Patients (AAKP), the largest kidney patient organization in America, partnered with the American Society of Nephrology (ASN), the world’s largest renal professional organization, to host their 9th Annual Kidney Health Advocacy Day on April 14th. The event centered on two specific Congressional kidney funding requests, $25 million for the KidneyX, a collaborative between ASN and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and an additional $285 million for the National Institutes of Health (NIH), each designed to accelerate groundbreaking advances in kidney disease research and innovation. Together, the organizations conducted dozens of joint, virtual meetings among key Congressional offices representing twenty-five states. The reach of the Kidney Health Advocacy Day event was further amplified as patients - including many undergoing dialysis treatments in real-time, families, living kidney donors, and renal doctors across the nation, engaged through AAKP’s Center for Patient Engagement and Advocacy via smart phones and iPads in a simultaneous contact campaign with Congress. AAKP is a national leader in efforts to expand the impact of patient insight information in all Congressional and federal agency discussions and decisions (read article).
AAKP President Richard Knight, a former hemodialysis patient and current 14-year transplant recipient stated, “We appreciate our ongoing collaboration with ASN and believe our shared views provide a unique doctor and patient perspective to Congress on how they can make a substantive impact on kidney disease and improve patient outcomes, especially among communities of color who are disproportionately impacted by both this disease and COVID-19.” Knight is a small business consultant and business strategy instructor at Bowie State University (HBCU) as well as a former Congressional staff member and liaison to the Congressional Black Caucus.
Congressional leaders were asked to accelerate innovations in kidney treatments by providing an investment in FY22 of $25 million to support the KidneyX prize competition aimed at supporting the development of artificial kidney technologies, including wearable and implantable artificial kidneys, and other novel innovations. KidneyX launched the Artificial Kidney Prize in 2020 as a long-term commitment to the development of an artificial kidney and the first round of prizes will be awarded in FY21. Parallel sign-on letters in support of the $25 million KidneyX request are circulating in the House and Senate, led by multiple leaders including Rep. Suzan DelBene (D-WA), Rep. Larry Bucshon (R-IN), Senator Ben Cardin (D-MD), and Senator Todd Young (R-IN). Learn more about KidneyX by watching a presentation hosted during an AAKP Global Summit on Kidney Innovations, held in partnership with the George Washington University School of Medicine & Health Sciences. (Watch OnDemand or click here to download slide presentation)
Additionally, Congressional leaders were asked to provide an additional $270-285 million in FY22 to support kidney research efforts at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), particularly those at the National Institute of Diabetes, Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK). AAKP formulated the NIH request to keep pace with medical research cost inflation, to make-up for lost NIH kidney research grant funding due to the impacts of COVID-19 on NIH operations, and to substantively increase investments in kidney health research to lead to more discoveries to slow and prevent kidney failure, determine long-term impacts of COVID-19 on kidneys, and address health disparities.
In 2019, AAKP declared 2020-2030 The Decade of the Kidney ™ (www.decadeofthekidney.org) and substantial increases in Federal, academic, and private sector investments in kidney disease research were identified as a top priority to combat the disease, spur innovation, expand patient consumer treatment choice, and to better serve communities most impacted, especially communities of color. A recent AAKP kidney patient and stakeholder survey, conducted under the AAKP Center for Patient Research and Education, indicated overwhelming support for additional and substantial long-term increases to the NIH budget for kidney research. In 2020, AAKP initiated a national patient consumer grassroots education campaign to lay the groundwork for greater investments in kidney research across all sectors. AAKP has increased its education campaign on the link between kidney research and health outcomes through its KidneyVoters™ initiative (https://bit.ly/KidneyVoters), the first and largest voter registration effort in the kidney stakeholder community.
AAKP Vice President and Chair of the AAKP Veterans Health Initiative, Edward V. Hickey, III, USMC, a chronic kidney patient, stated “AAKP appreciates the Congressional commitment to kidney disease and their demonstrated interest in working directly with kidney patient experts and professionals on a long-term, research-based framework for addressing kidney disease and treatment.” Hickey is a former Congressional staff member who was involved in the first comprehensive Congressional initiative on brain diseases. He has served in two presidential administrations, including roles as liaison to Veteran Service Organizations, such as the Vietnam Veterans of America, AMVETS, the Veterans of Foreign Wars, and the American Legion.
Current NIH/NIDDK funded research efforts include the groundbreaking Kidney Precision Medicine Project (KPMP), a research consortium led by an equal partnership of kidney research and patient experts. KPMP is designed to better understand and discover new means to treat chronic kidney disease (CKD) and acute kidney injury (AKI) through kidney tissue samples altruistically provided by patient research collaborators. Learn more about the KPMP from Dr. Jonathan Himmelfarb, Co-Director of the University of Washington Center for Dialysis Innovation (CDI) and Director of the Kidney Research Institute (KRI), from his presentation at the 2020 AAKP Global Summit on Kidney Innovation: Emerging Research with Global Implications: Identification & Diagnosis of Kidney Diseases – The Kidney Precision Medicine Project. NIH is also heavily involved in patient-centered research related to APOL1 genetic variants, a key risk factor for CKD and kidney failure among African, Caribbean, and Latin Americans, and a factor related to disparate kidney health outcomes. Learn more about APOL1 research in an AAKP webinar featuring Dr. Barry I. Freedman, Wake Forest School of Medicine and Principal Investigator, APOLLO Scientific Data and Research Center, along with fellow research and patient colleagues – Who is at risk: Understanding the connection between APOL 1 gene and kidney disease.
AAKP Chair of Policy and Global Affairs Paul T. Conway, a 24-year kidney transplant patient and former dialysis patient stated, “Kidney disease is a health, disability, and workforce issue that costs taxpayers and the economy $130 billion in annual Medicare spending, including $50 billion just to manage kidney failure and dialysis care. Less than one percent of this cost is invested in kidney health research, so The Decade of the Kidney™ is a time for all stakeholders, including elected leaders, to think more strategically about saving lives through increased research funding, expanded talent pipelines to draw in experts from more diverse disciplines, and new policies to encourage private investors and market forces to create new technologies and jobs that target disease prevention, detection, and treatment.” Conway has served in three presidential administrations and is a former Chief of Staff of both the U.S. Department of Labor and the U.S. Office of Personnel Management with a background in labor, workforce and health policy implementation and stakeholder relations.
More than 37 million Americans are living with kidney diseases, which for nearly 800,000 Americans progresses to kidney failure, a life-threatening condition for which there is no cure. This under-recognized epidemic disproportionately affects communities of color. For instance, Black Americans comprise 13 percent of the U.S. population but represent 33 percent of Americans receiving dialysis, the most common therapy for kidney failure. The COVID-19 pandemic is especially deadly for kidney patients. Americans with kidney diseases are the most at risk among Medicare beneficiaries for severe outcomes from COVID-19, including hospitalization and death, and COVID-19 damages the kidneys of as many as 50 percent of all hospitalized COVID-19 patients, even those without a prior history of kidney diseases.
About the American Association of Kidney Patients (AAKP): Since 1969, AAKP has been the largest kidney patient organization driving policy discussions on kidney patient consumer care choice and treatment innovation. By 1973, AAKP patients had collaborated with the U.S. Congress and White House to provide dialysis coverage for any person suffering kidney failure, a taxpayer-funded effort that has saved over one million lives. Over the past decade, AAKP patients have helped gain lifetime transplant drug coverage for kidney transplant recipients (2020); new patient-centered policies via the White House Executive Order on Advancing American Kidney Health (2019); new job protections for living organ donors from the U.S. Department of Labor (2018); and Congressional legislation allowing HIV positive organ transplants for HIV positive patients (2013). AAKP virtual platforms and social networks are internationally known for their impact. Follow AAKP on social media at @kidneypatient on Facebook and @kidneypatients on Twitter and visit at www.aakp.org.
Jennifer Rate Marketing and Communications Manager

instruction: What factors can influence the results of a creatinine clearance test, and how might these factors affect the interpretation of the test?
response: The results of a creatinine clearance test can be influenced by various factors, which can impact the interpretation of the test. One of the primary factors is dietary intake, particularly the consumption of protein. High-protein diets can increase creatinine production, leading to higher creatinine clearance values. Muscle mass is another important factor; individuals with more muscle mass generally produce more creatinine, which can affect the clearance rate. Hydration status can also play a role; dehydration can concentrate creatinine in the blood and urine, while overhydration can dilute it. Certain medications, such as diuretics, can increase urine output and affect the creatinine clearance calculation. Additionally, conditions that affect blood flow to the kidneys, such as congestive heart failure, can reduce the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and thus the creatinine clearance. It is crucial to consider these factors when interpreting the test results to avoid misdiagnosis or incorrect assessment of kidney function. For example, a high creatinine clearance in a well-hydrated individual with a high muscle mass might not necessarily indicate optimal kidney function, and a low creatinine clearance in a dehydrated individual might suggest worse kidney function than actually present. Therefore, a comprehensive patient history and clinical context are essential for accurate interpretation.

instruction: What are the main factors that contribute to the risk of developing chronic kidney disease, and how can these be managed or prevented?
response:
The primary factors that contribute to the risk of developing chronic kidney disease (CKD) include diabetes, hypertension, a family history of kidney disease, and advanced age. Diabetes is a significant risk factor because elevated blood sugar levels can damage the kidneys' filtering units, leading to impaired function. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is another major risk factor, as it can cause damage to the small blood vessels in the kidneys, reducing their ability to filter waste and excess fluids. Family history is also a critical factor, as genetic predispositions can increase the likelihood of developing CKD. Additionally, older age is associated with a higher risk of CKD, as the kidneys naturally lose some function over time.

To manage or prevent CKD, it is essential to maintain good control over blood sugar levels if you have diabetes. This involves a combination of dietary changes, regular physical activity, and medication. For those with hypertension, managing blood pressure through lifestyle modifications such as reducing salt intake, maintaining a healthy weight, and taking prescribed medications is crucial. Regular monitoring of kidney function through check-ups with a healthcare provider can help detect any issues early. Other preventive measures include following a balanced diet, staying well-hydrated, and avoiding excessive alcohol and tobacco use. These steps can significantly reduce the risk of developing CKD and help preserve kidney health.

instruction: What are the potential kidney side effects of Mobic, and how can patients mitigate these risks?
response: Mobic, or meloxicam, is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that can have adverse effects on the kidneys. Potential kidney side effects of Mobic include acute kidney injury, which can occur in patients who are dehydrated or have pre-existing kidney conditions. NSAIDs reduce the production of prostaglandins, which are important for maintaining proper kidney function. This reduction can lead to decreased blood flow to the kidneys, potentially causing damage or failure. To minimize these risks, patients should ensure they stay well-hydrated, avoid exceeding the recommended dosage, and discuss any pre-existing kidney issues with their healthcare provider. Additionally, regular kidney function tests can help in early detection and management of any kidney-related complications.

- Kidney disease can affect children in various ways, ranging from treatable disorders without long-term consequences to life-threatening conditions.
- Acute kidney disease develops suddenly, lasts a short time, and can be serious with long-lasting consequences, or may go away completely once the underlying cause has been treated.
- Chronic kidney disease (CKD) does not go away with treatment and tends to get worse over time.
Kidney disease in children can be caused by
- birth defects
- hereditary diseases
- nephrotic syndrome
- systemic diseases
- urine blockage or reflux
A health care provider diagnoses kidney disease in children by completing a physical exam, asking for a medical history, and reviewing signs and symptoms. To confirm diagnosis, the health care provider may order one or more of the following tests:
- urine tests
- blood test
- imaging studies
- kidney biopsy
Treatment for kidney disease in children depends on the cause of the illness.
- Children with a kidney disease that is causing high blood pressure may need to take medications to lower their blood pressure. Improving blood pressure can significantly slow the progression of kidney disease. As kidney function declines, children may need treatment for anemia and growth failure.
- Children with kidney disease that leads to kidney failure must receive treatment to replace the work the kidneys do. The two types of treatment are dialysis and transplantation.
- For children with CKD, learning about nutrition is vital because their diet can affect how well their kidneys work. Parents or guardians should always consult with their child’s health care team before making any dietary changes.
What are the Symptoms Associated with Pediatric Kidney Disease?
Kidney disease often goes undetected in the general population, but children and adolescents are at an even greater risk due to the nature of the causes of the diseases and the ambiguity of the symptoms.
Children might not be aware of some of the changes that are impacting their body and will not always let their parents know of potential issues.
Common symptoms for children are:
- Swelling (even mild) of the hands and feet and/or puffiness around the eyes caused by excess fluid build-up, to the point where the child’s ability to move around normally is compromised
- After initial swelling, socks or a belt can leave an indentation in the skin that will persist
- Lack of or decrease in appetite.
- In children with ESRD it is especially important to keep their appetite up because transplant eligibility is based partially on growth.
- Decreased or increased frequency of urination. Children who can normally use the toilet without assistance may suddenly begin to wet the bed at night
- Long-lasting changes in the color of the urine such as unusually dark or red, which can indicate blood, and changes in appearance of urine such as extra foam that can indicate protein
- Headaches resulting from high blood pressure
- Flu-like Symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, weakness, fatigue, loss of appetite
- Stunted or poor growth as compared to similar age group peers
- Difficulty concentrating and poor school performance
Another potential indicator of pediatric kidney disease is family history of kidney disease. Genetic related disease is much more common in children than in adults. If there is family history, it is a good idea to get a check-up.
Looking at the list of common symptoms it is easy to see how CKD can go undiagnosed. As a parent or caregiver, it is important to have conversations with your children to understand the severity and duration of the symptoms and follow up with pediatric nephrologist.
instruction: What are some common symptoms that parents should be aware of in children that might indicate the presence of pediatric kidney disease, and how can these symptoms be distinguished from other common childhood illnesses?
response: Pediatric kidney disease can present with a variety of symptoms that parents should be vigilant about. These include swelling in the hands and feet, puffiness around the eyes, and persistent skin indentations from socks or belts. Other symptoms to watch for are changes in urination patterns, such as increased or decreased frequency, and changes in urine color or appearance, like dark or foamy urine. Children may also experience headaches, flu-like symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and fatigue, and stunted growth. To distinguish these symptoms from other common childhood illnesses, parents should note the duration and combination of symptoms. For instance, while a cold might cause temporary changes in appetite or urination, kidney disease symptoms tend to be persistent and involve multiple symptoms. Additionally, a family history of kidney disease can be a red flag. If these symptoms persist, it is crucial to consult a pediatric nephrologist for a proper evaluation.

Although there’s no cure, working with specialists can help maintain a patient’s quality of life
According to the National Kidney Foundation, 37 million American adults have chronic kidney disease (CKD) and millions of others are at increased risk. Though there’s currently no cure, treatment and some lifestyle changes may help slow CKD’s progression for some. Working with specialists to help manage CKD’s effects is important and can help with maintaining quality of life.
Dr. Jonathan B. Woods, MD, a nephrologist of Eastern Nephrology Associates who sees patients at 1302 Medical Center Drive in Wilmington, Jeana Koen, group facility administrator at DaVita Wilmington Dialysis Center, and Mary Tyndall, facility administrator at DaVita New Hanover Dialysis Center, have shared some information about CKD.
1) Kidneys are vital to the body’s health, and lab tests are necessary to make sure they are functioning well.
“Kidneys do a lot,” said Woods. “The main thing they do is remove waste products from the body and put them out into the urine and creates the urine that eliminates a lot of toxins from the body. They are also important in controlling electrolytes in the body and acid levels.”
Woods said kidneys also play a role in blood pressure, preventing anemia, and bone health.
“Kidney disease means abnormal kidney function, and that’s detected by a simple lab test that’s called serum creatinine,” Woods said. “Creatinine is a lab that tells you how your kidneys are functioning.”
Chronic kidney disease is a gradual loss of kidney function over time. “Chronic just means it’s been present for months to years,” Woods said.
2) Most with Chronic Kidney Disease Have No Symptoms to Alert Them There’s a Problem.
When kidneys aren’t working well, waste products and fluid can build up in one’s body and other complications can occur. If the decrease in kidney function worsens over time, one’s kidneys can eventually stop working, which can be life-threatening. A big issue with CKD, however, is many don’t know they have it until it’s in an advance stage.
“I don’t want anyone to have symptoms or be sick, but at the same time 9 out of 10 people who have mild chronic kidney disease don’t know it,” he said. “And actually 1 out of 2 people with advance chronic kidney disease don’t know about it because there are no symptoms that go with it, and it’s only detected by blood test.” Woods said some with less than 10 percent kidney function indicate no symptoms. This can pose a big problem as some may believe they are fine and may not realize their need for potentially life-saving treatment, such as dialysis.
Routine lab tests for kidney damage and kidney function are important. Koen and Tyndall said early detection can help slow down or even stop progression of CKD into chronic kidney failure where one needs a kidney transplant or dialysis to live.
3) People with high blood pressure and diabetes are at a higher risk for chronic kidney disease
Diabetes and high blood pressure are two main causes of CKD. According to Koen and Tyndall, “1 in 3 people with diabetes and 1 in 5 people with hypertension also have kidney disease.”
“If you have high blood pressure and you have diabetes you really have to watch your kidney function more closely,” Woods said.
4) There are five treatment options and ways to possibly slow CKD’s progression if caught early
According to Koen and Tyndall, changing eating habits can be effective in slowing CKD’s progression in some cases. Some of their other recommendations include: maintaining a healthy blood pressure, maintain a healthy weight, adopt a kidney-friendly diet as prescribed by a renal dietitian, see doctor regularly, avoid smoking, reduce or avoid alcohol consumption, and manage blood glucose if you have diabetes.
Treatment options are: In-center hemodialysis, occurs in a dialysis center and uses a machine to filter toxins from the blood; Home hemodialysis, uses a machine to clean the blood but is administered at home; Peritoneal dialysis, a needle-free treatment done at home that uses the lining of the abdomen to filter waste from the blood; In-center nocturnal dialysis, where patients dialyze in a dialysis center overnight or after working hours while they sleep; and a kidney transplant where a patient receives a kidney from a living or deceased donor.
5) If it’s determined one needs dialysis, one can still have a productive life.
Woods said working with a nephrologist can be beneficial when it comes to preparing for dialysis or exploring the possibility of a kidney transplant. “Dialysis has changed a lot over time,” said Dr. Woods. “I understand how people are fearful of dialysis. But If you follow with us, we have time to talk about the different ways of doing dialysis … There’s people who still work full time. There’s people who still travel. I’m not going to say it’s a joy, but it’s improved a lot.”

instruction: How can early detection and management of chronic kidney disease (CKD) help in slowing its progression, and what are some lifestyle changes that can be beneficial for patients with CKD?
response: Early detection and management of chronic kidney disease (CKD) can significantly slow its progression and improve a patient's quality of life. The kidneys perform critical functions, including waste removal, electrolyte balance, and blood pressure regulation. Since CKD often presents no symptoms until advanced stages, regular lab tests, such as serum creatinine, are essential for early detection. Individuals with high blood pressure and diabetes are at higher risk and should monitor their kidney function closely. Lifestyle changes, such as adopting a kidney-friendly diet, maintaining a healthy weight, and managing blood glucose levels, can help slow the progression of CKD. Other beneficial changes include avoiding smoking, reducing alcohol consumption, and regular medical check-ups. Treatment options like in-center and home hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, and kidney transplants are available, and working with a nephrologist can help patients understand and manage these treatments effectively, ensuring a more productive and fulfilling life.

According to the Oxalosis & Hyperoxaluria Foundation (OHF), Primary Hyperoxaluria is a rare genetic inherited disorder that is present at birth and comes in different forms. Type I affects an estimated 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 1 million people.
In Type I, “the liver creates too little of the enzyme alanine: glyoxylate aminotransferase or AGT. The (enzyme) deficiency causes increased amounts of oxalate and glycolate to be formed in the body … which cannot be metabolized,” according to the foundation’s website.
Typical symptoms include kidney stones, which some people may develop as early as birth but most by their mid-20s. The kidneys can be irreparably damaged when excessive amounts of oxalates are present in the urine, and sometimes kidney failure is the first clue that someone has the disease, according to OHF.
“Oxalosis occurs after the kidneys fail and the excess oxalate builds up in the blood and then deposits oxalate salts in the eyes, blood vessels, bones, muscles, heart and other major organs, according to OHF.
instruction: What are the primary symptoms and health complications associated with Primary Hyperoxaluria Type I, and how does the disease typically progress over time?
response: Primary Hyperoxaluria Type I is a genetic disorder affecting the liver's production of the enzyme alanine: glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT). The lack of this enzyme results in the overproduction of oxalate and glycolate, which can build up to toxic levels in the body. The most common initial symptom is the development of kidney stones, which can begin from birth but are more commonly observed by the mid-20s. As the disease progresses, the excessive oxalate can cause irreversible damage to the kidneys, eventually leading to kidney failure. When the kidneys fail, oxalosis occurs, a condition where oxalate accumulates in the bloodstream and is deposited in various tissues and organs, such as the eyes, blood vessels, bones, muscles, and heart. This deposition can cause significant health complications, including organ dysfunction and systemic issues, making the management of the disease increasingly complex over time.

instruction: How does insufficient water intake affect kidney function, and what are the potential long-term consequences of this deficiency?
response: Insufficient water intake can have serious repercussions on kidney function and overall health. When the body is dehydrated, the blood becomes more concentrated, leading to reduced blood flow to the kidneys. This impairs the kidneys' ability to filter toxins and waste products from the blood, causing a buildup of substances like urea and creatinine. Over time, this can lead to kidney damage and degeneration. Chronic dehydration can also contribute to the formation of kidney stones and increase the risk of urinary tract infections. Additionally, the long-term consequences of insufficient water intake can include chronic kidney disease, which may progress to kidney failure if left unaddressed. Early symptoms of kidney disease are often absent, making it crucial to maintain adequate hydration to support kidney health.

Research we're watching
Image: © wildpixel/Thinkstock
Can a high-tech water bottle help prevent painful kidney stones? The National Institutes of Health is hoping to find out. As many as one in every 11 people in the United States today has experienced a painful kidney stone. Kidney stones, a condition also referred to as nephrolithiasis or urolithiasis, are hard deposits that form inside the kidneys. They can be as small as a grain of sand or the size of a marble or larger. Symptoms of a stone include excruciating pain, interrupted urine flow, or bleeding inside the urinary tract. In short, kidney stones are definitely something you want to avoid. One way to keep stones from developing is to drink lots of water. The problem is, people who have had a stone often don't drink enough water to prevent new ones from forming, even when they're told how important it is to stay hydrated.
This trial, which will enroll 1,642 people, is trying to change that by using a "smart" water bottle that not only encourages people to drink a target amount of water each day, but also tracks their consumption using an app. People in the test group who reach their daily fluid intake targets will get financial incentives. Health coaches will provide added support to help participants achieve their goals. The findings could shed new light on how to get people to change their behavior to prevent this common and painful condition. For more information on the trial or to see if you qualify, visit www.health.harvard.edu/push.

instruction: What behavioral and motivational strategies, beyond the use of technology, could be effective in encouraging individuals to maintain adequate hydration to prevent kidney stones?
response: Behavioral and motivational strategies beyond the use of technology to encourage adequate hydration for preventing kidney stones can be multifaceted. One effective approach is to **set specific and achievable goals**. Individuals can start by setting a daily water intake goal, such as drinking 2 liters of water per day, and gradually increasing it as they become more comfortable. **Creating a routine** can also help, such as drinking a glass of water with each meal or at specific times throughout the day. **Social support** is another powerful tool. Individuals can involve family, friends, or colleagues to remind them to drink water and to share their progress, which can provide motivation and accountability. **Positive reinforcement** can be used by rewarding oneself for meeting hydration goals, such as treating oneself to a favorite activity or snack. **Educational programs** that explain the importance of hydration and the risks of kidney stones can also be beneficial, as knowledge often leads to better compliance. Finally, **environmental cues** can be set up, such as placing a water bottle on the desk or setting reminders on a phone, to serve as constant prompts to drink water.

instruction: What are the key responsibilities of a Dialysis Technician in the context of patient care and equipment maintenance?
response: In the role of a Dialysis Technician, the primary responsibilities encompass both direct patient care and the maintenance of dialysis equipment. Key duties include: 1) Setting up and sterilizing dialysis machines, ensuring they are calibrated and functioning properly for each patient. 2) Administering dialysis treatments according to prescribed protocols, including inserting needles and starting the dialysis process. 3) Continuously monitoring patients during treatment to observe for any signs of distress or complications, and taking appropriate actions to address issues. 4) Recording patient data, such as treatment parameters, vital signs, and any changes in the patient’s condition. 5) Assisting patients with personal care and mobility as needed, and providing emotional support. 6) Ensuring the dialysis unit is clean and adheres to infection control standards. 7) Working collaboratively with nephrologists, nurses, and other healthcare providers to optimize patient outcomes and manage the overall care of patients with kidney failure.

instruction: What are the potential long-term effects of dialysis on kidney function, and how does it compare to alternative treatments like Toxin-Removing Therapy in managing kidney failure?
response: The long-term effects of dialysis on kidney function are significant and often detrimental. Dialysis is essential for managing kidney failure by removing waste and excess fluids from the blood, but it does not restore kidney function. Over time, dialysis can cause further damage to the kidneys, leading to a complete loss of kidney function and the need for a kidney transplant. In comparison, Toxin-Removing Therapy, an alternative treatment developed in China, takes a more comprehensive approach. This therapy involves a series of Chinese medicine-based treatments, including Medicated Bath, Hot Compress Therapy, and others, designed to clean the blood of toxins and improve the kidney environment. These treatments aim to enhance the self-healing ability of the kidneys and gradually recover renal function. Unlike dialysis, which is primarily symptomatic, Toxin-Removing Therapy seeks to address the underlying causes of kidney failure, potentially offering a more sustainable and effective long-term solution for patients.

instruction: What are the key considerations and precautions one should take before starting a potassium supplement regimen, and why are these precautions important for maintaining health and safety?
response: Before starting a potassium supplement regimen, several key considerations and precautions are essential to ensure safety and health. First, it is crucial to consult a healthcare provider, especially if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, taking prescription medications, or under medical supervision. Second, do not exceed the recommended dose, which is typically 2 tablets per day providing 1000mg of Potassium Chloride (524mg elemental potassium). Third, take the supplement with water and preferably with food to enhance absorption and reduce the risk of gastrointestinal issues. Fourth, monitor your body for any adverse reactions and discontinue use if you experience symptoms such as nausea, weakness, or irregular heartbeat. Finally, ensure that the supplement is stored properly and out of reach of children. These precautions are vital because potassium is an essential electrolyte that supports muscle function, electrolyte balance, and blood pressure, and maintaining the right balance is crucial for overall health.

Obesity is an independent risk factor for the development and progression of chronic kidney disease and one of the emerging reasons for end-stage renal disease owing to its dramatic increase worldwide. Among the potential underlying pathophysiologic mechanisms, activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone-system (RAAS) plays a central role. Increased angiotensin II (AngII) levels also are central in hypertension, dyslipidemia, and insulin resistance, which, taken together with obesity, represent the metabolic syndrome. Increased AngII levels contribute to hyperfiltration, glomerulomegaly, and subsequent focal glomerulosclerosis by altering renal hemodynamics via afferent arteriolar dilation, together with efferent renal arteriolar vasoconstriction as well as by its endocrine and paracrine properties linking the intrarenal and the systemic RAAS, adipose tissue dysfunction, as well as insulin resistance and hypertension. The imbalance between increased AngII levels and the angiotensin converting enzyme 2/Ang (1-7)/Mas receptor axis additionally contributes to renal injury in obesity and its concomitant metabolic disturbances. As shown in several large trials and experimental studies, treatment of obesity by weight loss is associated with an improvement of kidney disease because it also is beneficial in dyslipidemia, hypertension, and diabetes. The most promising data have been seen by RAAS blockade, pointing to the central position of RAAS within obesity, kidney disease, and the metabolic syndrome.

instruction: What are the potential benefits of RAAS blockade in the treatment of obesity-related kidney disease, and how does it address the broader aspects of the metabolic syndrome?
response: The use of RAAS blockade in treating obesity-related kidney disease is supported by its multifaceted benefits, particularly in addressing the broader aspects of the metabolic syndrome. RAAS blockade, by reducing the levels of angiotensin II (AngII), helps in alleviating the renal hemodynamic changes that lead to hyperfiltration, glomerulomegaly, and focal glomerulosclerosis. These conditions are critical in the progression of chronic kidney disease. Furthermore, RAAS blockade has been shown to improve hypertension, a common comorbidity in obese individuals, by reducing the vasoconstrictive effects of AngII. It also helps in managing dyslipidemia and insulin resistance, which are other components of the metabolic syndrome. The imbalance between AngII and the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)/Ang (1-7)/Mas receptor axis, which is often seen in obesity, is another target of RAAS blockade. By restoring this balance, RAAS blockade can further protect the kidneys and improve overall metabolic health. These comprehensive effects make RAAS blockade a promising treatment strategy for obesity-related kidney disease and the metabolic syndrome.

instruction: What are some of the common symptoms and underlying causes of Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis (NSF), and how is it typically diagnosed and treated?
response: Nephrogenic Systemic Fibrosis (NSF) is a disease that primarily affects individuals with kidney disease, particularly those with advanced renal failure or on dialysis. The condition is characterized by the thickening and hardening of the skin, which can lead to severe mobility issues. Common symptoms include hardened skin, unexplained skin lesions, and dark patches, often affecting the extremities and trunk. Patients may also experience itching, although this symptom tends to subside over time. The underlying cause of NSF is primarily linked to exposure to gadolinium-based contrast agents used in MRI scans. These agents can accumulate in the body when kidney function is compromised, leading to fibrotic changes in the skin and sometimes internal organs. Diagnosis of NSF typically involves a thorough medical history, physical examination, and may include skin biopsies to confirm the presence of characteristic fibrotic changes. Treatment options are limited and focus on managing symptoms and preventing further progression. This can include discontinuing the use of gadolinium-based contrast agents, optimizing kidney function, and using medications to reduce inflammation and fibrosis. Physical therapy and supportive care are also crucial to maintain mobility and improve quality of life.

ATLANTA—Phosphate binder use by chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients does not lower their risk of death, according to a study presented at the American Society of Nephrology’s Kidney Week 2013 meeting.
Sankar D. Navaneethan, MD, and colleagues at Cleveland Clinic studied 939 CKD patients on phosphate binders (238 on non-calcium-based binders and 701 on calcium-based binders) who were propensity matched to those not on phosphate binders.
Phosphate binder use was not significantly associated with mortality among patients who took the drugs for at least six months. Patients who took a binder for one year had a non-significant 15% reduced mortality risk. Results showed no difference in death risk between calcium-based and non-calcium-based binders.
Additionally, the study found that each 5 kg/m2 increment in body mass index, 1 mg/dL increment in serum phosphorus, and 1 mg/dL increment in serum calcium was associated with a 12%, 35%, and 35% increased likelihood of being prescribed a non-calcium-based binder.
instruction: What factors are associated with an increased likelihood of being prescribed a non-calcium-based phosphate binder in CKD patients?
response: The study conducted by Dr. Sankar D. Navaneethan and colleagues at Cleveland Clinic identified specific factors that are associated with an increased likelihood of CKD patients being prescribed non-calcium-based phosphate binders. These factors include higher body mass index (BMI), serum phosphorus levels, and serum calcium levels. For each 5 kg/m² increase in BMI, the likelihood of being prescribed a non-calcium-based binder increases by 12%. Similarly, a 1 mg/dL increase in serum phosphorus and serum calcium levels is associated with a 35% increased likelihood of being prescribed a non-calcium-based binder. These findings indicate that patients with higher levels of these parameters may be more likely to receive non-calcium-based binders, possibly due to clinical considerations related to their overall health status and the potential benefits of these binders in managing phosphorus levels.

A dietitian, for example, plays a crucial role by tailoring nutritional plans that support kidney health. Social workers are essential in addressing the psychosocial aspects of kidney disease. They can provide counseling, assist with financial planning, and help patients access necessary resources, such as transportation to medical appointments and social services. Pharmacists, on the other hand, ensure that patients are adhering to their medication regimens and are aware of the potential risks and benefits of their medications. They can also coordinate with other healthcare providers to optimize medication therapy. By combining the expertise of these professionals, patients receive comprehensive care that not only manages their medical condition but also enhances their overall well-being and quality of life. This collaborative approach fosters a supportive environment that empowers patients to better manage their health and live more fulfilling lives.

instruction: How does the blood flow through the kidneys, and what is the significance of the glomerulus in the filtration process?
response: The blood flow through the kidneys follows a specific pathway that ensures efficient filtration and reabsorption. Blood enters the kidneys via the renal arteries, which branch from the abdominal aorta. The renal artery then divides into smaller segmental, lobar, and interlobar arteries, eventually forming arcuate arteries and interlobular arteries. These arteries lead to the afferent arterioles, which supply blood to the glomerulus, a network of capillaries. The glomerulus is crucial in the filtration process because it acts as a sieve, filtering out waste products and excess substances from the blood. The filtered blood then exits the glomerulus through the efferent arteriole and passes into the peritubular capillaries, where further reabsorption and secretion occur. Finally, the blood leaves the kidney through a series of veins, including the interlobular, arcuate, interlobar, lobar, segmental, and renal veins, ultimately emptying into the inferior vena cava.

Based on these diagnostics, a nephrologist will develop a comprehensive treatment plan that may include dietary and lifestyle modifications, medication, and dialysis for severe cases. For patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) or end-stage renal disease (ESRD), nephrologists ensure that dialysis treatments, such as peritoneal dialysis, are properly managed.
